# Agent operations guide

A cold-start checklist for a coding agent that must build this repository, or
install and operate Phantom. Every command here exists in the current source
(`phm --help`, `phm help <topic>`, `phm <command> --help`); where a capability
is gated or unverified, this guide says so. The binary you run is the authority:
an older install may lack commands described here.

`phm` and `ashlr` are the same binary (`package.json` `bin`). Help text uses
either name.

## 1. Working on this repository

`ashlr router rank --tier frontier --routes routes.json --slots codex-cmp=2 --json`
returns `{schema: "fleet.lane-rank.v1", tier, lanes}` ordered by nearest budget reset.
`routes.json` maps pool names to existing `routeBackend` decisions, e.g.
`{"codex-cmp":{"backend":"codex","tier":"frontier","reason":"prior route"}}`.
Supply currently free slots; missing routes, slots or usable budgets exclude a lane.
This reads the pool-budget ledger without writes or reservations. Decisions remain
advisory: the dispatcher must recheck policy, account admission and capacity.
The command consumes route evidence because invoking the legacy router can publish usage.

| Need | Command |
| --- | --- |
| Node version | `>=22.15.0` (`package.json` `engines`) |
| Install dependencies in a trusted local worktree | `npm run install:worktree` (pnpm 10.28.2; shared same-volume store; see [setup](../CONTRIBUTING.md#shared-installs-for-trusted-local-worktrees)) |
| Install dependencies in CI or for release packaging | `npm ci` |
| Build `dist/` (CLI, assets, web console, build identity) | `npm run build` |
| Run the CLI from source, no build | `npm run dev -- <command>` or `npx tsx src/cli/index.ts <command>` |
| Run the built CLI | `node bin/ashlr <command>` (shim that imports `dist/cli/index.js`) |
| Install the source build on `PATH` | `./install.sh` (builds, symlinks `bin/ashlr` into `~/.local/bin`) |
| Type check (backend + web) | `npm run typecheck` |
| Fast type check via the native compiler (same projects as `typecheck`) | `npm run typecheck:fast` |
| Lint (ESLint + real-I/O lane + Phantom console sync-I/O guards) | `npm run lint` |
| Backend tests | `npm test` (all), `npx vitest run test/<file>.test.ts` (focused) |
| Fast unit lane with per-file timing | `npm run test:fast` (report: `.ashlr-gate/test-fast-durations.json`) |
| Backend tests with isolated homes and a runtime cap | `npm run test:ci -- <files>` |
| Web console tests | `npm run test:web` |
| Safety invariant suites | `npm run test:invariants` |
| Documentation links and anchors (offline) | `npm run check:docs` |
| Duplicate test names across `test/` (describe path + title) | `node scripts/check-test-names.mjs` |
| Fast local gate: build, static checks, related tests, smoke set | `npm run gate` (`-- --base <ref>`, `-- --json`) |
| Full gate: complete backend and web suites | `npm run gate:full` |
| Release-readiness subset | `npm run check:release` |

`npm run gate` writes to `.ashlr-gate/` and `dist/`. It selects tests through
the import graph, so a test that reads a changed file as text is not selected;
name it explicitly or use `gate:full`. Neither replaces hosted CI or the
[release guide](RELEASING.md).

**Hosted CI.** A pull request or merge-queue commit runs only the fast gate:
the secret-shape scan, lane classification, and — unless the change is
docs-only — the quick typecheck, all on Ubuntu. `Merge Gate` is the one
required check and fails unless exactly that selection ran and every full lane
was skipped. No pull request or merge-queue commit may occupy a macOS or
Windows runner: the `ci` Ubuntu/Windows matrix, the Mac exhaustive lanes
(`Mac exhaustive (N/4)`, `Mac exhaustive (isolated)`), the shared-macOS and
native-broker lanes, and the Windows service authority run only in the daily
scheduled run on master, on manual dispatch (optionally sliced by `mac_shard`),
or on the reusable release call — where the caller's push event still defers
the macOS and Windows-service legs to the daily run while the `ci` matrix,
including its Windows portability legs, stays the release's native gate
(`.github/workflows/ci.yml`).

**Fast test timing.** `npm run test:fast` runs the unit project with the existing isolated-home watchdog. It records Vitest file elapsed times in milliseconds and flags files over 20 seconds with a suggested split. The budget is advisory; test failures still fail the command. Pass Vitest filters after `--` for a focused run. Each run replaces the local report, so focused runs only contain selected files.

**Tests.** Backend suites live in `test/` and are named after the milestone or
release that introduced them: `test/m<N>.<topic>.test.ts`, invariant suites
`test/h<N>.*.test.ts`, and `test/<topic>-<release>.test.ts`. Web tests sit next
to their components as `src/web-ui/**/*.test.{ts,tsx}`. Tests that do real I/O
must be listed in `test/config/realio-lane-membership.mjs` (`npm run lint`
checks this). Every test runs with an isolated `HOME` (`test/setup/home.ts`),
and writes under the real `~/.ashlr` fail the test.

**Layout.** `src/cli/` holds thin argv dispatchers, one file per command group;
`src/core/` holds the logic; `src/web-ui/` the React console; `desktop/` the
desktop app; `scripts/` build, gate and check tooling. See
[CONTRIBUTING.md](../CONTRIBUTING.md#project-layout) and
[ARCHITECTURE.md](ARCHITECTURE.md).

**Docs.** The map is [docs/README.md](README.md). `scripts/check-documentation.mjs`
checks the operator entrypoints in its `OPERATOR_DOCUMENTATION` list. Each of
those (except `README.md`) must also appear in `package.json` `files`
(`test/documentation-navigation.test.ts`). A packaged guide must link to an
unpackaged one through a `https://github.com/ashlrai/phantom/blob/master/...`
source link, which the checker resolves locally.

### Merged-PR router queue

`phm fleet queue` supplies the RQ bridge with follow-up work. It does not run
jobs or grant review/merge authority. The bridge must deliver **every** verified
GitHub merge (including manual and external merges), retry failed ingestion,
and replay missed events after downtime. The internal `merge:shipped` event
also enqueues authenticated inbox merges when configured; that event is best
effort and is not a complete GitHub event feed.

The operator provisions `~/.ashlr/router-queue/` (0700) and `config.json`
(0600) in the supervisor's HOME, outside every job HOME. Configuration has
exactly the keys `v: 1` and `repositories`, an array of exactly seven unique,
lowercase `ashlrai/<repo>` names from the owner's approved scope. There is no
inferred/default repository list, and forks are not queue targets. Keep this
configuration and the queue's metadata sidecars inaccessible to jobs. Do not
give workers this HOME or the supervisor's environment/credentials.

After independently verifying a PR is merged, the bridge pipes a JSON object
to `phm fleet queue merged --json` on stdin, with exactly these fields:

```json
{
  "v": 1,
  "state": "MERGED",
  "prUrl": "https://github.com/ashlrai/phantom/pull/42",
  "headSha": "aaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaa",
  "mergeSha": "bbbbbbbbbbbbbbbbbbbbbbbbbbbbbbbbbbbbbbbb",
  "mergedAt": "2026-01-01T00:00:00.000Z"
}
```

This is an example envelope, not evidence that this PR merged. The stdin
adapter validates shape and scope; it cannot authenticate a GitHub event by
itself. Only the trusted bridge should call it with verified metadata.
An accepted PR creates one deterministic follow-up asking for the next bounded,
evidence-supported improvement. Replay is idempotent, even after completion;
conflicting SHA/time metadata for the same PR is refused.

### Outcome learning

`phm fleet outcomes --events <log> --json` reads a dispatch event log and
prints, for each resource, model, job type, and repo, the merge rate, time to
merge, usage, and breakage rate. It also lists improvement jobs for recurring
failures. `phm fleet outcomes route` adds the next assignment and a
plain-language reason. The same types are exported from
`src/core/routing/outcome-learning.ts` for the desktop app. There is no
routing setting to tune: the log is the memory. Critical jobs are never held
for an exhausted resource, and allowance that resets soon is still spent when
that resource can finish the job.

### Selector

`phm select --json` ranks candidates in `~/.ashlr-runs/selector/candidates.jsonl`
by value x leverage / (time + usage), using the outcome log for what a candidate
leaves out. It prints the top five as `READY` lines, appends them with their
predicted value to `~/.ashlr-runs/selector/picks.jsonl`, and never funds an id
twice. `--dry-run` writes nothing. `phm select schedule --write` installs the
hourly launchd agent on the Mac. See
[the selector contract](contracts/CONTRACT-SELECTOR.md).

`phm fleet queue ask --json` reads one `ask.v1` record on stdin —
`{schema:"ask.v1",id,tier,pool,priority,repos,task}` — and prints its fanout
as a `queue.v1` document: N READY jobs, one repo each, N by tier (work 1, mid
2, frontier 3) over the first N listed repos. Every repo must be one of the
seven configured `ashlrai/<repo>` names; a malformed or out-of-scope ask fails
whole. The projection is deterministic, so replayed asks dedupe by job id at
the queue store, and it mutates nothing: no receipts, queue file or audit log
are written. `task` stays untrusted prompt data on each emitted job.

`phm fleet queue read --json` returns `{v:1,jobs:[{jobId,repo,prompt}]}`.
The bridge passes `prompt` only as untrusted model input, never as shell,
command arguments, configuration, an execution path, or authority. It must
not copy prompts into `fleet.json` or logs. This command is a snapshot, not a
worker lease: the existing supervisor must serialize assignment/claim work
before dispatch. When work finishes, the trusted supervisor acknowledges it
with `phm fleet queue complete <job-id> --json`.

`router-queue.md` holds JSON data in Markdown job sections. Operators can edit
task strings; identities, repositories and SHAs must still match durable
receipts in `state.json`. Every successful read records an ordered, hash-only
replacement hunk in `read-diffs.jsonl` before any task is returned, including
unchanged reads and malformed edits within the size bound. No task/model/diff
text or environment is written to metadata or audit logs. Invalid or unreadable
state fails closed. Queue reads and mutations share the existing process lock;
atomic writes and write-ahead receipts recover an interrupted queue write on
the next read/replay. Deleted outstanding entries are restored; use `complete`
to acknowledge work. Completed receipts are retained for deduplication.

The queue is bounded to 2 MiB and 10,000 lifetime PR receipts; capacity errors
require operator attention, not silent eviction. Missing audit/deduplication
state, unsupported pre-existing Markdown, and scope changes affecting retained
receipts require operator reconciliation. Do not reset sidecars to bypass a
refusal. Review isolation, sensitive-path checks, PAUSE, rate limits, CI/revert
halts and credentials remain the supervisor's independent gates.

### Publish preflight for a proposed PR

Run `node scripts/check-publish.mjs --base origin/master --body /path/to/pr-body.txt --held-path path/to/held` before handing a branch to a publish workflow. Repeat `--held-path` for each held file or directory, or explicitly use `--no-held-paths` when none apply. Supply the actual target base and exact proposed PR body; the script does not discover either or fetch remote state. It checks committed changes since the merge base plus staged, unstaged, and untracked files, reporting `.github` paths, recognized lockfiles under held paths, and em dashes in the body. It does not create a PR or certify CI, permissions, or mergeability. Rerun it after changes to the branch, held paths, or body.

## 2. Installing and running Phantom

```sh
npm install -g @ashlr/phantom
phm --version
phm doctor            # health check; exits 1 when any check fails
phm verse             # console at http://127.0.0.1:7777/verse/
```

- `phm verse [--port N] [--no-open] [--json]` binds `127.0.0.1` only (default
  port 7777) and prints a read token and a mutation token. Keep both private.
  `--json` prints them too, so do not log that output.
- `phm doctor [--json] [--fix]` checks Node, git, config, Phantom Secrets, Locus,
  local providers and MCP registration, and prints a `fix:` line for each problem.
  A missing Locus or local model is a warning, not a failure. The MCP fix lines
  name `phm mcp install claude` and `phm mcp ecosystem --write`.
- `phm init [--wire] [--yes] [--json]` is idempotent onboarding. It writes the
  config, creates `~/.ashlr/genome`, symlinks `ashlr` into `~/.local/bin`, and
  with `--wire` registers the MCP gateway in detected editors. `phm init --help`
  prints help and writes nothing. With `--json`, the `ready` field matches the
  exit code. A new `config.json` carries only generic defaults (one tidy keeper,
  `github`); an existing one keeps its saved keepers and categories. Its roots
  are `~/Desktop/github` and `~/Desktop` when those exist, otherwise whichever
  of `~/code`, `~/src`, `~/projects`, `~/dev`, `~/Developer` and `~/repos`
  exist, and there are no tidy rules without a `~/Desktop`.
- `phm status [--json]` is the attention board (dirty, off-sync and stale
  repos). `--json` prints one object (`schemaVersion: 1`) with no ANSI.
  In a GitHub repository, status also lists advisory per-PR merge ETA ranges
  (JSON: `github.mergeEtas`). It reads up to ten oldest open PRs and their
  actual GitHub merge-queue positions; PRs outside the queue show `unknown`.
  Supply historical **required** check durations in
  `~/.ashlr/merge-check-history.json`, a JSON array such as
  `[{"repo":"ashlrai/phantom","name":"Merge Gate","durationMs":300000},
  {"repo":"ashlrai/phantom","name":"Merge Gate","durationMs":480000}]`.
  Use completed-check timestamps from your CI history exporter; status never
  writes history or changes a PR. Each currently required check needs at least
  two samples from that repository. The range uses the slowest parallel
  check's observed 10th–90th percentile durations, multiplied by queue position
  under a conservative serial-slot assumption. Reviews, reruns and queue
  batching can change actual timing; these ranges are estimates, not deadlines.
  Missing/malformed history, unavailable required checks, or an unknown queue
  position yields `unknown`. History is bounded to 1 MiB / 10,000 rows.
  Each row also attributes the PR's merge-queue wait (`waitingOn`): `position`
  when entries ahead must land first, `checks` when the head entry waits on
  the merge-group's required checks, or `conflict` when GitHub reports the PR
  conflicting; `waitingMs` is the observed queue time from `enqueuedAt`.
  A conflicting PR carries exactly one idempotent recut request,
  `RQ-RECUT-<repo>-<pr>-<head7>` — the same conflicting head re-read yields
  the same key, so consumers dedupe by it; a moved head makes a new request.
- `phm preflight [--json]` is a read-only readiness check (exit 0 ready, 1 blocked).
- `phm onboard [--yes] [--json]` walks through the first safe activation (preflight, enroll
  one repo, dry-run plan, inbox). `--json` never prompts and prints one object.
  `phm onboard --rollback <repo> [--kill]` undoes it.
- `phm setup` and `phm worker setup` are currently unavailable and refuse
  before changing anything. `phm setup` first lists what to run instead
  (`phm init`, `phm doctor`, `phm verse`, `phm run "<goal>"`). Off macOS,
  `phm authority setup` exits 1 and changes nothing; its `--dry-run` and
  `--help` still run.
- `phm update [--check] [--json]` self-updates (`--check` is read-only);
  `phm upgrade` runs the same command.
- `phm docs --agent [--json]` prints the command registry for agents. `phm docs
  --json` without `--agent` prints a JSON usage error and exits 2.

**Output for agents.** `--help` and `-h` print usage and exit 0 without acting,
including on commands that mutate (`fleet pause`, `worker setup`, `roadmap run`,
`gh pr create`, `swarm approve`). Set `NO_COLOR` to any non-empty value to drop
ANSI codes from human output. Commands that take `--json` print one JSON object
on stdout; `enroll add --json` and `authority stop --json` send their prose to
stderr.

For the desktop app and the first useful turn, follow the
[Quickstart](QUICKSTART.md) and [desktop/README.md](../desktop/README.md).

### Inspecting a router job session

`phm fleet session <job> --json [--follow] [--queue-dir <abs>]` reads
`jobs.jsonl` in `~/.ashlr-runs/queue` (or the supplied queue directory).
It combines matching transitions into a `fleet.session.v1` snapshot with
job id, lane, status, repository, tier, timestamp, PR URL, provider session
URLs and the last 64 KiB of log text. Missing links are null; a missing log
is empty. It reads `logPath`, `log_file`, `logFile` or `log` from the ledger,
falling back to `<queue-dir>/logs/<job>.log`. Recognized secret patterns in
log text are redacted. Ledger reads cover the latest 4 MiB.

`--follow` emits complete JSON Lines snapshots whenever the metadata or log
tail changes, polling every 500 ms, and exits on a terminal job status or
SIGINT/SIGTERM. Finished jobs emit once. Unknown jobs return a JSON error
and exit 1; malformed arguments exit 2. This command is read-only and
never contacts providers.

### MCP server

`phm mcp` runs the MCP aggregation gateway on stdio. Its subcommands are `list`,
`doctor` (exit 1 when a required server is down), `install <claude|ashlrcode>`
and `ecosystem [--write] [--json]`.

`phm wire [claude|codex|cursor|all] [--config <path>] [--json]` registers the
gateway as server `ashlr-hub` with command `ashlr` and args `["mcp"]`. It backs
up the target config first and is idempotent.

`phm mcp install claude` also writes `~/.claude.json`, under the same
`ashlr-hub` key (with an absolute path to this package's `bin/ashlr`), so
running both commands leaves one gateway entry. Each of them also removes a
legacy `ashlr` entry when it launches this product's own gateway, and refuses
to overwrite an `ashlr-hub` entry that is not the gateway. Releases up to
3.29.15 register `phm mcp install claude` as a second server, `ashlr`; with one
of those, use one registration command, or delete one of the two entries from
`mcpServers` if the agent sees every gateway tool twice. `phm mcp install
ashlrcode` still writes the `ashlr` key.

| Client | Default config | How `wire` writes it |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Claude Code | `~/.claude.json` | JSON merge into `mcpServers` |
| Codex | `~/.codex/config.toml` | runs `codex mcp add ashlr-hub -- ashlr mcp` |
| Cursor | `~/.cursor/mcp.json` | JSON merge into `mcpServers` |

Without a target, or with `all`, it wires only the editors it detects. An
editor counts as detected when its config exists (`~/.claude` or
`~/.claude.json`, `~/.codex`, `~/.cursor`) or its CLI (`claude`, `codex`,
`cursor`) is on `PATH`, so a fresh Claude Code install is found before its
first run. `phm init --wire` and `phm doctor --fix` use the same
detection. To test
without touching real configs, pass one explicit target with `--config`, for
example `phm wire claude --config /tmp/x/.claude.json` or
`phm wire codex --config /tmp/x/config.toml` (Codex still needs the `codex` CLI).
`phm wire --claude-md` prints a CLAUDE.md snippet and writes nothing.

`phm wire status [claude|codex|cursor|all] [--config <path>] [--json]` is read-only: for each client it reports the config path, whether the client is detected, whether the `ashlr-hub` entry is registered, whether it matches what `wire` writes, and whether a `<config>.bak` exists. It reports all three clients unless one is named, never writes or creates files, never runs a vendor CLI (Codex is read from `config.toml`), and never prints entry env values. Exit code 1 means a config could not be read or parsed.

`phm wire status gemini` (also included in the default all-client report) reads Gemini CLI's `mcpServers` object from `~/.gemini/settings.json` ([source](https://github.com/google-gemini/gemini-cli/blob/main/docs/tools/mcp-server.md)). Gemini is status-only for now: `phm wire gemini` refuses and changes nothing, and `phm wire` with no target never includes it. A write path will be dry-run by default with a backup.

The Codex check matches `[mcp_servers.ashlr-hub]` in `config.toml` with line-based regexes, not a TOML parser. An entry that uses multi-line `args` or an inline table is reported as `wired, entry differs` even if it is equivalent; re-run `phm wire codex` or inspect it with `codex mcp get ashlr-hub --json`.

### Daemon

`phm daemon status|doctor|pause|resume|stop|service-status`. In this build,
`daemon start --once` refuses before taking any action because the compiled
daemon trust roots are empty. `daemon start --once --dry-run` only plans, and
`daemon install` is withheld. `phm authority resident start|stop|status` manages
the resident daemon under an active grant. See
[RESIDENT-RUNTIME.md](RESIDENT-RUNTIME.md).

### Where state lives

Everything is under `~/.ashlr/`. Verified paths:

| Path | Contents |
| --- | --- |
| `config.json` | configuration (`phm config path`, `phm config effective --json`) |
| `KILL` | the global kill switch / Stop marker |
| `account-connections/connections.json` | native account roster that Phantom seats come from |
| `authority/ledger.jsonl` | hash-chained authority ledger |
| `manager/<ts>.json` | `phm manager` reports |
| `logs/` | supervised local-runtime stdout and stderr |
| `daemon.launchd.out.log`, `daemon.launchd.err.log` (macOS), `daemon.systemd.log` (Linux) | daemon service output |
| `fleet/mirrors/` | the fleet's own mirror clones (`phm mirror`) |

[RELIABILITY.md](RELIABILITY.md#where-state-lives) lists the rest
(`enrollment.json`, `daemon.json`, `inbox/`, `sandboxes/`, `audit/`).

## 3. Operating

| Group | Purpose (from `phm help`) |
| --- | --- |
| `phm sweep report [--repo <dir>]` | Weekly, local deletion review report; see [DELETION-SWEEP.md](https://github.com/ashlrai/phantom/blob/master/docs/DELETION-SWEEP.md) |
| `phm orient [--repo <r>] [--json]` | Read-only session-start context: memory hits, health, backlog, pending proposals |
| `phm enroll list\|add\|remove\|kill` | Repos open to autonomous work, plus the global kill switch (`enroll add <repo> --json` never prompts) |
| `phm backlog [refresh]` | Scored work queue across enrolled repos |
| `phm inbox [show\|approve\|submit\|reject] <id>` | Approval gate for proposals; `approve` applies to a local branch, `submit` hands off to a protected PR and never merges main |
| `phm goals add\|plan\|advance\|status\|pause\|resume` | Objectives decomposed into milestones; `advance` runs a sandboxed, proposal-only swarm on an enrolled repo |
| `phm goal "<objective>" --project <repo>` | One owner-invoked plan plus one proposal-only advance on an enrolled repo (`--plan-only` plans without advancing and needs no repo) |
| `phm run "<goal>"` / `phm swarm "<goal>"` | Local agent run / contracts-first multi-agent run (`run --engine <id>`; both accept `--allow-cloud`) |
| `phm fleet status\|watch\|lanes\|direction\|doctor\|scorecard\|oversight` | Read-only fleet snapshot, per-lane engineering console, direction report, engine readiness and quality metrics |
| `phm manager [--apply-rejects]` | Judges pending proposals; shadow mode by default, never merges |
| `phm leader show\|run\|tick\|say\|thread\|approve\|veto\|directives` | The Leader: memos, actions, directives and veto ([LEADER.md](LEADER.md)) |
| `phm improve propose [--open-pr --repo <dir>]` | Evidence-backed self-improvement proposals; `--open-pr` opens draft PRs from an isolated worktree and never merges or deploys |
| `phm cloud ...` / `phm devin ...` | Claude Code cloud and Devin lanes ([CLOUD.md](CLOUD.md), [DEVIN.md](DEVIN.md)) |
| `phm automations ...` | Turn triggers (labels, red CI, schedules, webhooks) into fleet tasks |
| `phm website status\|auto\|pause\|off` | Inspect or pause automatic phm.dev publication |
| `phm top [--once] [--json]` | Read-only per-account pool capacity and reset-pressure snapshot; always includes codex-personal. JSON schemaVersion is 1; missing telemetry stays unknown. Local subscription readings are engine-wide, with no account attribution. |
| `phm resources [--json]`, `phm usage` | Per-backend capacity and usage, read-only |
| `phm audit [N] [--json]` | Tail the append-only audit trail |

### Metrics levers

`phm metrics levers --json` returns a versioned report with the top three
opportunity proxies from the activity rollup and fleet digest. Use
`--window 7d` (default) or `--window 30d`; omit `--json` for a ranked list.
The command reads local metadata without model calls or writes.

Scores are opportunity indices from 0 to 100, not predicted gains:

| Lever | Score basis | Limitation |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Lane imbalance | (largest minus smallest active project session count) / attributed sessions | Projects are not execution lanes; needs two active projects. |
| Template merge rate | 1 minus window witnessed merges / window proposals, clamped to [0, 1] | Fleet flow is not a template cohort; the digest excludes pending from proposals, and merges can belong to older proposals. |
| Wait time | Live pending / (live pending + window merges + window declines) | Mixed live/window backlog share is not elapsed wait duration. |
| Empty jobs | Sessions in projects with zero window commits / attributed sessions | Research or uncommitted work can be useful; this does not prove empty jobs. |

Every reason names the proxy limitation. Missing samples and incomplete or
legacy proposal read quality yield `score: null` and `evidence: "unavailable"`.
Known scores sort first, descending, rounded to two decimals. Ties use the table
order, including unavailable entries, so the report always contains three rows.
Use the reasons to investigate before changing routing or templates.

### Stop and pause

| Control | Effect |
| --- | --- |
| `phm authority stop [--no-wait] [--json]` / `clear-stop` | Engages Stop (`~/.ashlr/KILL`): halts running agents and cancels armed merges. With `--json`, stdout carries only the JSON result. Clearing is written to the ledger first. |
| `phm authority revoke [--reason <text>]` | Stop, set autonomy off, and require a new signed grant to resume |
| `phm authority switch off\|propose\|autonomous` | Lowers autonomy at once; can raise it only as far as the grant allows |
| `phm fleet pause` / `phm fleet resume` | Engage or release the global kill switch (idempotent) |
| `phm enroll kill on\|off` | Same global kill switch |
| `phm daemon pause` / `resume` | Halt autonomous dispatch only |
| `phm daemon stop` | Orderly shutdown; also sets the global kill switch |
| `phm website pause` | Pause automatic site publication |

### Per-agent Auto-merge

Agents started from the Agents board in the Phantom app can Auto-fix CI and
Auto-merge their PR. Both are off for each agent until the operator turns them
on. Auto-merge also needs `ASHLR_VERSE_AUTOMERGE_CHECKS` set to the exact,
comma-separated names of the required code checks; an unset or malformed value
holds every automatic merge. The gates run in this order, and the first refusal
is shown on the agent (`src/core/verse/agents/checks.ts`):

1. Auto-merge is on for this agent.
2. Stop (`~/.ashlr/KILL`) and pause (daemon or comms) are both clear.
3. The PR is open, not a draft, mergeable, and green on the head the checks
   ran on.
4. Git's own diff from the merge base to that head is readable, not empty,
   does not weaken tests (deleted tests, removed `it(` or `expect(`, added
   `.skip` or `.only`), and touches no protected path: CI, manifests,
   lockfiles, CODEOWNERS, hooks and, in Phantom itself, its Tier-1 authority
   code.
5. In Phantom's own repository, the standing grant's self-land policy is
   `merge-non-authority`. The repository is recognised by package name
   (`@ashlr/phantom` or `@ashlr/hub`) or by an `ashlrai/phantom` or
   `ashlrai/ashlr-hub` origin.
6. GitHub's branch protection. The squash merge is pinned to the head commit
   and never uses `--admin` or `--auto`.

The merge runs under the machine-wide outward-mutation fence, and Stop and
pause are read again inside it, so Stop or unenroll cannot report quiescence
while a merge is in flight. A busy fence holds the merge for a later pass.

Seats are not allowed to merge on their own. A seat's terminal asks the
operator before `gh pr merge`, a `gh api` merge or auto-merge call, or
`gh pr review --approve` (rule `gh-merge`). When Auto-fix sends failing CI log
tails back to the seat, they arrive fenced and labelled as untrusted data.

### Authority

`phm authority status [--json]` shows grant state, the switch, Stop, the
rollout stage, the ledger chain and custody. Grants (`authority grant`,
`re-approve`) are signed with Touch ID through custody and verify only against
the standing-grant trust roots compiled into the release
(`src/core/authority/trust-roots.ts`). The separate daemon and conductor
activation trust roots are empty, so permit-based daemon and conductor
execution stays dormant. `phm authority setup --dry-run` previews
Phase 0. Agents do not sign grants. The policy reserved for the owner is in
[AGENTS.md](../AGENTS.md). Design and procedures:
[STANDING-AUTHORITY.md](STANDING-AUTHORITY.md) and [AUTHORITY.md](AUTHORITY.md).

### Offline router backlog planning

`phm backlog plan` (RQ-BACKLOG-GEN) proposes READY jobs from captured VISION
checklists, open issues and repository scanner findings. Invoke it after each
bridge queue refresh. Below three READY jobs per active slot it refills toward
five per slot; at or above three it emits nothing. Zero slots emits nothing.
Existing excess work is preserved. If sources run out, it emits the available
jobs and reports the remaining gap rather than inventing work.

```sh
phm backlog plan --config rq-config.json --input rq-sources.json \
  --queue router-queue.md --previous-queue previous-queue.md
```

The command is offline and read-only: no model, GitHub, subprocess, credential
access, queue writes or dispatch. The bridge supplies fresh source snapshots
and the active slot count, invokes the planner repeatedly, and applies output
under its own queue lock only if the current queue SHA-256 matches the `sha`
in the stderr `rq-plan` record. If the queue changed, replan. READY here means
available work data; it grants no execution, review or merge authority. The
supervisor still owns isolated review, exact-head checks, denylist/sensitive-path
checks, credential isolation, merge caps, PAUSE and post-merge stop controls.

Configuration is separate from untrusted queue/source data. Its allowlist must
contain exactly the bridge's seven approved `ashlrai/<repo>` identities. The
following names are illustrative; replace all seven with the approved list.
The command cannot discover or expand that authority:

```json
{
  "v": 1,
  "activeSlots": 2,
  "allowedRepos": [
    "ashlrai/repo-0", "ashlrai/repo-1", "ashlrai/repo-2", "ashlrai/repo-3",
    "ashlrai/repo-4", "ashlrai/repo-5", "ashlrai/repo-6"
  ]
}
```

Source snapshots have this shape (repositories may be an approved subset):

```json
{
  "v": 1,
  "repositories": [{
    "repo": "ashlrai/repo-0",
    "vision": "# VISION\n- [ ] Restore offline search",
    "issues": [{
      "number": 42, "state": "open", "title": "Fix search pagination",
      "body": "Reproduce duplicate results on the second page."
    }],
    "scans": [{
      "id": "search:test:pagination", "source": "test",
      "title": "Cover empty search pages", "detail": "Add a regression case.",
      "value": 4, "effort": 2
    }]
  }]
}
```

`vision`, `issues` and `scans` are required; use empty text/arrays for a known
empty source. Collectors must surface failed or incomplete discovery themselves,
never replace unknown evidence with empty arrays. VISION accepts explicit
unchecked `- [ ]`, `* [ ]` or `+ [ ]` tasks outside fenced code; narrative and
completed tasks do not generate jobs. Issues require a unique positive number,
`open`/`closed` state, title and body (empty body allowed); closed issues are
excluded. Scans accept the existing `WorkItem` fields shown above (extra fields
are ignored), with a unique ID, a backlog source and integer value/effort 1–5.
Ranking reuses portfolio value/effort and source weighting, with stable ID order
for ties. VISION uses value 5/effort 2 and goal weighting; issues use 3/2.

stdout contains **only new jobs as JSON Lines** with fields `v:1`, `id`, `repo`,
`status:"READY"`, `source` (`vision`, `issue`, `scan`), `sourceId`, `title` and
`prompt`. The queue uses that same row schema, with status one of `READY`,
`RUNNING`, `BLOCKED`, `DONE`, `FAILED`, `CANCELLED`; initialize it as an empty
file. Despite its `.md` name, `router-queue.md` contains JSON Lines, without
Markdown fences or headings. Escaped prompt newlines remain within one row.
All source/task text is untrusted model prompt data and must never enter shell
commands. The planner does not approve paths or interpret source instructions.

Stable IDs, source identities and normalized per-repo titles prevent duplicate
work, including against every terminal and in-progress queue status. Keep queue
history (or equivalent tombstones); removing history permits replay. Existing
READY capacity counts distinct source identities and titles rather than copied
rows with different IDs; the bridge owns stale-job reconciliation.

A READY row whose ID belongs to the `REFILL-*-SALVA` or `REFILL-*-TEST` family
is **parked** until the row's title or prompt names both an absolute
(multi-segment) worktree path and a `*.test.*` file. These families repeatedly
produced empty runs from unanchored task text. A parked row is not READY
capacity and does not suppress refill, but it remains valid queue history and
still deduplicates its ID, source objective and title — unpin it by editing
the row to name the concrete worktree and test file, not by appending a
duplicate. The `rq-plan` record reports the count as `parked`.
stderr is JSON Lines too: each successful queue read emits `rq-queue-read`,
with before/after hashes and added/removed/changed row identities, states and
hashes. Task and diff text never appear in audit logs. Supply `--previous-queue`
to compare against the last read; without it, the baseline is empty. A malformed
queue produces a rejection hash record and no work. Invalid UTF-8, oversized,
missing or symlinked files are refused. File reads are capped at 8 MiB, queue
rows at 20,000, slots at 1,000, and issues/scans at 1,000 each per repo. Titles
are capped at 240 characters, issue bodies/scan details at 16,000, VISION at
128,000, and queue prompts at 20,000.

Exit 0 means no refill needed or target reached; exit 1 means source exhaustion
with possibly usable partial rows; exit 2 means bad usage or invalid snapshots
and no rows. Bridge collectors and the supervisor are separate components;
this command does not install or activate either.

### Restock/queuegen admission lint

`phm backlog lint` gates the Markdown router queue that the bridge's restocker
and queue generator admit work from. This is the `- READY` line format, not the
JSON Lines schema used by `phm backlog plan` above:

```sh
phm backlog lint --queue router-queue.md [--landed landed.txt] \
  [--repos-root ~/Projects/ashlrai] [--pools devin,codex-personal] [--json]
```

A candidate line `- READY <job-id> (<attrs>): <task>` is admitted only when all
of the following hold: the id starts with an uppercase letter and is unique
among candidates; `repo=` (or the `LAND-<repo>-<n>` id fallback) names one of
the seven fleet repositories — `phantom`, `phantom-secrets`, `locus`, `lexicon`,
`ashlr-stack`, `ashlr-plugin`, `ashlr-md`; the repo's folder exists under the
repos root; the task names a concrete file path (a `name.ext` token, a slash
path, or a known extensionless basename — schema handles like `queue.v1` do not
count); the task names a test or acceptance command (a package/verification
script, a test runner, a test-file reference, or an `Acceptance:`/`Tests:`
label); every `after`/`depends` reference is landed; and `pool=`, when
`--pools` is supplied, is in the allowlist (`pool=any` is always allowed).
`.github/` references outside an explicit negation are rejected.

Dependencies are job ids or PR references (`pull` URLs, `<repo>#<n>`, `PR#<n>`,
`#<n>` bound to the line's repo); a trailing `-<LETTER>` dep reuses the job's
own suffix base. `esc=<pool> after <N> failed` is parsed as an escalation spec,
never as a dependency. `--landed` supplies evidence one token per line: job
ids, or PR refs as a full URL, `ashlrai/<repo>/pull/<n>`, `<repo>#<n>`, or a
bare `#<n>` matching any repo. A job dep also counts as landed when the same
document marks it DONE, MERGED or LANDED. Anything else — including unmerged
PRs — is `unlanded-dep`.

Every rejected candidate is logged: one `rq-lint-drop` JSON event per line on
stderr with `line`, `job`, `reasons` and a SHA-256 of the line — never the
untrusted task text — followed by an `rq-lint` summary. Drop reasons:
`unparseable`, `bad-id`, `dup-line`, `no-repo`, `bad-repo`,
`repo-folder-missing`, `github-protected`, `no-file-path`, `no-test-command`,
`bad-dep`, `unlanded-dep`, `unknown-pool`. stdout carries only the admitted
lines verbatim (or the full report object with `--json`), so a restock or
queuegen step can pipe `phm backlog lint --queue q.md > admitted.md`. The
command is offline and read-only: no model, GitHub, subprocess, credential
access or queue writes. Exit 0 means no drops, exit 1 means at least one drop,
exit 2 means bad usage or an unreadable/oversized input.

## 4. Native engines

There are two registries:

- **Phantom chat routing** (`ROUTABLE_ENGINES` in
  `src/core/verse/multimodel/advisor.ts`): `claude`, `codex`, `devin`, `grok`,
  `local`. Native seats (claude, codex, grok) come from
  `~/.ashlr/account-connections/connections.json`. Local seats are Ollama
  models: the base URL is `cfg.models.ollama`, otherwise the default. Devin
  chat seats are separate: a cloud seat, and a CLI seat that is listed when the
  `devin` binary is found.
- **Fleet and run engines** (`src/core/run/engine-registry.ts`). The fleet
  dispatches only to `cfg.foundry.allowedBackends`, which defaults to
  `["builtin"]`. `phm fleet init [--write]` prints or merges a starter `foundry`
  block ([FOUNDRY-CONFIG.md](FOUNDRY-CONFIG.md)). `phm fleet doctor [--json]`
  probes each allowed engine.

How `fleet doctor` decides readiness (`src/core/fleet/engine-readiness.ts`):

| Engine id | Kind | Detected by | Auth signal |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `builtin` | built-in | always present | always ready |
| `claude` | CLI | `claude` on `PATH` | `CLAUDE_CODE_OAUTH_TOKEN` or `ANTHROPIC_AUTH_TOKEN` set, or `~/.claude/credentials.json` exists |
| `codex` | CLI | `codex` on `PATH` | `codex login status` output |
| `grok-cli` | CLI | `grok` on `PATH` | not probed |
| `devin-cli` | CLI | `devin` on `PATH` | not probed by `fleet doctor` |
| `aw`, `ashlrcode` (`ac`), `hermes`, `opencode` | CLI | binary on `PATH` | not probed |
| `claude-api`, `grok`, `kimi`, `nim`, `meta-muse`, `openai-compat` | API | env key set (`ANTHROPIC_API_KEY`, `XAI_API_KEY`, `MOONSHOT_API_KEY`, `NVIDIA_NIM_API_KEY`, `MODEL_API_KEY`, `OPENAI_COMPAT_API_KEY`) | a set key counts as ready |
| `local-coder` (Ollama), `llama-server` | local API | loopback `/models` lists the configured model ID (`OLLAMA_BASE_URL`, `LLAMA_SERVER_BASE_URL`) | not applicable |

**Not verified by these probes:** that a credential is valid or unexpired, that
a model completes a request, quota or plan entitlement, and auth for any CLI
marked "not probed". A key that is present, or a `codex` that reports logged
in, can still fail at runtime. For per-account capacity, use
[RESOURCE-POOLS.md](RESOURCE-POOLS.md) and `phm resources`. For local models,
use [LOCAL-FLEET.md](LOCAL-FLEET.md), `phm models` and `phm local-runtime status`.

## 5. Troubleshooting

| Symptom | Command |
| --- | --- |
| Not sure what is wrong | `phm doctor` (then `phm doctor --fix` for safe fixes), `phm preflight` |
| `phm` not found after install | `phm doctor` checks `~/.local/bin` on `PATH`; from source run `./install.sh` |
| Agent does not see Phantom tools | `phm mcp doctor`, `phm mcp list`, then `phm wire <client>` |
| No local provider reachable | `phm models`, `phm models start`, `phm local-runtime status\|logs` |
| `phm run --engine claude --sandbox-engine` refuses with exit 2 | Run as a non-root user (Claude Code refuses unattended mode as root), or hand the task to `phm cloud launch "<task>"`. Inside a Claude Code cloud container the session's sign-in is not passed into the sandbox: export `CLAUDE_CODE_OAUTH_TOKEN` (from `claude setup-token`) first |
| `repo not enrolled for autonomous work` | `phm enroll add <repo>` |
| An engine is not ready | `phm fleet doctor` and its `fix:` line. For a Claude engine with no credential under the daemon, the line names this platform's way to set `CLAUDE_CODE_OAUTH_TOKEN` (`launchctl setenv`, `systemctl --user set-environment` or `setx`) |
| `phm resources profile prepare` refuses the executable | The error names the failed check. Install symlinks are refused by design: pass the real path the error prints. The file must be a regular, executable file that is not group- or world-writable, and the profile's parent must be an existing owned mode-0700 directory |
| `daemon status` reports a state issue | `phm daemon recover-state --dry-run --expected-sha256 <sha256>`, then `--execute --plan-id <uuid> --plan-sha256 <sha256> --authorize <plan-sha256>` to quarantine; resolve the quarantine with `phm daemon resolve-state --dry-run --quarantine-plan-id <uuid> --quarantine-receipt-sha256 <sha256>` (see `phm daemon <sub> --help`) |
| Daemon claims running but is not | `phm daemon doctor`, then `phm daemon doctor --clear-stale` |
| Goals stuck in progress with no proposal | `phm goals recover-stale --dry-run` |
| Leftover sandbox worktrees | `phm sandbox list`, `phm sandbox gc` |
| Agent worktrees using too much disk | `phm disk` (read-only: each folder's size and lifecycle state, and the bytes safe to reclaim; `phm disk --json` for agents) |
| Rebuildable disk growth (logs, sessions, staging, worktrees) | `phm disk-maint` (dry run: bytes reclaimable per class; `--apply` frees them; `phm disk-maint schedule --install` installs the daily job; the protect-list keeps `~/.codex*`, model weights, Docker, client trees and secrets always) |
| Log roots using too much disk | `phm steward disk` (dry run; `--apply` deletes expired or over-quota plain logs and gzip-archives cold Codex and Claude sessions to `~/.ashlr/archive`; files modified in the last 24 hours are untouched) |
| Ledger integrity questions | `phm authority ledger verify` |
| Safety invariants | `phm verify-safety` |
| Ledger-specific diagnosis | `phm fleet evidence doctor <source> [--json]` |
| Undo a first activation | `phm onboard --rollback <repo> [--kill]` |

For more failure modes and their recovery, see
[RELIABILITY.md](RELIABILITY.md#failure-modes--recovery).

## Per-pool budget ledger

`phm budget show --json` returns `{ "budgets": ... }`; fleet status includes the
same `budgets` projection. Its schema is `fleet.budgets.v1`. It is an advisory
observation ledger, with no dispatch or spending authority. Pools are
`codex-cmp`, `codex-personal`, `devin`, `claude`, `grok-build`, `local-omlx`, and
`grok-ultra`. Claude remains `held`; local oMLX reports capacity only.

```sh
phm budget add codex-cmp --bucket weeklyPct --remaining 0 --reset-at 2026-11-01T12:00:00Z --json
phm budget add codex-cmp --bucket credits --remaining 42 --json
phm budget add devin --bucket acus --remaining 12.5 --json
phm budget add local-omlx --bucket capacity --remaining 2 --json
phm budget add codex-cmp --source log --input ./quota.log --json
phm budget show --json
```

Manual is the default source. `--at` sets an observation's UTC ISO timestamp;
future readings are rejected. Manual readings override later automatic readings
in the same pool and bucket until their explicit reset. Without a reset, that
manual override persists until another manual reading. Record a new manual
reading to correct it. A reset makes an old balance unknown until a new reading
arrives; it never assumes a full refill. Weekly percentages and credit balances
are independent, including when the weekly allowance is exhausted.

Automatic imports accept `--source cli|log --input <file|->` (`-` is stdin).
The caller supplies the pool explicitly, so personal and company accounts cannot
be inferred from account identifiers. Input is limited to 1 MiB. Supported
labelled lines are `weekly remaining: 25% reset: 2026-11-01T12:00:00Z`,
`weekly used: 75%`, `credits remaining: 42`, `acus remaining: 12.5`, and
`capacity remaining: 2`, optionally prefixed with `rate-limit`. Codex native
`event_msg` / `token_count` JSONL rate-limit records are also supported: only
10080-minute windows, finite credit balances, and observation/reset times are
kept. Unknown output is ignored; an import with no recognized readings fails.
No provider CLI is launched, no authentication file is read, and no raw log,
transcript, account identifier, or credential is stored.

Records are immutable batches under `~/.ashlr/fleet/budgets/`. Concurrent
imports cannot overwrite each other's batches. Unreadable or malformed records
make the snapshot `unavailable`, with unknown balances. Bucket projections
include remaining amount, source, timestamp, reset, last-two and trailing-12-hour
burn per hour, and projected exhaustion. Rates use observations in the current
uninterrupted window; refills and resets break the series. The 12-hour rate uses
the earliest available reading within that interval, so it can cover less than
12 hours. Projection uses the last-two rate from the observation timestamp and
is unknown if exhaustion would occur after reset. Capacity has no burn estimate.

The router queue's external `fleet.v1` and `dispatchd/status.json` producers are
not present in this repository. Their consumer contract is to embed the same
`budgets` object from `phm budget show --json`; this change does not create or
replace those external files. The core reader is `readPoolBudgets` in
`src/core/fleet/pool-budget-store.ts`.

## Fleet event stream

`phm fleet events --json [--follow] [--cursor <cursor>] [--queue-dir <path>]`
replays complete JSON-object lines from `dispatch-events.log` and `jobs.jsonl`
in `~/.ashlr-runs/queue`. It needs no fleet state. `--follow` polls for appended
records (including files created later); SIGINT/SIGTERM stop it cleanly.
Each NDJSON row has `v: 1`, `id`, `cursor`, `source`, `at`, `type`, `job`, and
`pool`. Only these normalized fields are emitted. Timestamp aliases include
`ts`, `time`, `timestamp`; event aliases include `event`, `type`, `to`, `status`,
`state`. Missing fields are null, with `type` defaulting to `unknown`.

Save the last consumed row's opaque cursor and pass it to `--cursor` to resume
both files. IDs are stable for an unchanged record at the same file position.
Source order is dispatch then jobs per read batch, not global timestamp order.
Malformed complete lines are skipped; incomplete final lines wait for newline.
Lines are limited to 64 KiB. A replaced, shortened, or changed checkpoint
restarts that source, so consumers should deduplicate IDs after recovery.
Cursors are local to these log files; they cannot recover deleted history.

## Engineering lanes console

`phm fleet lanes [--json] [--queue-dir <abs>]` prints the `fleet.lanes.v1`
projection — one row per router lane (pool) with credit left, ready-queue
depth, live jobs and merges per hour — and the same projection is served on
the loopback console at `GET /api/fleet/lanes` and rendered in the Fleet
view. It is strictly read-only: bounded file reads, no writes, no spawned
readers, no provider calls, no secrets.

Inputs are the existing readers' artifacts. From the router queue directory
(`~/.ashlr-runs/queue` by default, `--queue-dir` overrides for fixtures):
`ready.tsv` (queue depth; LAND rows with timestamps count toward merges/hour),
`queue.v1.json` (authoritative live jobs plus the job→pool map), `jobs.jsonl`
(merge outcomes and transitions in the trailing hour), and `usage-readings.log`.
The merge rate counts a GitHub PR once across repeated observations and jobs;
legacy transitions without a PR URL deduplicate by job, including LAND rows in
`ready.tsv`. Rows with neither identifier remain separate observations. Event
timestamps must include a timezone; the trailing window includes both endpoints
and uses the event timestamp, not reconciliation time. The bounded ledger is
read in full because backfilled events need not be ordered by event time. Credit
comes from the pool-budget ledger; a queue-local `budgets/` directory or the
usage journal fill pools the ledger has not observed.

Every input degrades independently: a missing file reports `missing`, a
corrupt one `degraded`, and the affected cells come back null/`unknown` rather
than fabricated zeros. `test/fixtures/fleet-lanes/` is a captured queue
directory covering every source.

Proposal apply cleanup and crash-leftover reaping use plain `git worktree remove`,
which also reclaims ignored build directories such as `node_modules` and `target`. Dirty or locked
checkouts remain available for recovery. To retain an inbox checkout for a
FIXUP, put its absolute path in the JSON array at
`~/.ashlr/kept-worktrees.json`. Exact paths and their filesystem aliases match;
entries are not glob patterns. A missing file means no pins, while a malformed,
unreadable or symlinked file stops inbox reaping. These pins apply to proposal
apply cleanup and the crash-leftover reaper; sandbox and merge terminal cleanup
have separate retention controls.

The doctor storage line estimates logical GB in clean, inactive inbox worktrees,
excluding pinned checkouts and symlink targets. It does not delete files or
measure shared repository objects. A bounded or failed scan reports an unknown
total; reported logical bytes are not a promise of physical disk space freed.

`phm fleet repo-rate --json` reads merged PR outcomes from
`~/.ashlr-runs/metrics/jobs.jsonl` for the last six hours. It reports each repo's
merge count, median time to merge in seconds, and newest merge time. Each PR
counts once; missing durations remain unknown. `--hours N` changes the window.
The default target is 20 merges for `ashlrai/phantom`; `--target N` changes it
and `--all` checks every observed repo. Exit 1 means a checked repo is below
target or the ledger could not be read. No work is launched or changed.

`phm fleet slow-prs [--json]` lists open PRs at least 30 minutes old, measured
against the newest timestamp in the last 3000 lines of the jobs ledger. Plain
output shows one line per repository with its count and PR URLs; JSON returns
the typed `fleet.slow-prs.v1` report. This command only reads the local ledger.

`phm fleet pr-hygiene [--repo <owner/name>] [--stale-days <n>] [--limit <n>] [--json]`
audits one repo's open PRs and emits the `fleet.pr-hygiene.v1` triage report
for the merge cockpit: each PR is flagged superseded (the same merged-job
prompt evidence the fleet superseded report uses), conflicted, stale (idle at
least `--stale-days`, default 7), file-overlapping, behind or draft, then
triaged close-candidate,
refix, review or ok. A failed open-PR read still emits the versioned shape
with `reads.open: 'failed'` (exit 1); a failed merged or prompts read degrades
only the superseded leg. Read-only — `gh pr list` calls only. See
[pr-hygiene](fleet/pr-hygiene.md) for the report shape.

Source: https://verse.ashlr.ai/docs/AGENT-OS-DOCTRINE.md

# Agent OS Doctrine

Status: architecture doctrine. This document does not grant runtime authority or assert that the described end state is deployed.

## Mission

Ashlr Hub is the local-first operating system for an autonomous engineering fleet. Its purpose is not to maximize agent activity. Its purpose is to continuously convert available model capability, repository context, governed tools, and verified evidence into durable company value.

The end state is a system that can:

1. maintain a living, evidence-linked view of the best attainable product state;
2. generate multiple courses of action rather than lock onto the first plausible plan;
3. allocate Codex, Claude, local-model, human, compute, and time capacity to the highest-value verified bets;
4. execute reversible work within narrow identity- and capability-bound authority;
5. verify outcomes in the real environment, not merely source completion;
6. learn from effectiveness evidence and replan without waiting for routine human coordination; and
7. stop, isolate, or escalate when identity, evidence, budget, reversibility, or environmental assumptions no longer hold.

## Design inspiration: distributed decision advantage

NIWC Pacific describes *Sea Strike 2043* as distributed maritime operations in a contested environment using emerging technology, innovative strategy, and real-time intelligence. The film depicts a human-machine team comparing courses of action, fusing distributed observations, reconfiguring modular capabilities, using resilient communications, and synchronizing effects only after explicit authorization.

The engineering-system translation is direct, but not literal:

| Sea Strike concept | Agent OS design rule |
| --- | --- |
| Distributed operations | Repositories and agents remain independently useful but participate through one mission, evidence, and capability fabric. |
| Real-time decision aids | The cockpit leads with the current bottleneck, verified exceptions, capability headroom, and highest-value bets. |
| Course-of-action simulation | Generate competing implementation strategies, red-team their assumptions, and choose using expected value and evidence quality. |
| Human-machine teaming | Humans specify intent and exceptional constraints; the fleet handles routine planning, execution, verification, and replanning. |
| Pre-authorized capability | Standing permits are narrow, expiring, revocable, identity-bound, budget-bound, and effect-class-specific. Policy eligibility is never execution authority. |
| Modular systems | Models, harnesses, tools, and repositories expose typed capabilities and receipts instead of being hard-wired into one provider workflow. |
| Resilient communications | Durable state, leases, replay-safe events, checkpoints, and degraded-mode behavior survive process and provider failure. |
| Sensor fusion | Claims are projections over authenticated source evidence with visible completeness, freshness, and provenance. |
| Effect synchronization | Multi-repository or external effects use an explicit plan, preconditions, immediately rechecked authority, idempotency, and outcome receipts. |
| Contested spectrum | Prompt injection, stale context, compromised tools, account exhaustion, and conflicting concurrent agents are normal operating conditions. |

The `/VISION/` URL is a showcase for *Sea Strike 2043*, not evidence of a
separate published system named VISION. The film is a future-concept thinking
aid, not proof that its depicted capabilities are fielded. Likewise, public DON
material describes the electromagnetic-spectrum enterprise as policy,
governance, people, equipment, procedures, information, and infrastructure—not
as one verified software product named Spectrum. Agent OS adopts the control
patterns, not an unsupported equivalence or government-compliance claim.

Sources: [NIWC Pacific vision page](https://www.niwcpacific.navy.mil/VISION/),
[official DVIDS video record](https://www.dvidshub.net/video/950543/sea-strike-2043),
[DON Electromagnetic Battle Space Governance Board charter](https://www.doncio.navy.mil/FileHandler.ashx?id=16121),
and [DON Information Superiority Vision 2.0](https://www.doncio.navy.mil/FileHandler.ashx?id=22154).

## Capacity as contested spectrum

Codex and Claude subscriptions, local-model accelerators, context windows,
browser sessions, sandboxes, repositories, credentials, network paths, and
human attention are finite channels with interference, reset windows, variable
quality, and different consequence limits. The resource control plane must:

1. sense authenticated capacity and health without exposing credential values;
2. reserve capacity for high-priority and recovery work before opportunistic use;
3. route by mission value, measured model fitness, cost, latency, isolation,
   data sensitivity, quota, and current risk;
4. prevent double allocation through atomic, expiring leases;
5. apply fairness, backpressure, preemption, and circuit breaking;
6. degrade to smaller local scopes when providers or connectivity disappear;
7. reconcile interrupted work idempotently when capacity returns; and
8. learn from measured outcome per token and wall-clock time, not utilization.

This is an engineering inference from DON's closed-loop spectrum-on-demand
concept, which describes distributed sensing, interference monitoring,
predictive congestion management, dynamic allocation, and human oversight. It
does not claim that Ashlr implements or is endorsed by that system. Source:
[DON Spectrum on Demand](https://www.doncio.navy.mil/chips/ArticleDetails.aspx?ID=20514).

## Kernel architecture

The Agent OS kernel is a control loop with six planes:

1. **Intent plane** — living end state, mission graph, invariants, acceptance criteria, and current bottleneck.
2. **Identity and capability plane** — execution identity, workload identity, provider/model/tool capabilities, account headroom, reset windows, and environment binding.
3. **Planning plane** — competing value hypotheses, courses of action, dependency graphs, expected value, evidence plans, and reversible checkpoints.
4. **Execution plane** — sandboxed agents and tools operating through narrow leases and the existing effect-authority machinery.
5. **Evidence plane** — append-only authenticated observations, verification manifests, outcome windows, counterfactuals, and source-quality states.
6. **Command plane** — exception-first operator experience, kill/revoke controls, audit, replay, and explicit human authorization for materially consequential effects.

No plane may silently manufacture authority for another. A good plan is not a permit. A permit is not an execution. A passing source test is not a deployed effect. A deployed effect is not a valuable outcome.

## Zero-trust and ICAM rules

Zero trust in Agent OS means every workload, tool call, repository mutation, provider request, and effect is treated as untrusted until its exact identity, context, capability, and current policy are verified.

- Never trust an agent because it ran earlier in the same task.
- Bind authority to principal, workload, repository, mission, spec, tool, environment, budget, time window, acceptance criteria, rollback evidence, and revocation epoch.
- Separate observation authenticity from effect authority. Host-local HMAC evidence does not become a deployment or merge credential.
- Recheck kill state, revocation, budget, freshness, and scope immediately before an effect.
- Prefer short-lived, least-privilege capabilities over ambient credentials.
- Keep account locators and secrets private; expose only values-free capability state to planning and UI layers.
- Treat missing or incomplete evidence as unavailable, never as a healthy zero.
- Make every external or irreversible effect replay-safe, attributable, and recoverable where recovery is genuinely possible.

### Decision, administration, and enforcement

The control plane adapts NIST SP 800-207's policy-engine, policy-administrator,
and policy-enforcement-point model:

- **Policy engine:** evaluates signed identity, resource, environment,
  risk, budget, freshness, mission, and effect-class facts. It can allow, deny,
  or revoke eligibility, but it performs no effect.
- **Capability administrator:** a constrained specialization of NIST's policy
  administrator. It converts an allowed engine decision into one single-purpose,
  short-lived, audience-bound capability and commands only the named enforcement
  point. It cannot broaden the decision or reuse an expired/revoked grant.
- **Policy enforcement point:** the local broker immediately rechecks the
  capability and current posture, confines the process/tool session, mediates
  I/O, terminates access, and emits an outcome receipt.

The three roles require disjoint interfaces and audit events even when they run
on one desktop. No planner, model, dashboard, repository file, environment
variable, or self-authored score may call the enforcement point directly.

Sources: [NIST SP 800-207](https://csrc.nist.gov/pubs/sp/800/207/final),
[DoD Enterprise ICAM Reference Design](https://dodcio.defense.gov/Portals/0/Documents/Cyber/DoD_Enterprise_ICAM_Reference_Design.pdf),
and [DoD Zero Trust Reference Architecture v2.0](https://dodcio.defense.gov/Portals/0/Documents/Library/%28U%29ZT_RA_v2.0%28U%29_Sep22.pdf).

### Identity and evidence envelope

Every dispatch and effect must bind a canonical envelope containing:

- human or service principal, agent/workload instance, model endpoint, account,
  tool, broker, repository, worktree, revision, runtime, and device identities;
- mission, objective, hypothesis, acceptance contract, sensitivity, data
  lineage, retention, budget, deadline, and effect class;
- policy version and epoch, decision inputs and reason codes, capability ID,
  issuance/expiry, audience, nonce, and revocation state; and
- start/end state, resource use, verifier identity, produced artifacts,
  outcome observation, recovery status, and immutable receipt identity.

Unknown, stale, incomplete, unauthenticated, or conflicting fields produce an
unavailable or denied state. They never collapse into a healthy default.

## Autonomy ladder

Autonomy expands by proven effect class, not by a single global switch.

1. **Observe** — read and authenticate state; no effects.
2. **Recommend** — generate value hypotheses and courses of action; no effects.
3. **Simulate** — run tests, sandboxes, replay, and adversarial canaries.
4. **Build** — perform workspace-local reversible edits under a narrow permit.
5. **Propose** — create commits or change proposals with complete evidence.
6. **Integrate** — merge or push only through the existing authorization and effect journal.
7. **Operate** — deploy, communicate externally, or spend materially only under explicit current authority and acceptance monitoring.

Each rung has its own identity, evidence, budget, revocation, recovery, and acceptance contract. Evidence from one rung does not prove the next.

## Resource economics

Subscription tokens are perishable capacity, but utilization alone is not value. The scheduler should optimize expected durable value under uncertainty:

`priority = expected outcome value x information gain x strategic compounding x time sensitivity / (token cost x failure risk x coordination cost)`

The expression is a planning model, not a validated financial metric. Estimates must remain labeled, bounded, and replaceable by observed outcomes. Cheap or local models should absorb parallel exploration, classification, replay, mutation testing, and background verification when their measured reliability is sufficient. Frontier capacity should be reserved for high-leverage synthesis, difficult implementation, and independent criticism.

## Effectiveness and self-critique

The fleet may mark its own work effective only when the acceptance contract named the measurement in advance and an independent observation supplies the result. Self-authored prose is not outcome evidence.

Every value bet should close with one of four states:

- **effective** — the predeclared outcome threshold was met with complete evidence;
- **refuted** — evidence disproved the thesis;
- **inconclusive** — the observation window or source quality was insufficient; or
- **superseded** — the mission changed, with the replacement linkage recorded.

The learning loop retains failed hypotheses, verifier disagreements, elapsed time, token cost, operator intervention, and downstream outcome. It should reward calibrated prediction and durable impact, not code volume or agent agreement.

The DoD zero-trust roadmap distinguishes capabilities, their intended outcomes
and impacts, associated activities, responsibilities, and end states. The cATO
memo separately requires continuous visibility and retains revocable human
authorization. Inspired by those sources, Ashlr defines its own five-state
evidence model:

- **implemented** — source and artifact evidence exists for the capability;
- **enforced** — the exact runtime rejects bypass and degraded inputs;
- **effective** — a predeclared outcome threshold passed an independent
  observation window;
- **commissioned** — an authorized operator bound the exact identities,
  infrastructure, policies, keys, and rollback path; and
- **production-authorized** — a current, scoped, revocable grant admits this
  exact effect class.

Regression, expired evidence, changed configuration, identity drift, failed
adversarial checks, or revoked authority automatically lowers the state. A
component is never "fully complete" as a permanent self-assertion.

Sources: [DoD Zero Trust Capabilities and Activities v1.1](https://dodcio.defense.gov/Portals/0/Documents/Library/ZT-CapabilitiesActivities.pdf),
[DoD Continuous Authorization to Operate](https://dodcio.defense.gov/Portals/0/Documents/Library/20220204-cATO-memo.PDF),
and [CISA Zero Trust Maturity Model v2.0](https://www.cisa.gov/sites/default/files/2023-04/zero_trust_maturity_model_v2_508.pdf).

## Production acceptance contract

Before evaluating a candidate, the operator must sign and freeze a versioned
acceptance manifest. It names the exact candidate and rollback, host and policy
identities, verifier identities and independence constraints, mission corpus
and stratification, outcome oracle and normalization, paired FIFO comparison
protocol, credential-leak attack matrix, component-independence probes,
load/concurrency/warmup profile, timing boundaries, minimum sample counts,
allowed failure count, percentile estimator, and evidence retention. The
candidate cannot write or select its own oracle, corpus, baseline, or verifier.
A changed manifest creates a new acceptance run and cannot inherit results.

The control loop is not live until one exact release passes all of these gates
under that frozen manifest:

1. **Fresh composition:** the cockpit reconstructs an authenticated snapshot in
   under 60 seconds, remains fresh for 24 hours, rejects a forged or replayed
   source, and visibly degrades after a producer crash.
2. **Concurrent allocation:** two separately identified Codex accounts, one
   supported Claude capacity source, and one local model can run concurrently
   through atomic leases without double allocation and pass every declared
   credential-isolation attack in the manifest.
3. **Containment:** execution uses an authenticated deny-default broker;
   network, filesystem, process, environment, time, output, and cleanup limits
   are enforced, and a kill/revoke reaches the broker in under one second at
   p99 during the acceptance run.
4. **Course-of-action choice:** each material bet records at least two genuinely
   different plans, assumptions, predicted value/cost, red-team findings, and a
   deterministic selection reason before implementation begins. The manifest's
   diversity predicate decides whether the plans are materially different.
5. **Value-loop closure:** at most three active strategic bets each have a
   frozen hypothesis, baseline, budget, stop rule, independent outcome source,
   and terminal classification. A benchmark of at least 20 representative
   pre-stratified missions must show more than 20 percent improvement in
   oracle-scored outcome per token under the paired FIFO protocol before
   adaptive routing is promoted.
6. **Effect-class canary:** each new effect class completes at least 50 admitted
   actions over seven days with complete receipts, under 10 percent human
   intervention, zero unreceipted effects, and a tested rollback under five
   minutes before broader standing authority is considered.
7. **Golden ecosystem mission:** one mission crosses Plugin, Hub, Cortex or
   Locus, an isolated agent, Phantom, and Stack through typed contracts while
   each product passes its frozen stand-alone probe; every handoff retains
   identity, provenance, sensitivity, and acceptance linkage.
8. **Operator command:** physical and software kill/revoke controls are tested
   under load. The Work Louder emergency action must be authenticated and reach
   local enforcement in under 250 milliseconds at p99 without relying on a
   cloud round trip.

These thresholds are initial promotion criteria, not validated performance
claims. The manifest supplies the exact sampling and timing details; an
acceptance receipt must bind that manifest plus the exact release, host,
configuration, policy epoch, clock interval, raw measurements, and verifier.

## Current implementation boundary

The current tranche establishes source-level contracts for execution identity, capability spectrum, living end state, strategic investment, an observation-only kernel, an authenticated Agent OS snapshot path, an inert standing-permit evaluator, and a read-only cockpit.

It intentionally does not schedule a producer or grant live effect authority because a production source for the complete Agent OS read-model input does not yet exist. Until that source exists, the correct runtime state is missing or degraded. Historical rollback resistance also requires an anchor outside the same-user local store; host-local authenticated chains must publish that limitation.

## Next implementation sequence

1. Create durable production registries for verified mission, capability, portfolio, hypothesis, and redacted display inputs.
2. Add an observation producer after durable daemon ticks, with overlap suppression, deadlines, cancellation, and attempt receipts.
3. Add counterfactual course-of-action simulation and adversarial evaluation using isolated model pools.
4. Connect standing-permit eligibility to the existing activation/effect-authority path without adding a parallel trust root.
5. Introduce effectiveness observation windows and automatic portfolio reallocation.
6. Add cross-repository mission packages so Hub, Phantom, Cortex, Locus, MMCP, and Work Louder remain independent products while sharing typed identity, evidence, and capability contracts.
7. Add an external transparency or hardware-backed monotonic anchor before claiming historical rollback protection.


<!-- page: AGENT-OS-OBSERVATION-SANDBOX-V1 -->
Source: https://verse.ashlr.ai/docs/AGENT-OS-OBSERVATION-SANDBOX-V1.md

# Agent OS Observation Sandbox V1

Status: contract and commissioning preflight only. No backend is commissioned,
no daemon lane is enabled, and M562 continues to accept only a trusted in-process
observer callback.

## Honest boundary

`AgentOsObservationSandboxV1` is the protocol between the M562 observation
coordinator and a future local isolation backend. It does not turn a callback,
a child process, or a Node flag into a sandbox. A run is `enforced` only when a
fresh attestation is authenticated by a separately configured verifier and
binds the expected backend identity and policy.

The attested policy must prove all of the following at once:

- a separate process and an isolation boundary intended for untrusted code;
- denied network access, runtime/input-only filesystem reads, and denied filesystem writes;
- a minimal sanitized environment and denied ambient host IPC;
- denied child processes, worker threads, native addons, WASI, and inspector;
- backend-enforced deadline termination and bounded output collection; and
- a response-bound process identity.

The controller authenticates exact canonical request and response frames with
role-separated attestation, controller-request, and backend-response keys,
binds each request to the epoch, durable tick, attempt, start receipt, input,
deadline, output cap, backend, and policy, and rereads the exact backend
attestation after execution. Callback mutation, attestation drift, stale
evidence, oversized output, late completion, malformed Base64, digest mismatch,
and authentication failure all withhold the output.

This is still an observation-only capability. An authenticated sandbox result
grants no planning, execution, effect, credential, commissioning, activation,
or external-mutation authority.

## Why Node 22 is a seatbelt, not the boundary

Node 22.22.3 is installed on the inspected host. Node 22's stable Permission
Model can restrict `node:fs`, child processes, worker threads, native addons,
WASI, and the inspector when Node starts with `--permission` and the related
allow flags are omitted. The V1 helper returns a minimal defense-in-depth flag
set, but a `node-permission-seatbelt` attestation is hard-coded to remain
`seatbelt-only`.

This follows Node's own threat model: the Permission Model is a seat belt for
trusted code and does not provide guarantees against malicious code. The Node
22 documentation also says filesystem restrictions apply through `node:fs`
and do not guarantee that another API cannot access the filesystem. A local
probe confirmed child-process creation was denied by the listed flags while
`fetch()` still reached the network; Node 22 does not provide the newer network
permission described by later Node releases.

Primary references:

- [Node.js 22.18 Permission Model](https://nodejs.org/download/release/v22.18.0/docs/api/permissions.html)
- [Node.js 22.17 command-line permission flags](https://nodejs.org/download/release/v22.17.0/docs/api/cli.html)

## Why the existing macOS launcher is not auto-commissioned

The inspected host has `/usr/bin/sandbox-exec`, and a trivial SBPL profile ran
successfully. Hub's existing `src/core/sandbox/confine.ts` uses it effectively
for a different threat model: interactive engineering agents working in a Git
worktree. That profile begins with `(allow default)`, re-allows vendor homes,
and intentionally retains broad process functionality. Its launcher builder
does not produce a fresh authenticated proof that the child actually started
under the expected profile, remained there, was killed at its deadline, and
had bounded output.

Reusing that launcher would therefore overstate the M562 guarantee. A future
macOS adapter can qualify only after it uses a dedicated deny-first observation
profile and independently demonstrates each required control through an
authenticated commissioning and runtime attestation. A local container or VM
backend can implement the same protocol without changing M562 records.

## Commissioning sequence

1. Choose a local backend and pin its executable/image and policy digests.
2. Implement a dedicated producer process that accepts only authenticated V1
   request frames and emits only authenticated V1 response frames.
3. Red-team filesystem writes, egress, subprocesses, workers, addons, WASI,
   inspector, deadline termination, output flooding, and process substitution.
4. Install a distinct attestation trust root and frame keys through an explicit
   ceremony. Do not accept a key ID supplied by the backend as its own trust.
5. Run crash, timeout, cancellation, and attestation-rotation acceptance with
   M562 still disabled.
6. Add the sandbox dependency to the composition root, then enable one
   observation lane through the separately governed daemon activation path.

Until those steps complete, the exact residual is: authenticated framing and a
fail-closed commissioning gate exist, but no local isolation backend is proven
or active and the M562 callback must remain trusted and side-effect-free.

# Agent profiles

Portable agent metadata lives at `~/.phantom/agents/<id>.toml`. A doctrine
is a Markdown path, never executed or expanded by the profile reader. Profiles
never grant project access, transport access, credentials or spending authority.

```toml
id = "helper"
version = 1
displayName = "Helper"
doctrine = "doctrine.md"
resourceClass = "any"
channels = []
tools = []
mcpServers = []
skills = []

[policy]
send = "drafts-only"
perMessageApproval = true
limitsTodo = true

[policy.recipients]
allow = []
deny = []
```

`resourceClass` accepts any, codex, claude, glm or local and expresses a router
preference only. `mcpServers` contains connector profile ids, never server
commands or credentials. The writer rejects ids absent from the local connector
profile. Unknown fields are rejected. Writes use a directory lock, atomic
replacement and mode 0600. Unchanged writes keep their version; changed writes
increment it. Stale versions are refused. Missing dailyCap means unlimited;
a nonnegative integer sets the cap. `limitsTodo = true` always means drafts only.

The pure send policy denies unlisted channels and denied recipients, then drafts
when limits are incomplete or a cap is reached. Portable allowlists cannot prove
a verified self identity, so this implementation never grants automatic send.
All recipients require approval until a trusted identity integration is reviewed.

Copy-paste command contract:

```sh
phm agents list --json
phm agents show helper --json
phm agents validate helper --json
phm agents versions helper --json
```

Integration status: the command implementation is provided in src/cli/agents.ts;
the existing top-level agents bus dispatcher is outside this change's named-file
scope, so these commands are not yet registered. Versions lists current and archived revisions. Changed writes retain the previous
revision in a private `<id>.versions/` directory. `pinAgentProfile` resolves an exact
revision and refuses missing versions. Session/job integration is not implemented. The email outbox calls a main-PR drafts-only stub and refuses transport execution
until the policy integration is reviewed. There is no iMessage outbox module in
this checkout. The existing chief-of-staff approval path is outside the named-file
scope and remains unchanged. Security must review send-policy.ts and its test in a separate PR.
The main metadata changes have no runtime dependency on that Security PR.

Mapping reference: [Managed Agents setup](https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/managed-agents/agent-setup).
The local format keeps provider-neutral resource classes and connector references.
