# Duration-balanced Bun shards

`scripts/bun-shards.mjs` plans explicit Bun test inventories using the existing
longest-processing-time-first allocator. It does not change CI workflows or
the Vitest backend runner. Workflow adoption needs a separate G1 change.

Create an inventory JSON array of repository-relative Bun test paths, for example
`["test/example.test.ts", "test/other.spec.ts"]`. Supply the same complete
inventory to each shard planner, from the same checkout and timings snapshot.
Only include tests compatible with Bun; this script does not convert Vitest tests.

```sh
node scripts/bun-shards.mjs plan inventory.json bun-timings.json 4 > shard-plan.json
HOME=$(mktemp -d) node scripts/bun-shards.mjs record inventory.json bun-timings.json
```

`plan` prints JSON with one-based shard indices, sorted file lists, total weights,
and fallback files. Consume each file list as separate argv entries prefixed
with `./` when invoking `bun test`; do not join paths into shell code. Empty
shards must exit successfully without invoking Bun (which would run all tests).
Every inventory file appears exactly once, including files absent from timings.
Inventory paths must resolve to regular test files within the current directory;
duplicates and symlink escapes are rejected.

`record` runs each file separately with `bun test ./path`, inherits test output,
and records elapsed wall-clock milliseconds including Bun startup. Each file has
a five-minute timeout. Any failure, signal, timeout, or missing executable stops
calibration without replacing the previous timings. A passing complete inventory
atomically replaces the snapshot, removing stale entries. Use separate output
paths for concurrent recorders; record on representative hardware with the same
Bun version and test configuration used by consumers. Isolate HOME as above.
The timings format is `{ "schema": "phantom-bun-timings/v1", "files": { "test/example.test.ts": 125 } }`.

Missing timings use file size, calibrated to aggregate observed milliseconds per
byte when measurements exist. A missing snapshot is a normal cold start; malformed
snapshots fail visibly. Cold plans report `bytes`; calibrated plans report
`estimated-ms`. Size is a heuristic, and a single dominant file can prevent tight
balance. The fixture test requires the maximum-minus-minimum shard load to stay
within 15% of the mean for 2, 3, 4, and 6 shards. This is a planning guarantee on
those fixtures, not a claim that PR CI already meets the 75-second target.

Regression checks:

```sh
HOME=$(mktemp -d) npm run test:ci -- test/bun-shards.test.ts test/test-shard-plan.test.ts
```


<!-- page: BUS-THREADS -->
Source: https://verse.ashlr.ai/docs/BUS-THREADS.md

# Bus threads and task board

`phm bus` coordinates cooperating local agents and machines using private
filesystem state. It does not run tasks, grant execution authority, or send
messages to external services. Every command returns JSON (except `--help`):
exit 0 is success, 1 is an operational refusal, and 2 is invalid usage.
`phm fleet bus ...` reaches the same board through the fleet dispatcher.

## Work together

```sh
phm bus thread create 'Release review' --peer alice --json
# Use the returned result.id as THREAD.
phm bus thread join THREAD --peer bob
phm bus thread post THREAD 'Tests are ready for review' --peer alice
phm bus thread read THREAD --peer bob
phm bus thread pending THREAD --peer bob
phm bus thread hops THREAD --peer bob
phm bus thread list --peer alice

phm bus task create THREAD fleet-item-123 'Review test results' --peer alice
# Use the returned task id as TASK.
phm bus task claim TASK --peer alice
phm bus task handoff TASK bob --peer alice
phm bus task renew TASK --peer bob
phm bus task list THREAD --peer bob
phm bus task release TASK --peer bob
```

Quote titles and bodies as single arguments. `--` permits content beginning
with a dash. Peer defaults to `fleet.sharedQueue.machineId`, or the hostname.
Peers are cooperative routing labels, not authentication. Anyone with the
same OS account and store access has that account's authority; this is not a
multi-tenant messaging service. Joining requires knowing the thread ID.

Posts snapshot the joined members, including the sender. Joining twice does
not duplicate deliveries; joining later does not expose earlier messages.
Reads are historical inspection, repeatable, and do not acknowledge or delete
messages. Wire messages use P2 priority and a 60-second TTL; live observers
receive only the remaining lifetime, while board history retains the original
metadata. The durable board is authoritative; `bus:delivery` lifecycle
observers are best effort and cannot invalidate a committed post. Retrying a
post creates another message.

## Fleet ownership

Each task names the exact fleet item ID, which may appear only once on the
board. A claim uses `SharedStore`'s queue ID, token, generation, phase and
lease fences (`src/core/fleet/shared-store.ts`). Handoff transfers a live,
claimed item under the same queue lock, creates a fresh generation, and
invalidates the previous capability. It cannot transfer executing or expired
work. Only the current board owner can hand off, renew, or release, and the
recipient must have joined the thread.

Default state is `~/.ashlr/bus/state.json`; the local coordination queue is
`~/.ashlr/fleet/bus-queue`. In single-machine mode this queue coordinates bus
clients; the fleet's in-memory local coordinator is separate. For integration
with the fleet's shared queue, configure `fleet.sharedQueue.mode: filesystem`,
an absolute `path`, and `trustedCoherentStorage: true`. The bus then uses that
queue and stores its board in `<path>/bus`. The existing coherent-filesystem
attestation is required; replicated sync folders are unsuitable. All writers
must access the same private, owned filesystem state. `--root <abs>` and
`--queue-root <abs>` override both paths for development and tests.

Capabilities are stored only in private board state, never CLI output or
messages. The board and fleet queue are separate durable files: if disk failure
occurs after a queue mutation, the command fails and the orphaned **claimed**
lease remains fenced until expiry. There is no success response, automatic
execution, or attempt to steal it back. Retry claiming after expiry. A corrupt
board is refused, never silently reset. Retention is bounded at 10,000 records
per collection and 16 MiB total; a full store refuses new writes instead of
silently dropping messages. There is no automatic pruning.

## Untrusted delivery and audit

Bodies and titles are data, framed with an explicit untrusted warning and a
fresh unpredictable delimiter. Deliveries carry `content.trust: untrusted`.
Consumers must not execute instructions found inside peer content. Every
outbound read rewraps persisted content; lifecycle observers receive frozen
envelopes. `foundry.eventBus: false` disables bus operations before writes.

`thread hops` is a durable-delivery log projection containing only envelope ID,
thread ID, sender, recipient and timestamp. A separate `<bus-root>/hops.jsonl`
records the hop-log allowlist: `id`, `from`, `to`, `inputTokens`, and
`outputTokens` (unknown counts are null). Neither log contains bodies, titles,
capability tokens, or payload hashes. Posts report `unlogged` if the append
fails or its 8 MiB bound is reached; board delivery remains durable.

## Module contracts

Each post validates the shared bus envelope (`src/core/fleet/bus-envelope.ts`)
before storage; the complete wire JSON lives only inside the untrusted content
wrapper, while `message` exposes body-free routing metadata. Durable delivery
records and their projections live in `src/core/fleet/bus-delivery.ts`; the
metadata-only hop sink is `src/core/fleet/bus-hoplog.ts`, and the advisory
`bus:delivery` lifecycle event rides `src/core/fleet/event-bus.ts`.

Peer IDs are accepted when they match the bus identifier grammar (1 to 128
ASCII letters, digits, dots, underscores, colons, @ signs or hyphens,
beginning with a letter or digit). `BusBoard` also accepts an injected peer
allowlist for callers that want admission tied to an external registry; the
CLI leaves admission open because every label is only a cooperative routing
hint on a private store anyway.

## Explicit delivery receipts

A thread routes each post to the membership snapshot at posting time. After
reading, a recipient may record `phm bus thread ack <thread-id> <delivery-id>
--peer <recipient> --json`. Retrying returns the original receipt and timestamp.
`phm bus thread receipts <thread-id> --peer <sender> --json` lists receipt
metadata for that sender's deliveries; it contains no message body. Reading or
posting does not acknowledge a delivery. Existing board state without receipts
remains valid; malformed receipts make the board unavailable rather than being
discarded. Receipt records share the board's bounded private local storage.

Labels are cooperative routing labels, not authenticated identities: a receipt
records an assertion under a label, not proof that a particular person or agent
read, understood, or acted on content. It grants no execution authority. Do not
put secret values in messages. This local board does not contact remote peers.

`thread pending` reads only deliveries addressed to the caller that have no
explicit receipt. It is a repeatable polling view over the same durable board:
polling never acknowledges a message, and an acknowledgement removes only that
delivery from subsequent pending reads. Historical `thread read` is unchanged.
The view and receipt check share one locked snapshot; labels remain cooperative
and neither a pending read nor a receipt grants execution authority.


<!-- page: CHANNEL-DELIVERY-CONTRACT -->
Source: https://verse.ashlr.ai/docs/CHANNEL-DELIVERY-CONTRACT.md

# Channel delivery contract

`createChannelReceiver` is the shared inbound boundary for a trusted channel
adapter, not an authentication or transport service. Before calling it, the
adapter must authenticate the sender using its channel's trusted evidence and
map that identity to a canonical `verifiedSenderId`. Use the same canonical ID
for the same person across channels, and configure `allowedSenderIds` with the
permitted IDs. When the channel's evidence id is per-channel (for example
`telegram:<userId>` or `email:<address>`), the adapter also supplies
`canonicalSenderId`: the shared person id the dedupe receipt and cross-channel
merge key on (`OPERATOR_SENDER_ID` for the operator surfaces). Never use a
sender or channel asserted in the message body as proof of identity. The
receiver checks the supplied ID against the allowlist; it does not
independently verify the adapter's claim.

The default inbox records the receiving channel as its displayed `source`; it
does not record `verifiedSenderId`. Source is presentation, not identity or
evidence of who sent the message. A duplicate does not replace the original
entry's source. Applications needing durable sender attribution must provide
their own trusted persistence; they cannot recover it from the inbox source.

## Receipt and acknowledgement

The receiver normalizes the body to Unicode NFC, converts CRLF and CR to LF,
and trims surrounding whitespace. For ten minutes from the first successful
receipt, the same canonical sender and normalized body deduplicate across
channels. A duplicate does not extend that window. Different canonical senders
remain distinct. The first receipt returns an `accepted` ack; a duplicate returns
`duplicate` with the same dedupe key and the current receiving channel.

With the default inbox sink, receipts persist in the shared `runsDir` (default
`~/.ashlr-runs`), so separate receivers using that directory share deduplication.
A custom `write` sink with no `runsDir` and no `receiptStore` keeps receipts only
in that receiver's memory. A custom sink with `runsDir` uses its local receipt
store, or the caller can supply a `receiptStore` that serializes lookup, sink
write and receipt commit across its users. A custom sink must report success
only after persistence.

The sink write and receipt commit are separate operations. A crash or receipt
commit failure after a successful write can leave an inbox entry without a
receipt; a retry may append again. This is not an exactly-once guarantee. A
refused or failed sink write does not reserve a receipt or trigger an ack, and
receipt-store failures return an error without an ack.

The optional `acknowledge` callback is attempted after an accepted or duplicate
receipt. It is best effort: a callback failure is swallowed, and a successful
receive result does not prove delivery of the ack. Route the callback through
the same authenticated channel and reply context that received the message.
The callback receives a detached ack and is awaited while calls to that receiver
are serialized; it must not await another receive on the same receiver.
`accepted` means the sink accepted the entry and the receipt was committed; it
does not mean a leader read or acted on it. `duplicate` means a matching receipt
was already recorded within the window, not that the leader acted on it.

## Agent-bus mirroring

An `accepted` receipt is also mirrored onto the durable local agent bus as a
`mason` → `leaders` P0 envelope whose body is
`{ kind: 'interjection', channel, text, receivedAt, dedupeKey }`, so
`phm comms bus read` and the fleet agent-bus API observe the interjection
without reading the inbox. The bus id derives from the dedupe key, so a retry
after a restart cannot double-post one receipt. Mirroring is best effort: it
runs after the durable write and before the ack, outside the ack timeout, and
a `duplicate` receipt is never republished. A successful result carries a
`publishState` of `published`, `skipped` or `failed`; a failed mirror never
changes the receipt, the result or the ack. `publish: null` disables mirroring
and a `publish` function replaces the default sink. `busRoot` selects the store
root for the default sink; the default stays hermetic for runsDir-scoped
receivers that name no `busRoot`, while adapters that pass neither option
publish to the canonical store.

A pending mirror receipt stores only the source channel and a hash-only
`envelopeDigest` (SHA-256 over the exact raw body, channel, verified sender and
thread; not `receivedAt`, which the receipt pins). A duplicate retry rebuilds
and republishes the original envelope only when its own tuple hashes to that
digest. Case, whitespace, channel, thread or sender variants, and legacy
receipts without a digest, still dedupe and ack as `duplicate` but never
reconstruct a body: the mirror stays pending and the result reports
`publishState: 'failed'`. A malformed digest makes the receipt store refuse the
receive (`dedupe-store-unavailable`).

The same binding gates every retried effect, not only the mirror. Each accepted
record whose receiver has a background effect (mirror or COS queue) stores the
digest, with `pending: false` when mirroring is disabled. On a duplicate, the
COS queue write and the bus mirror use only the envelope rebuilt from a
matching digest (original body, channel, thread and `receivedAt`); the receipt
channel must also equal the hashed channel, otherwise the record fails closed.
Variant and legacy unbound duplicates still ack as `duplicate` but enqueue and
publish nothing.

The inbox reader keeps ordinary Markdown headings inside a structured message.
A dated legacy entry still starts a separate record when old and current
writers share the inbox. The writer escapes entry-like headings in message
bodies so they cannot create an extra record.

### Fleet dispatch events

The dispatch log's own events — launches, publishes, lane holds, incidents,
inbox arrivals and the other kinds the live bus feed parses — are mirrored by
`mirrorDispatchToBus` as `fleet` → `all` P2 envelopes with body
`{ kind: 'fleet-event', event, at, text, job?, lane? }`. `event` is the feed
kind, `at` the log timestamp, `text` bounded to 500 characters, `job` the
first `RQ-PHX-[A-Z0-9]+` token and `lane` the first known lane name. The bus id
is `fleet-<kind>-<16 hex of sha256(at + text)>`, so a re-scan of the same rows
dedupes in the store; a `{at, key}` cursor file skips them earlier. Mirroring
is bounded and headroom-aware: it stops when the store approaches its caps so
room remains for agents and Mason, and a failed run leaves the cursor for the
next pass to retry.

## Minimal use

The following assumes the adapter has already authenticated the request,
resolved its canonical ID and captured the same-channel reply function. These
values are supplied by the adapter, not parsed from the body.

```ts
import { createChannelReceiver } from '../src/core/fleet/channel-envelope.js';

const receive = createChannelReceiver({
  runsDir, // shared by the channel adapters using the default inbox
  allowedSenderIds,
  acknowledge: async (ack) => { await replyOnThisChannel(ack); },
});
const result = await receive({ channel: 'email', verifiedSenderId, body });
// Handle !result.ok as a refusal; no successful ack was attempted for it.
```

Bind `replyOnThisChannel` to this request's authenticated reply destination.
If a receiver is shared across requests, its callback must instead route each
ack to the appropriate originating channel and reply context; the channel field
alone does not identify a particular conversation.

Source: https://verse.ashlr.ai/docs/CHANNEL-HOST.md

# Hosting channel input

[`examples/channel-host.ts`](../examples/channel-host.ts) is a source-level integration example, not a server or a provider client. Run its fake in-memory demonstration from the repository root:

```sh
npx tsx -e 'import { runInMemoryDemo } from "./examples/channel-host.ts"; runInMemoryDemo().then(console.log)'
```

The import alone does nothing. The demo uses fake sessions, an in-memory sink and in-memory acknowledgment transports; it opens no connection and reads no credentials.

Create one `createChannelHost` per host and retain it while handling desktop, Telegram and email events. Inject a port for each channel, an allowlist of canonical identities, and a sink that reports success only after persistence. Call the corresponding `host.desktop`, `host.telegram` or `host.email` with a body and transport evidence. Each port's `verifyIdentity` must authenticate that evidence using the provider or host's actual security boundary and map its verified account to the same canonical Mason ID. Return `null` when it cannot verify the sender. The sample fake verifier is only a fixture, not an authentication scheme.

The evidence must come from a trusted transport and bind the authenticated sender, message and reply destination; do not derive identity or a reply destination from a sender string in the message body. The host chooses the channel handler, and the example constructs the receiver message only after verification, using that channel and the adapter's canonical ID. The receiver separately enforces the allowlist and validates the body. Never pass credentials in the body or canonical identity.

All three handlers share one receiver. It normalizes message text and deduplicates by canonical identity and normalized body across channels for ten minutes from the first successful receipt. Its dedupe state is **process-lifetime in memory**, scoped to that receiver: a restart or another host instance does not share it. The stored first envelope retains its originating channel; a duplicate is acknowledged on the channel that delivered the duplicate.

On a successful receiver result, the example calls that channel's injected acknowledgment transport with the accepted or duplicate acknowledgment and the original transport evidence. `acknowledgement: 'sent'` means the transport resolved, not that a person received it. A rejected transport produces `acknowledgement: 'failed'` while the successful receipt remains intact; the receiver has already recorded the write, so a retry within the window is a duplicate. A failed or rejected sink returns the receiver's failure reason and sends no acknowledgment; a retry can be accepted. Unverified or failed authentication also sends no acknowledgment and writes nothing. The host must decide how to observe and retry delivery failures. This example sends after `receive` returns so it can report transport failures; the receiver's optional callback itself swallows transport errors and is best effort. Do not use both acknowledgment mechanisms for the same delivery.

# Channel guide

Every external message — Mason on Telegram, a CLI inbox post, a mobile
interjection, the desktop composer, the Phantom page, or a drop-folder
email — lands in one shared inbox, gets deduplicated, carries its source,
and receives a same-channel acknowledgement.

## Where messages land

- `~/.ashlr-runs/leader/MASON-INBOX.md` — the durable receipt store
  ([`appendInboxEntry`](../src/core/fleet/mason-inbox.ts)).
- The durable agent bus (readable via `phm comms bus read`) — mirrors
  accepted receipts through [`publishChannelEnvelope`](../src/core/fleet/channel-bus-publish.ts).
- Both paths are driven by the shared [`createChannelReceiver`](../src/core/fleet/channel-envelope.ts), so a duplicate never writes a second entry.

## Channels

`INBOUND_CHANNELS` lists **email · telegram · mobile · desktop · page · cli**
and each channel has display labels in
[`fleet-channels-model.ts`](../src/web-ui/routes/verse/fleet-channels/fleet-channels-model.ts).

### Telegram

Private chat to the configured bot ([`telegram-inbox-bridge.ts`](../src/core/comms/telegram-inbox-bridge.ts)).
Verified as Mason when `comms.telegram.chatId` in the config matches the event's
`senderUserId` (canonical ID: `telegram:<id>`). Explicitly enroll that private owner
with `phm comms pair-telegram` on the local host, or send `/pair <code>` from the
configured account using the existing private operator secret. A later identity
is refused; setup never overwrites an existing pairing record.
Plain language is enough: "how's the fleet?" returns the short glance, and any
other sentence is an order in `MASON-INBOX.md`. Setup is the existing bot token
and chat id ([operator glance](OPERATOR-GLANCE.md)).

### CLI

`phm comms inbox post --file <file|->`
([`comms-inbox.ts`](../src/cli/comms-inbox.ts)).  Verified as Mason when the
CLI operator's sender ID is in the allowlist (canonical ID: `local-operator`).

### Email

Run `phm comms setup-email` for local drop paths and the Mail.app rule / trusted
forwarder recipe. Save only Mason's independently verified addresses with
`phm comms email-drop <inboxDir> --from <verified-address> --save-config`.
The saved `~/.ashlr-runs/queue/email-drop.json` enables email in the existing
`phm comms cycle`; `phm comms email-cycle` runs that same email pass directly.
Set `enabled: false` to pause both ingestion and reply sending (omitting it
preserves enabled behavior for existing saved configs). Unknown senders remain
in the processed archive, without inbox steering or replies. Message-ID dedupe
prevents a second inbox entry or bus publication.

Drop-folder delivery via [`email-drop-bridge.ts`](../src/core/comms/email-drop-bridge.ts):
an external mail path saves raw RFC 822 files (`*.eml`) into an inbox directory;
Phantom parses, checks the allow-listed From address, writes the body, and drops a
`.reply.eml` into the outbound folder.  Sending those replies is opt-in on
macOS: `phm comms email-drop … --save-config --send-replies` stores
`sendReplies: true`, after which each `phm comms cycle` pass drains the outbox
through Mail.app — claimed atomically, sent exactly once, never retried from a
crashed claim.  Replies go only to the config's allow-listed `from` senders;
`ashlr fleet email-outbox [--send] [--json]` shows what is queued, sent or
stuck.  Mail.app cannot set `In-Reply-To`, so replies start a fresh thread.
Pairing and exact-domain DKIM are mandatory. When `PHANTOM_OPERATOR_SECRET` (or `~/.ashlr/comms/operator-secret`) is set, mail
also needs a DKIM pass for the sender's domain and that secret once; later mail
from the paired address stays plain language. See [operator glance](OPERATOR-GLANCE.md).

### Desktop

Sent from the desktop composer; source string is `"Phantom desktop"`
([`mason-inbox.ts`](../src/core/fleet/mason-inbox.ts) default source).  No
separate verification gate — the source is the channel label.

### Mobile

The remote phone gateway sends through the mobile channel
([`channelKey`](../src/web-ui/routes/verse/fleet-channels/fleet-channels-model.ts)
matches `mobile` / `remote` / `phone`); the gateway pins `"Phantom mobile"`
as the source for phone-originated writes.  Not a separately-verified sender.

### Phantom page

Messages sent through the Phantom page are captured under the `page` channel
label in the Channels pane (`"page"` / `"7790"` source match).  No separate
verification — the page source is the channel label.

## Dedupe · attribution · acknowledgment

- **Dedupe window** — 10 minutes (first receipt, across restarts);
  [`CHANNEL_DEDUPE_WINDOW_MS`](../src/core/fleet/channel-envelope.ts).
- **Duplicate acknowledgement** — `"Already received by Phantom; no duplicate interjection added. Receipt: <key>"`
  (see [`formatChannelAck`](../src/core/fleet/channel-ack-text.ts)).
- **Attribution** — the `source` field in every inbox entry (e.g. `"telegram"`,
  `"Phantom mobile"`); the default source falls back to `"Phantom desktop"` when
  a channel omits one ([`mason-inbox.ts`](../src/core/fleet/mason-inbox.ts)).
- **Ack timeout** — 2 000 ms per [`CHANNEL_ACK_TIMEOUT_MS`](../src/core/fleet/channel-envelope.ts);
  the transport is best-effort and never unwrites a durable receipt.

## Setup and status from the CLI

`phm channels` is the one path: `add` writes a channel's config and nothing
else — no transport, no pairing, and no credential. Tokens and secrets stay in
their existing custody (`TELEGRAM_BOT_TOKEN`, `PHANTOM_OPERATOR_SECRET`, or the
private files above) and are never accepted on the command line or printed.

```sh
phm channels add telegram 123456789          # your numeric chat id; token stays in TELEGRAM_BOT_TOKEN
phm channels add email /path/to/mail-in --from you@example.com
phm channels status --json
```

`phm comms setup-telegram` still discovers the chat id. `status` reports each
channel's `configured`/`credential`/`paired` state plus `received`,
`pendingOutbound`, and `lastSeenAt` — measured numbers, or `"unknown"` when a
source cannot be read. `cli`, `desktop`, and `page` need no setup and always
report ready; `mobile` needs the `~/.ashlr/verse-remote.json` gateway file
([REMOTE-PHONE.md](REMOTE-PHONE.md)).

## Where to watch it

- **Desktop console** — the Channels pane (top-level navigation) and the Inbox pane.
- **CLI** — `phm channels status [--json]` rolls all six kinds up;
  `phm comms bus read` shows every accepted bus envelope;
  `phm comms inbox read` reads the inbox file directly.
- **API** — the `GET /api/verse/fleet/runs/inbox` route exposes the inbox in JSON.

## Gmail triage building block

[`pollGmailBridge`](../src/core/comms/gmail-bridge.ts) is a local programmatic
triage function, not a configured Gmail integration or CLI command. Its caller
must provide a read-only inbox adapter and classification, composition and
summary functions. A poll accepts at most 100 messages; updates return summaries,
and eligible replies become local drafts. A reply is drafted only when the
provider's `autoSubmitted` value is `no` (case-insensitive); missing or other
values go to review. Duplicate or empty IDs in one poll also go to review.
The function has no provider send operation; drafting is not delivery.

# Daily CI trigger plan

Run these commands from the repository root:

```sh
ashlr fleet ci-plan
ashlr fleet ci-plan --patch | git apply
```

The first command reads workflow YAML and prints a table and owner follow-ups.
The second applies the printed patch and is for Mason to run after reviewing it.
The fleet cannot apply it itself: workflow files require owner review and cannot
be edited and auto-merged by fleet workers. The planner never writes files.
Use `--json` for the full result or `--cron "3 9 * * *"` to override newly
added schedules. Default new schedules use 09:03–09:30 UTC, ordered by filename
and wrapping after 28 workflows. Existing schedules, including weekly ones,
are preserved. Parse failures are reported as skipped with their errors.

The planner removes `pull_request`, `pull_request_target`, and branch `push`
triggers. Tag-only pushes are retained. Manual, reusable, release, repository
dispatch and merge-group events remain, as do existing schedules. Therefore
this is a trigger migration proposal, not a global once-per-day rate limiter.
Review retained events and workflows whose jobs depend on PR event payloads
before applying; adding a schedule does not adapt those jobs automatically.

After CI stops running for PRs, the required **Merge Gate** check never
completes. Mason must remove that requirement in branch protection/rulesets
and require **ashlr/verify**, the host-verified gate implemented in
`src/core/fleet/host-merge.ts` and `src/core/fleet/verify-check-run.ts`.
Read current branch protection checks with:

```sh
gh api 'repos/{owner}/{repo}/branches/master/protection/required_status_checks'
```

This command only reads settings. Review rulesets separately and ensure host
verification is configured before switching merge requirements.


<!-- page: CI-IMPACT-MAP -->
Source: https://verse.ashlr.ai/docs/CI-IMPACT-MAP.md

# PR impact map

This read-only view reuses `.github/scripts/ci-impact-shadow.mjs` and its immutable
Git input graph. It maps changed files to current test modules through direct and
transitive imports in each source version. Deleted files retain their old-tree
relationships. Edges from different source versions are not combined into paths
that never existed. Cycles are handled without repeated traversal.

```sh
node .github/scripts/ci-impact-map.mjs ROOT BASE_SHA HEAD_SHA mac-general-1
node .github/scripts/ci-impact-map.mjs ROOT BASE_SHA HEAD_SHA mac-general-1 --html
```

`ROOT` is a clean checkout of the exact `HEAD_SHA`; both revisions must already be
available locally. Redirect stdout to a JSON or HTML file outside that checkout.
Use `web` for frontend test candidates. The other supported role names come from
the existing impact policy. The HTML is self-contained, searchable, and expands
each changed file's known test connections. No assets or scripts are fetched.

The map distinguishes observed role modules from source candidates. Source-only
analysis is not Vitest collection or shard membership. It preserves the analyzer's
incomplete-coverage status and changes no test selection or release policy.
Filesystem reads, generated inputs, workflow invocations, environment, computed
imports and package behavior can introduce dependencies outside known import edges.
Tests without a known path are labeled coverage-unproven, not safe to omit.

The JSON retains available reporter timing metadata without treating overlapping
test spans as CPU time or claiming a speedup. Use the map for focused review and
to identify the next dependency edges to verify. Whole-tree equality, when shown,
is a source observation here; a separate trusted CI proof decides whether a history
merge can avoid duplicate checks. No historical results are inherited by this view.


<!-- page: CI-TEST-FEEDBACK -->
Source: https://verse.ashlr.ai/docs/CI-TEST-FEEDBACK.md

# CI test feedback and failure-first ordering

The stateless processor in `.github/scripts/ci-test-feedback.mjs` replays module-result
metadata and produces a complete ordering of the caller's collected tests. It retains
the original objects and project slots. It does not select tests or reuse results.

Each event binds a source revision, run, attempt, job, role, original log digest and
module occurrence. A filtered second execution is another occurrence. Identical
redeliveries deduplicate; conflicting observations refuse the whole replay. Missing,
skipped and unknown results stay distinct from passes. A final incomplete JSONL record
is corruption. `encodeFeedback` and `decodeFeedback` define the replay format; they do
not themselves provide durable storage or authenticate a GitHub log.

An external collector must retain the original logs and verify their digests before
projecting events. Keep raw errors, titles, fixture values and private content out of
the metadata. Append events to the collector's existing durable storage, then rebuild
snapshots statelessly. Do not introduce an independent source of release authority.

The existing Vitest sequencer accepts an optional JSON snapshot:

```json
{"schema":"phantom-ci-test-feedback-snapshot/v1","events":[]}
```

Set `ASHLR_TEST_CI_FAILURE_FIRST=1`, `ASHLR_TEST_CI_FEEDBACK_SNAPSHOT` to its canonical
file path, and `ASHLR_TEST_CI_FEEDBACK_ROLE` to the exact historical job role. No new
dependency or service is required. The existing bounded descriptor reader validates
the snapshot file. Missing or invalid metadata preserves the normal sequencer order.
The default remains unchanged until a caller enables the option. Shard membership,
project groups, worker caps, deadlines and the isolated runner's final ledger task
remain owned by their existing code.

Vitest already orders locally cached failures first. Those locally known result
slots retain their default positions; historical feedback only orders slots without
local results, which are common on fresh hosted runners.

Within each project's existing slots, historically failed modules run first, ordered
by their measured median elapsed time where known; unobserved or skipped-only modules
follow, then observed passing modules. Equal priorities preserve caller order. A
historical failure can already have been repaired. A matching path is not proof of
unchanged dependencies, runtime, hardware or current performance. History affects
only priority and never supplies a current pass, quarantine or acceptance decision.

Measure actual time to first actionable failure, full-run wall time, complete module
coverage, rerun rate and revert/incident rate before widening usage. Do not sum
overlapping module spans and call that CPU time. A replayed ordering is a scenario,
not a measured CI speedup. Keep a full default-order comparison and retain failures.

This applies the listener/selector separation described in [Anthropic's test-impact
analysis report](https://claude.com/resources/articles/agentic-coding-is-straining-ci-heres-how-we-scaled-test-impact-analysis-at-anthropic).
Its distributed storage architecture is not required for this local metadata step.
Future test omission needs independently established dependency coverage; this
component changes no omission or release policy.


<!-- page: CLI-REFERENCE -->
