# Persistent Linux nodes for Phantom

Status: research and design, with an offline planning CLI and a Lima template.
Research checked 2026-10-26. Nothing has been provisioned. The command does not
measure capacity, log in, join a registry, or enable dispatch.

## Evidence and attribution

The closest verified video title is [Stanford CS146S: How always-on agents
work](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=L1OBRtfPS34), published by `leerob`, confirmed by [YouTube metadata](https://www.youtube.com/oembed?url=https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=L1OBRtfPS34&format=json).
The accessible YouTube page identifies CS146S, not Stanford GSB. The requested
GSB attribution, speaker's exact SpaceX engineering title, spoken Linux-instance
wording, and a timestamp for that wording are **unverified**: the primary video
page did not expose captions in this research environment. Do not present a
third-party transcript as a verified quotation or silently substitute CS146S
for GSB. No spoken quotation is asserted here.

Primary product documentation does establish the useful pattern:

- [Grok Bot overview](https://docs.x.ai/grok-bot/overview) describes persistent
  cloud computers with a browser, filesystem and terminal, and retained context.
- [Grok Bot FAQ](https://docs.x.ai/grok-bot/faq) explicitly says:
  "The computer is assigned per user, not per Bot." This is a documentation
  quotation, not a quotation from the talk.
- [Computer and apps](https://docs.x.ai/grok-bot/computer-and-apps) says bots on
  an account share files, browser sessions and command-line credentials.
- [Deployment documentation](https://docs.x.ai/grok-bot/deployment) identifies
  the hosted computers as Linux, separate from the operator's managed device.

Phantom should adopt persistent storage and resumable work, while choosing
**one VM per node trust boundary**. Multiple bot identities inside one VM would
share that boundary; they must not be advertised as mutually isolated. This is
our design, not a claim that Grok allocates a VM per bot. Specific Grok RAM,
cloud provider, hypervisor, price and lease protocol are not established here.

## Local choice and capacity gate

Use Lima with Apple's Virtualization.framework (`vmType: vz`) on Apple silicon,
macOS 13 or newer. The supplied template is ARM64 only. Intel Macs need a
separately reviewed native x86_64 image/template, not implicit ARM emulation.
[Lima's VZ documentation](https://lima-vm.io/docs/config/vmtype/vz/) describes
this backend. No paid service is required; existing hardware and electricity
are not literally free, and model/vendor subscriptions remain separate.

These are planning allocations, **not measured footprints or benchmarks**:

| Option | Guest allocation | Host overhead reserve | Assessment |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Lima + VZ, terminal only | 4 GiB, 2 vCPU | initially 1 GiB | Recommended CLI lifecycle, reproducible YAML, no GUI required |
| UTM + Apple virtualization, same Linux image | 4 GiB, 2 vCPU | initially 1 GiB plus measured GUI overhead | Useful interactive console; no evidence it consumes less RAM than Lima |
| Direct Virtualization.framework app | 4 GiB, 2 vCPU | initially 1 GiB until measured | Can omit a manager UI, but we must implement image boot, networking, storage and lifecycle; no measured savings justify this work yet |
| Optional desktop/browser, any backend | 6 GiB starting budget | initially 1 GiB plus measured UI overhead | Re-admit against host capacity; tabs and builds can exceed this budget |

[UTM](https://mac.getutm.app/) offers a free direct download; the paid App Store
version is unnecessary. Its [directory sharing controls](https://docs.getutm.app/settings-apple/sharing/)
must stay empty. [Apple's framework](https://developer.apple.com/documentation/virtualization)
is a building block, not an already configured node manager. None of these
sources supplies an apples-to-apples memory benchmark. Use the same guest,
workload, RAM cap and cold/warm phases before comparing them.

Apply the queue's MEMORY P0 invariant as a hard admission gate:

```text
H = total physical host RAM
B = peak host usage excluding the candidate VM, including other VMs
G = configured guest RAM, not its optimistic idle RSS
O = max(1 GiB provisional reserve, measured VM-manager overhead)
admit only if H - B - G - O >= 0.30 * H
```

For a 4 GiB guest and 1 GiB overhead, the maximum B is 6.2 GiB on a 16 GiB Mac,
17.4 GiB on 32 GiB, or 28.6 GiB on 48 GiB. A 6 GiB desktop guest reduces each
limit by 2 GiB. Reserve per VM, account for all running nodes, and reject
unknown/stale samples. Do not treat swap or compressed memory as extra RAM.
Keep memory pressure green with no sustained swap growth. If the budget fails,
queue work or stop the candidate VM; never silently weaken the 30% reserve.

The template caps its persistent guest disk at 40 GiB. Treat the **20 GB free
disk floor** as 20,000,000,000 bytes on both host and guest before admission.
For host admission reserve the full 40 GiB even when the image is sparse, plus
5 GiB for the downloaded image/cache and installation work, plus the floor:
roughly 68.3 decimal GB free initially. Add separate capacity for snapshots,
logs and extra images. Guest jobs must also leave 20 GB free after their
estimated checkout/build output. Neither thin provisioning nor APFS purgeable
space is a promise of capacity. Stop admission at the floor, preserve work,
and request operator cleanup instead of deleting data automatically.

Measure Activity Monitor's memory pressure and VM process footprint, `vm_stat`,
and swap growth during idle, one dependency install/build, and a browser task.
Use `df -k` on the actual VM storage volume and inside the guest. Record hardware,
OS/Lima/image versions, elapsed time, peak memory and minimum disk free. Idle
for ten minutes and sample the workload for at least thirty. No VM measurements
were taken in this change; the capacity rules are proposed admission criteria,
not enforcement implemented by the dry-run stub.

## Template and operator sequence

The [template](../contrib/nodes/lima/phantom-node.yaml) uses an Ubuntu 24.04
ARM64 release image and SHA-256 from the dated
[Ubuntu image manifest](https://cloud-images.ubuntu.com/releases/noble/release-20261017/SHA256SUMS).
A missing image or digest mismatch must fail, never fall back to an unpinned
image. Update URL and digest together after reviewing the publisher manifest.

[Lima's versioned default configuration](https://github.com/lima-vm/lima/blob/v2.0.0/templates/default.yaml)
defines the fields used here. The template has no inherited base, mounts,
provision scripts, container runtime, copied certificates, environment values,
SSH-agent forwarding or X11 forwarding. Proxy environment propagation is off.
A catch-all rule suppresses automatic application-port forwarding. Lima still
manages its SSH transport; its generated public access key is infrastructure,
not a copy of the operator's private key or vendor login. No tokens are created
by this change. No host vendor directory, including `~/.codex`, is accessed.

Preview from a source checkout:

```sh
npm run dev -- node bootstrap --dry-run
npm run dev -- node bootstrap --dry-run --json
```

After a human has measured capacity, the following is the proposed manual local
procedure. These commands were **not run** as part of this change:

```sh
# Use a new dedicated directory, never an existing Lima configuration tree.
mkdir -m 700 "$HOME/.phantom-node-lima"
export LIMA_HOME="$HOME/.phantom-node-lima"
limactl validate contrib/nodes/lima/phantom-node.yaml
limactl create --name=phantom-node contrib/nodes/lima/phantom-node.yaml
# Inspect $LIMA_HOME/phantom-node/lima.yaml locally before starting.
limactl start phantom-node
limactl shell phantom-node
# Later, stop without deleting the persistent disk:
# limactl stop phantom-node
```

Lima merges global defaults/overrides. A new dedicated LIMA_HOME prevents
inheriting ordinary personal Lima mounts, scripts or environment settings;
inspect the effective instance configuration and verify no unexpected shares
before boot. Do not add personal `_config` files. Do not print the process
environment. Run vendor login only in a guest shell, never in cloud-init or
recorded bootstrap logs. Install Node >=22.15.0 and a reviewed Phantom build
inside the guest, using reviewed source/artifacts without `.env`, auth files,
SSH keys, cookies, agent state or personal dotfiles. Do not mount the repository
from a parent containing credentials. Use Locus for approved companion access
and Phantom Secrets references for later secret needs, not copied secret files.

Device-code authorization belongs to RQ-PHM-CONNECT-WIZARD: the guest initiates
a vendor-supported device authorization; the owner confirms on the vendor's
verification page; resulting vendor state remains inside the guest. Never copy
host login state to make an unsupported flow work. A vendor without a supported
flow remains disconnected. This stub does not implement that wizard or claim
any particular vendor currently supports it. Do not snapshot an authenticated
VM as a reusable template; snapshots can contain guest credentials.

A VM protects host files only to the extent its configuration permits. Default
NAT is **not an egress firewall** and does not guarantee host/LAN isolation.
Before untrusted execution, enforce and test a guest/network policy blocking
host services, private networks and cloud metadata while allowing only required
vendor and registry destinations. This template alone is not admission for
hostile jobs. Guest root, browser sessions and code share one trust boundary.

## Registry and lifecycle contract

RQ-DRIVER-NODES-1-LEASE is not present in this checkout. The CLI prints a stub
handoff, not a fake registration or a successful readiness check. The proposed
adapter boundary is:

1. `join(identity, capabilities, capacity)` proposes a stable node identity,
   boot incarnation, Linux architecture, Phantom version and measured resources.
   Repeated joins must be idempotent. No credentials appear in the plan.
2. Registry acceptance returns a bounded lease and fencing generation through
   the registry's approved enrollment/authentication mechanism. This change
   invents neither an endpoint nor a new enrollment token.
3. `heartbeat(nodeId, incarnation, generation, health)` renews only while the
   registry permits it. Use the eventual NODES-1 TTL/renewal policy, not a
   second hard-coded lease schedule. Server-side expiry is authoritative.
4. Jobs carry lease generation and idempotency identity. Check lease, Stop,
   enrollment and resource limits before admission and before committing an
   external effect. Reject stale generations after a reboot or reconnect.
5. Lost connectivity, expired lease or Stop closes admission and fences work.
   Suspend/resume never revives an old lease. Rejoin before becoming ready.
   Drain jobs before planned shutdown; preserve the disk and work receipts.

Future states: planned -> provisioned -> joined -> ready -> draining -> stopped;
lease failure moves ready to unavailable. Persist work and receipts inside the
node, but keep registry authority outside it. VM presence or a successful SSH
connection is not readiness. Persistence survives stop/start, not disk deletion;
Mac sleep/offline periods interrupt local service. Cloud independence from the
laptop is a separate deployment choice.

## Optional headless browser and desktop

Keep both off by default. For browser-only work install a maintained browser
inside the guest and run it as the unprivileged node user, with its normal
sandbox enabled. Do not use `--no-sandbox`. Keep any debugging endpoint on guest
loopback and grant access only for an active authorized session.

For visual workflows, add a minimal desktop such as Xfce on a virtual display
and a maintained VNC server bound to guest loopback. Disable clipboard/file
transfer, retain guest authentication, and use an explicitly requested SSH tunnel
bound to host loopback. Never expose VNC, noVNC or browser debugging to a public
interface. The catch-all forwarding rule remains in place. A separate reviewed
profile must implement and test this; the base YAML does not install a desktop.
Re-budget at 6 GiB or measured peak, whichever is larger. Shut down the desktop
when idle; do not confuse a stopped display with a stopped agent or revoked login.

## Cloud alternative, priced only

[DigitalOcean Basic Droplet pricing](https://www.digitalocean.com/pricing/droplets),
checked 2026-10-26, lists the following regular shared-CPU plans in USD:

| Candidate | RAM / vCPU | Disk / included transfer | Monthly base cap |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Terminal node | 4 GiB / 2 | 80 GiB / 4,000 GiB | $24 |
| Desktop/browser node | 8 GiB / 4 | 160 GiB / 5,000 GiB | $48 |

Base annual arithmetic is $288 or $576 for twelve fully billed months. Taxes,
backups, snapshots, transfer overages, extra disks and model subscriptions are
excluded; re-price the actual region and options before approval. Reserve guest
memory for the OS and keep the same 20 GB free guest disk floor. A stopped cloud
VM is not assumed free. Cloud images need a separate provider configuration;
the Mac VZ template is not a cloud deployment manifest. No cloud API, account,
credential, Terraform apply or provisioning command is part of this change.
Spending and provisioning require owner approval under repository policy.

## Validation and remaining work

`test/node-bootstrap.test.ts` covers text/JSON planning, fail-closed arguments,
help, no side effects, and the explicit registry stub. The offline schema/profile
test parses the YAML, validates its constrained Lima field schema, and rejects
credential-sharing regressions. Tests fetch no images and make no network calls.
If Lima is installed, also run `limactl validate` against the template in a fresh
LIMA_HOME. Offline schema validation is not a boot or hypervisor compatibility test.

Remaining runtime work is explicitly separate: measured capacity enforcement,
network isolation, guest installation/login, the NODES-1 adapter, fencing and
recovery integration tests, and optional desktop provisioning. This change
provides a reviewable design and safe preview surface without claiming those
systems are active.


<!-- page: NODES -->
Source: https://verse.ashlr.ai/docs/NODES.md

# Multi-Mac compute pool

## Implemented SSH pool

The node router now has an opt-in SSH transport and a designated backup witness.
Use Macs on a network they already share and explicit SSH config aliases approved
for team devices. No DNS registration, paid service, discovery broadcast, provider
auth transfer or agent forwarding is added. See [Agent network](AGENT-NETWORK.md)
for complete setup and the runner contract.

The primary keeps queue input and publication custody. The backup durably records
every node-router transition as its replica and fencing witness. It accepts no
backup-origin admissions while the primary is live. Every primary admission must
reach this witness, so a disconnected primary stops admitting. After 15 minutes
without a primary heartbeat, the witness promotes the backup, increments its
fencing epoch and invalidates the old leader. A returning primary is demoted and
cannot reclaim leadership by sending a heartbeat. There is no independent election
from a copied queue. The witness clock is authoritative and clock regression fails
closed. Loss of the witness holds admission; two isolated machines cannot safely
provide both availability and exclusive admission without a shared authority.

Run `phm node watch --json` on both runner Macs. On the primary it sends heartbeats;
on the backup it checks for promotion. This is a foreground command, not an
installed service. Workers can also trigger the timeout check when they contact
the backup after primary transport fails. The primary's private mirror is evidence
only and is never loaded as admission authority. Do not reset either store to
recover an unavailable witness.

Secondary workers probe their own native Codex and Claude CLI sign-in status,
advertise only those lanes, pull fenced owner-scoped jobs and return result
references. They check host-local PAUSE and KILL and stop the runner process group
when a lease cannot be renewed. Auth stays device-bound: never copy `~/.codex`,
`~/.claude` or any auth directory. Publication remains exclusively on the primary
through the existing `publish.sh` path. Backup promotion grants compute admission,
not publication authority.

`phm node list --json` and `phm node status --json` on a configured Mac show the
configured team scope, per-node lanes, load (`usage`, permille), heartbeat and
expiry timestamps, plus the active runner and fencing epoch. Expired nodes remain
visible. Unknown local sign-in never qualifies a provider lane.

This transport extends the existing DriveNodes queue adapter. It does not migrate
`ready.tsv`, install or modify dispatchd, or make the provisional node queue the
production driver queue. A host-owned runner must implement the documented worker
contract; existing dispatchd work must remain isolated until a shared claim adapter
is commissioned. The Agent Bus and A2A contracts remain coordination and context
surfaces, not a second admission authority. No message sending is introduced.
No new log paths are created; child diagnostics and provider output are discarded,
and only references and bounded metadata enter private node state.

## Small Mac enrollment and admission

After installing the reviewed Phantom build, enroll each additional Mac with
`phm node join --owner mason --primary primary-mac --backup backup-mac --json`.
The node ID defaults to a sanitized hostname. Subsequent `phm node join --json`
uses the saved identity and preserves primary/backup roles. SSH trust and each
provider's local sign-in remain prerequisites; join does not discover devices or
install a runner.

The 16 GiB Air has a two-slot RAM ceiling; the 8 GiB Pro has one. Reserve at least
4 GiB or 30% of RAM, whichever is larger, and budget 4 GiB per job. Memory below
30% available, swap in use, disk below 20 GB free or unknown telemetry holds
admission; runtime pressure stops the worker. A worker launches one bounded batch
of up to its RAM slot ceiling concurrently under one session, waits for every
started slot, then leaves. No permanent supervisor is installed. Disk telemetry
covers the home filesystem; the runner's existing DISKGUARD must also cover
checkout and artifact volumes. Pressure checks target three seconds, subject to
bounded synchronous telemetry and SSH delays. These checks add to DISKGUARD.
Use independent per-node lanes; no sharded-inference speedup has been measured.
iPad Pro and phone are mobile control surfaces, not compute nodes.

Share reviewed project MCP and skill files with the same checkout revision, and
credential-free Phantom connector profiles with local vault bindings. There is no
automatic profile sync or Cursor credential copy. The
[agent-network guide](AGENT-NETWORK.md) and
[example](../examples/node-pool/README.md) describe the boundaries.

## Earlier hosting decision

The historical decision below describes the original single-Mac deployment and
hosted-box options. Its hardware inventory and recommendation predate the opt-in
multi-Mac pool above; its auth, publication, cost and host-control boundaries remain
applicable to hosted-box pilots.

### Drive node options

This is a decision document for where `phm drive` capacity should run. The
supervisor and queue come from the queued driver change sets: `phm queue`
(DRIVER-1) owns the `queue.v1` store at `~/.ashlr-runs/queue/queue.v1.json`,
and `phm drive` (DRIVER-2) runs serial ticks that reap finished workers,
publish successful jobs through `publish.sh`, and admit READY jobs into
pools within their floors, ceilings and a global ceiling. Neither change set
is merged yet; this document uses their documented contracts and decides the
node layout they should target. It does not re-decide those contracts. For
the system they plug into, see [Architecture](ARCHITECTURE.md).

A "node" here is wherever a claimed job actually executes. Three things stay
fixed regardless of this decision:

- **The Mac keeps queue and publish custody.** `queue.v1` relies on
  local-filesystem atomic rename and an exclusive lock file, `publish.sh`
  runs under `phantom exec` on the trusted host, and dispatchd remains the
  fallback scheduler until an authorized cutover. Do not mount the queue
  directory over a network filesystem, and do not hand publication to a
  worker node.
- **Auth stays device-bound.** Provider CLI sessions live on the machine
  where a human signed them in. `~/.codex`, `~/.claude` and every other auth
  directory are never copied between machines; the driver bridge contract
  already excludes access to `~/.codex` auth.
- **PAUSE and KILL are host-local sentinels.** Every node that runs workers
  needs its own copies; a node without the sentinels is a node that cannot
  be stopped from here.

The Mac is the only local hardware. The existing Grok Bot box is a hosted,
vendor-operated Linux machine shared by all of Mason's Grok Bot agents.
It is remote capacity, with a different trust boundary from the Mac.
Existing subscriptions do not establish spare capacity or permission to spend.

## At a glance

| Node | Security boundary | Cost | Capacity | Latency | Worst failure mode |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Grok Bot box, headless | Hosted shared Linux; vendor and co-agent credential exposure | No new spend authorized; existing plan limits apply | One shared machine; headroom unverified | Remote dispatch plus process spawn | Shared-host compromise or outage |
| Cursor cloud agents | Vendor compute; untrusted PR back | Included pool, then API rates | Elastic burst | Minutes per task | Silent spend past intent |
| Devin and Codex cloud pools | Vendor compute behind existing lanes and gates | Devin ACUs; Codex plan limits | Elastic within plan caps | Minutes; async PR delivery | Budget holds; PR never opens |
| Small paid VM | Live auth on rented hardware | About $5 to $15 per month | Small fixed box | Always-on, remote | Credential surface on rented disk |

## Option A: the Grok Bot box as a headless node

The existing hosted shared Linux box provided with Grok Bot is a possible
remote worker, subject to qualification before any pilot.

- **Security boundary.** The vendor operates the host, and all of Mason's
  Grok Bot agents share that machine. Codex and Claude CLI sessions signed
  in there are usable by every agent on the box. Device-bound sign-in does
  not isolate one agent from another or remove vendor access. Mason must
  approve that exposure before signing in through each CLI's native flow.
  Never copy auth directories from the Mac. A fresh `~/.ashlr` home,
  worktrees and environment stripping are required hygiene, not proof of
  credential isolation from other agents or the host operator. The box
  needs its own PAUSE and KILL sentinels and a tested remote stop path.
- **Cost.** No new spending is authorized. Reuse is conditional on verified
  existing plan coverage, included usage and compute limits, with on-demand
  billing disabled. Remaining allowance, CPU, RAM and concurrent usage by
  other agents are unverified; hold admission until checked. Signing in on
  another host does not establish an additional account allowance. See the
  [Grok Bot companion's billing boundary](GROK-BOT-COMPANION.md#allowance-resets-and-billing).
- **Capacity.** One shared machine, contending with every agent on it.
  There is no measured throughput increase or qualified worker ceiling.
  Current engineer rules keep heavy builds and full suites on the Mac
  pools. This decision does not change those rules. Mason must explicitly
  approve any later routing change after capacity and isolation evidence;
  a pilot here is limited to approved lightweight work.
- **Latency.** Dispatch and result delivery cross a remote network boundary.
  Process spawn on the box is only part of the latency; transport and repo
  access must be measured. Existing authenticated access is a prerequisite,
  not an assumption that the box shares the Mac's LAN or credentials.
- **Failure modes.** Provider or network outage, shared-agent resource
  contention, host restart, disk exhaustion and cross-agent credential use.
  Lost transport leaves claims for reconciliation on the Mac; it must not
  trigger duplicate dispatch. Expired subscription sessions hold launches
  until Mason restores sign-in. Provider maintenance and host custody are
  outside the Mac's control.

## Option B: Cursor cloud agents as burst capacity

Cursor's hosted cloud agents, used as overflow when local pools saturate.

- **Security boundary.** A separate trust domain, same shape as the existing
  cloud lanes. Task text and repository access move to the vendor's
  infrastructure; the agent works from GitHub and returns a branch or pull
  request. That delivery is untrusted input until the standing merge gates
  and Needs-you triage evaluate it; a cloud PR is a proposal, never a merge.
  No local credential, token or auth directory crosses to the vendor.
- **Cost.** Usage-based, not free. Cloud agents exist on the Premium tier
  ($30 per month) and above, and bill at the selected model's API rate:
  draws on the plan's included usage pool first, then on-demand prepaid
  credit. A spend limit is configured at first use. Third-party models bill
  separately at API list price. Burst is cheap to start if the plan is
  already paid for; the marginal cost of real work is real API spend.
- **Capacity.** Elastic and the widest burst of any option: many agents in
  parallel, each in its own environment, bounded by the spend limit and plan
  rather than by local hardware.
- **Latency.** Minutes per task for environment provisioning and clone.
  Wrong for latency-sensitive serial dispatch; right for absorbing a sudden
  queue spike.
- **Failure modes.** The included pool or spend limit running out mid-burst
  quietly changes the marginal cost of the next job. Sessions time out. A
  session that never opens a PR leaves an expired task, not a delivery.
  There is no mid-session readback comparable to a local worker's
  transcript, so the delivery contract is the only evidence channel.
  Provider outage or model changes are outside local control.

## Option C: Devin and Codex cloud sessions as remote pools

The lanes Phantom already operates, modeled as driver pools with their own
floors and ceilings.

- **Security boundary.** Already answered, which is this option's strongest
  property. Devin runs on a `cog_` key held in the macOS Keychain behind an
  ACU ledger, and Devin PRs merge only at a stage that names Devin with
  judges from two different model families ([DEVIN.md](DEVIN.md)). Codex
  cloud tasks run under the account's own product limits and likewise
  deliver through pull requests. Every delivery lands behind the standing
  gates; nothing in this option changes the merge boundary. Devin's training
  opt-out and per-repository GitHub integration are the two decisions that
  matter before private code goes to it.
- **Cost.** Metered on both sides. Devin bills in ACUs against the
  configured ledger (default estimate $2.25 per ACU, per-session cap 10,
  per-day 30, reserve 10; the ledger is a local estimate, not a provider
  balance). Codex cloud draws on the ChatGPT plan's own included limits.
  Neither is free burst.
- **Capacity.** Elastic within plan caps. Devin's defaults cap concurrency
  at 2 sessions, fleet launches at 1 at a time and 3 a day; Codex follows
  its account limits. Giving each lane its own pool ceiling lets the driver
  mix local and remote work without one starving the other.
- **Latency.** Minutes to provision, asynchronous delivery by pull request.
  Remote pools suit parallel backlog work; they are the wrong shape for the
  serial supervisor tick itself, which stays local.
- **Failure modes.** Budget gates refuse launches (paused, reserve, per-day
  or concurrency caps). A lost create response holds the session's whole
  ACU cap until settlement evidence arrives (the uncertain-create rule in
  [DEVIN.md](DEVIN.md)). A refused key, a missing GitHub integration or a
  session blocked on a human all leave tracked, named failure states. A PR
  that never opens leaves an expired task (12 hours for Devin), not a
  delivery. These modes are already implemented and tested in the lanes,
  which is more than any new remote path can claim.

## Option D: a small paid VM

A rented always-on Linux box running workers headlessly. Cost is listed
here; nothing is provisioned.

- **Cost.** A Hetzner-class shared-vCPU VM (2 vCPU, 4 GB RAM, 40 GB disk)
  lists at about 4.5 euros per month before tax; a build-comfortable 8 GB
  class runs about 9 euros to 15 dollars per month depending on provider.
  Recurring spend is owner-reserved under AGENTS.md, so this option needs
  Mason's explicit approval before anything is created.
- **Security boundary.** Like option A, this is provider-hosted hardware.
  A separately administered VM could reduce co-agent sharing, but that
  isolation would need verification. The same device-bound rule
  applies, so Mason would sign in natively on the VM, which puts live Codex
  and Claude session material on hardware inside a provider's physical and
  hypervisor control. Add SSH attack surface, disk persistence on rented
  storage, an ongoing patching burden, and a real gap in today's auth model:
  Devin's key lives in the macOS Keychain only, and `phantom exec` needs
  Phantom Secrets installed and initialized on the VM. Neither hosted
  option inherits the Mac's physical custody; relative capacity is unverified.
- **Capacity.** Small and fixed. 4 GB is tight for typecheck-and-test-class
  heavy steps, so the memory-admission model would queue most parallel work;
  resizing upward costs more. Roughly one modest worker's worth of steady
  capacity.
- **Latency.** Remote like the Grok Bot box: every dispatch crosses the
  network. The queue stays on the Mac; a partition pauses admission and
  requires reconciliation before retry. Moving queue custody is outside
  this decision.
- **Failure modes.** Provider outage or billing suspension; SSH
  misconfiguration or lockout; unpatched vulnerabilities; OOM on heavy
  steps; snapshot and image drift; credentials persisting on rented disk;
  and the quiet one, a forgotten VM that keeps billing.

## Recommendation

Keep the Mac as the local execution, heavy-build and full-suite host, with
sole queue and publish custody. Prefer qualifying the existing Grok Bot box
(option A) for approved lightweight remote work before buying another VM.
This is conditional reuse, not permission to sign in or launch workers:
the hosted shared credential boundary and plan coverage must first be
accepted by Mason. Option A avoids a new VM bill if existing coverage is
verified; it has no owned-hardware security advantage over option D, and
sharing it with all Bot agents adds exposure. A separate VM might offer
better isolation, but its extra bill is not approved. Defer option D.

Keep Devin and Codex cloud sessions within their existing gated budgets
(option C), and Cursor manual-only (option B, no adapter exists). No new
spending, on-demand billing, tokens or paid resources are authorized by
this decision. If qualification fails, keep execution on the Mac and within
already authorized remote lanes; do not purchase replacement capacity.

## What Mason must do

1. Before any box pilot, verify existing plan coverage and limits with
   on-demand billing disabled, and decide whether every agent on the hosted
   shared Linux box may access the proposed CLI sessions. Only after Mason
   approves that exposure may he sign in to Codex and Claude there himself,
   through each CLI's own login flow. Never copy `~/.codex`, `~/.claude` or
   any other auth directory from the Mac or anywhere else.
2. Install Node 22.15 or later and Phantom on the box (published package or
   source checkout) and let it create a fresh `~/.ashlr` home; do not clone
   the Mac's `~/.ashlr`.
3. Sign in `gh` on the box under his own GitHub account so workers can fetch
   and push their branches.
4. Qualify an authenticated channel to the Mac's bridge using existing
   authorized access, such as SSH if already available; create no new
   tokens. The `phm-drive/v1` bridge is a local subprocess contract, not a
   remote transport. The Mac remains the sole `queue.v1` claim and custody
   authority; the box must not create an independent production queue.
   Do not share `~/.ashlr-runs/queue/` over a network filesystem. Without a
   qualified channel, hold the box pilot.
5. Give the box its own memory-admission state directory and its own PAUSE
   and KILL sentinels; confirm PAUSE prevents launches and KILL stops an
   active synthetic worker through the remote control path before trusting it.
6. Rehearse before cutover: `phm drive --once --dry-run` on the box against
   synthetic queue state, then an approved lightweight one-pool pilot.
   Keep heavy builds and full suites on the Mac pools. The pilot and
   dispatchd must share the Mac's atomic claim authority; otherwise stop
   or isolate dispatchd from pilot jobs before admission. Keep dispatchd
   available for rollback after pilot claims are reconciled.
7. Keep Devin's ACU budget and any future Codex cloud pool ceilings where
   they are today; set a Cursor spend limit before treating cloud agents as
   burst, and do not build the paid VM without a separate decision.

<a id="ashlr-universe--north-star"></a>

# Phantom — North Star

> Build for a factory whose models become ten times more capable. The objective
> should become more ambitious without replacing the factory.

> **Aspirational design context — not current runtime activation guidance.**
> This document defines the target state. The local Universe experiment kernel
> executes and measures bounded code experiments; it is not a resident engineering
> firm. Current compiled daemon and conductor trust roots remain empty.

## Vision

**Build Phantom into an agent-native operating system for engineers and builders: a self-improving engineering fleet optimizing verified engineering yield—useful accepted changes per token and hour.**

Give it an idea, a starting portfolio, resources, and the scope of work it may
undertake. It should discover worthwhile opportunities, design experiments,
build competing approaches, test real artifacts, judge outcomes, and invest its
next unit of effort using what it learned. Its product vision can evolve from
evidence rather than freezing into a backlog of the first ideas it generated.

The ambition is continuous invention, not only code maintenance. The fleet should
challenge its own plans, discover better features and methods, and carry useful
work through integration and operation. It should improve its harnesses and
coordination through the same evidence-led process it applies to products.

Phantom unifies the interactive workbench, execution and observation kernel,
and autonomous fleet: continuing search, resource allocation, and organizational
learning across connected resources. Universe remains the name of the existing
experiment runtime and its compatibility interfaces. Subscription capacity,
cloud models, and local compute are resources to allocate according to
measured usefulness and provider limits. More tokens spent is not itself progress.
Preserve operator reserves and compare outcomes before spending more; idle
capacity is useful only when the next task can produce value.

## Three pillars (in order of ambition)

1. **Recursive self-improvement.** Experiment on harnesses, tools, memory, model selection, and coordination using independent, comparable evidence.
   Keep diverse useful variants and retain their ancestry. A candidate may improve
   the evaluator, but cannot rewrite the acceptance evidence used to select itself.

2. **Ecosystem product factory.** Turn real engineering work into useful, tested, shipped products with users.
   Ideation, implementation, integration, operation, and learning belong in the
   same loop. Evaluate product outcomes, not only code quantity or benchmark wins.

3. **The composition platform.** Independently valuable projects become stronger through shared interfaces and evidence.
   Phantom, Cortex, Phantom Secrets, Locus, Lexicon, Plugin, Stack, and Core
   Efficiency compose through their existing repositories and compatible
   interfaces. The desktop console and physical agent board are views and
   controls for the same system, not separate sources of truth.

## The engineer

Sets intent and delegates scope and resources. Routine decisions and effectiveness
assessment should run automatically from observable evidence. Bring the engineer
decisions that require new direction or authority, not every implementation step.
An operator can inspect, interrupt, redirect, and reproduce the system's work.
Autonomy should expand through demonstrated reliability and delegated scope,
without making the human approve every routine step or treating an agent's
confidence as independent proof of success.

## How we measure "grand" (not vanity)

- **Verified engineering yield:** useful accepted changes per measured token and hour.
- **Products shipped + adopted:** real features, releases, reliability, and users.
- **Capabilities invented:** useful net-new functionality, not just maintenance.
- **Compounding capability:** compare current and prior systems on the same tasks.
- **Measurement integrity:** unknown tokens remain unknown; local test scores are
  not customer acceptance, revenue, or deployment proof. Preserve raw dimensions.

## Near-term ambitious bets (vs internal plumbing)

- Run competing implementations, retain per-niche winners, and use them as the next generation's parents.
- Connect measured experiments to a real ecosystem product's local acceptance suite.
- Allocate frontier and local model work using observed quality and resource use.
- Learn from accepted and rejected changes, operational behavior, and user feedback.

## From parallel agents to an integrated engineering loop

The target is an objective-to-candidate loop, not a larger collection of agents:
an approved objective, explicitly enrolled repositories and a resource envelope
produce independently verified improvements on retained local candidate branches.
The engineer can delegate routine decomposition, implementation, testing and
effectiveness assessment within that envelope. New product direction and new
external authority remain explicit decisions.

Model roles are configurable starting hypotheses, not account identities or
guarantees of capability:

| Role | Selection guidance | Evidence required from the role |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Design and challenge | A capable planner selected by task fit, available allowance, quality and latency | Alternatives, a dependency graph, scoped interfaces, acceptance criteria and reasons to reject the plan. |
| Integrate and implement | Tool-capable workers selected by task fit and measured outcomes | Composable changes and a freshly tested combined candidate, not only independently passing branches. |
| Implementation and test repair | Eligible local, efficient or frontier models selected by task complexity | Useful changes, reproducible checks, and escalation when the evidence shows another approach is needed. |

Route these roles through enrolled workers; preserve account exclusions, shared
capacity and operator reserves before considering model preference. An account
used by the engineer can remain unavailable to the unattended fleet, including
all aliases of that capacity. Percentage allocation is an admission policy, not
a guarantee that already-running work cannot cross a usage threshold.

### Three implementation milestones

These are planned capabilities, not activation instructions. The current
[portfolio runtime](ASHLR-UNIVERSE.md#coordinate-campaigns-with-a-dependency-graph)
orders campaigns and can require local branch delivery. Explicit integration
handoff can now seed a new downstream experiment. A separate
[checkpointed portfolio controller](ASHLR-UNIVERSE.md#restart-a-checkpointed-portfolio)
preserves campaign dispatch history and one deadline across invocations; it does
not yet schedule integration handoff automatically.

The first milestone now has four executable local primitives:
[checked composition planning](ASHLR-UNIVERSE.md#inspect-a-combined-delivery-plan)
and [fresh combined evaluation](ASHLR-UNIVERSE.md#evaluate-a-pinned-combined-candidate),
followed by [explicit new-branch delivery](ASHLR-UNIVERSE.md#inspect-and-deliver-an-evaluated-combination)
and [downstream experiment registration](ASHLR-UNIVERSE.md#hand-a-combined-commit-to-a-new-experiment).
Evaluation retains the combined artifact and fixed-suite measurements without
rerunning a settled request. Delivery pins that passing outcome and preserves
existing branches. Handoff records the verified source lineage with a new
manifest and fresh comparator, without inheriting scores or starting work.
Automatic branch advancement, portfolio-triggered handoff, and recovery of
partially initialized seeds remain unfinished; existing manifests are not
silently rewritten.

**Later: automatic branch advancement.** This is a planned extension, not enabled
by new-branch delivery. An advancement request must name the expected current
commit and delegated target branch. A changed base requires newly evaluated
combined evidence; prior passing evidence cannot stand in for that check.
Use an atomic compare-and-swap update, retain durable intent and completion,
and reconcile interruption before another update. Preserve unexpected human
changes instead of overwriting them, and keep local advancement separate from
remote push or deployment authority.

1. **Accept the combined product.** Define a one-repository integration contract
   with pinned upstream delivery commits/trees, base revision, permitted paths,
   fixed acceptance suite and target candidate branch. One integration owner
   composes changes in an isolated worktree and tests the combined tree. A new
   dependent manifest pins the accepted result; existing manifests stay immutable.
   Acceptance: both upstream changes are present, jointly failing or conflicting
   changes never advance the candidate ref, changed input evidence is rejected,
   and replay of settled integration does not duplicate work.
2. **Continue reliably across interruption.** Persist invocation identity,
   pending transitions, fenced ownership, next observation time and remaining
   aggregate allowance above existing campaign and resource ledgers. Retry clean
   capacity withholding within the authorized budget; retain uncertain work and
   owner pauses. Acceptance: crash injection before dispatch, after reservation,
   after settlement and during delivery causes no duplicate dispatch or ref
   advancement. Restart preserves budgets; cancellation drains owned work. Start
   with a restartable foreground command before commissioning a resident service.
   The checkpointed campaign DAG is the first implemented slice: recorded
   completions can release dependants, untouched branches can continue on
   restart, and completed calls with a lost controller receipt can be reconciled
   using their unique campaign start/settlement identity and exact history.
   Untouched campaigns can wait for a busy execution lock within that same
   deadline; authoritative ownership precedes durable dispatch intent. Waiting
   never repeats a started attempt or silently refreshes enrollment.
   Planned delivery must already be verified; recovery neither repeats workers
   nor creates missing branches. Legacy, incomplete and mismatched dispatches
   remain held. Separate-process SIGKILL tests cover pre-intent, pre-start and
   post-completion boundaries, including an existing planned delivery. Restart
   can reclaim proven-dead controller writer locks only with empty staging;
   this is not arbitrary mid-publication or machine-reboot recovery.
   Automatic interrupted-session resumption, integration/handoff
   nodes and resident supervision remain separate work; this is not yet an
   end-to-end always-on controller.
3. **Learn the division of labor.** Compare baseline and role-based policies on
   the same enrolled tasks using accepted improvements, rework, elapsed time and
   reported usage with coverage. Keep each repair loop finite and retain consumed
   allowance on escalation. Hold acceptance evidence fixed while evaluating a
   candidate, including a proposed harness change. Unknown usage stays unknown.

Dependency layers and blocker impact are observations, not new scheduling
authority. Keep declared task priority while collecting evidence for later
ranking experiments. Structural descendant counts are neither predicted time
savings nor proof of product value. Reserve enough capacity to finish integration
and independent review of work already started, rather than spending the entire
allowance generating more disconnected changes.

## Wiring

`docs/NORTH-STAR.md` and `docs/ECOSYSTEM-MAP.md` ground strategy and invention.
Prioritize useful outcomes in concrete repositories and decompose work into
shippable milestones. Documentation, release work, tests and maintenance are
valuable when they improve the product or unblock delivery; judge their effect,
not their category. The [Phantom user guide](VERSE.md) describes the workbench;
the [Universe experiment guide](ASHLR-UNIVERSE.md) describes the separate
experiment runtime and its current executable scope. Reuse task playbooks and
recorded strategic lessons for shared engineering guidance across providers.

## Chat-first delivery plan

The [chat-first child jobs](https://github.com/ashlrai/phantom/blob/master/docs/plans/CHAT-FIRST-NORTH-STAR.md)
translate this vision into dependency-ordered assistant work, with acceptance
criteria and a combined journey gate. This is a planning handoff, not runtime
activation or evidence that the planned capabilities have shipped.

# Console Notifications

Every notification the Phantom desktop console bell can raise, what it means,
and which pane it opens.  Id prefixes are listed so agents can distinguish
a warning from noise across the six derivation sources.

The bell icon opens a stacked attention queue.  Notifications are sorted
**worst-first** (critical > high > medium > low > info) and then by age.
They live until acknowledged, retired, or aged out of the recent window.
Multiple notifications with the same id prefix for the same runtime key
are deduplicated — a fresh incident gets a fresh entry, the same one
updates in place.  The notification centre (the full scrollable list)
provides detail; clicking a notification navigates to its target pane.

| # | Id prefix | Severity | When it fires | Opens |
|---|-----------|----------|---------------|-------|
| 1 | `daemon-health-degraded` | high / medium | Daemon source quality is degraded or missing. | Control ▸ Daemon |

| 3 | `proposal-backlog` | high / medium | Pending proposals exceed the age threshold. | Inbox |
| 4 | `readiness-blocked-*` | varies (blocker severity) | Autonomous readiness verdict is blocked. | Control ▸ Fleet |
| 5 | `readiness-unknown` | medium | Autonomous readiness verdict is unknown. | Control ▸ Fleet |
| 6 | `run-failed-*` | high | A run finished with status failed or aborted (recent). | Work ▸ Runs |
| 7 | `run-stalled-*` | medium | A running run has not updated in 3 minutes. | Work ▸ Runs |
| 8 | `security-critical` | critical | One or more critical security findings exist. | Control ▸ Security |
| 9 | `security-high` | high | No critical but high security findings exist. | Control ▸ Security |
| 10 | `budget-over-*` | high | A backend is over its usage limit. | Control ▸ Daemon |
| 11 | `budget-warn-*` | medium | A backend is approaching its usage limit. | Control ▸ Daemon |
| 12 | `fleet-stall` | critical | Fleet has not started or merged for 30 minutes. | Fleet ▸ Lanes |
| 13 | `fleet-switches-on` | high | A HOLD switch file is stopping dispatch. | Fleet ▸ Lanes |
| 14 | `fleet-runs-dir-missing` | critical | Fleet runs directory is missing. | Fleet ▸ Host |
| 15 | `fleet-host-pressure` | critical / high | Disk < 10 GB or memory < 5 % (critical). Otherwise high. | Fleet ▸ Host |
| 16 | `fleet-claude-lane-down` | high | Claude lane state is down / rejected / invalid. | Fleet ▸ Host |
| 17 | `fleet-lane-usage-*` | high | A lane is out of usage (quota / rate limit). | Fleet ▸ Lanes |
| 18 | `fleet-lane-held-*` | medium | A lane is held for a non-usage reason. | Fleet ▸ Lanes |

| 25 | `fleet-release:*` | high | A release PR merged (version bump). | Settings ▸ Updates |
| 26 | `fleet-merge:*` | info | An individual PR merged. | (PR link or Fleet ▸ Merges) |
| 27 | `fleet-merge:rollup:*` | info | More than 5 PRs merged in the last hour. | Fleet ▸ Merges |
| 28 | `update-ready:*` | high | A new update (native or server) is ready to install. | Settings ▸ Updates |
| 29 | `update-held:*` | high | An update is staged but held by policy. | Settings ▸ Updates |
| 30 | `update-failed:*` | critical | Applying an update failed or was refused. | Settings ▸ Updates |
| 31 | `update-applied:*` | info | An update was recently applied (within 24 h). | (Updates row) |

# Managed OpenAI Agents API integration

Verified against official documentation on 2026-09-30. This document covers the managed **Agents API**, distinct from the Agents SDK and Ashlr's existing Codex CLI/subscription integration.

## What this release implements

The managed API hosts an agent harness with durable sessions, turns, recovery and environment management. Ashlr now exposes a **read-only inventory foundation**:

```sh
ashlr openai-agents sessions --limit 20 --json
ashlr openai-agents inspect <session-id> --json
ashlr openai-agents turns <session-id> --limit 20 --json
ashlr openai-agents sessions --after <nextCursor> --limit 20 --json
```

These commands use host-held `OPENAI_API_KEY` only when a read executes. Configure the variable through your existing secure environment/provider setup; never place keys in command arguments or chat. Help and invalid arguments perform no credential lookup or network request. Missing authentication gives setup guidance without asking for plaintext credentials. No key is stored, sent to an executor, or exposed in output. This release adds no SDK dependency or startup connection probe.

Every call is one GET to `https://api.openai.com/v1/agents/sessions` or an ID-scoped session/turn endpoint, with `OpenAI-Beta: agents=v1`. Redirects are refused. Limits are 1–100 records per page, 2 MiB per response and 15 seconds across headers/body; declared or streamed overflows fail explicitly. `hasMore` and `nextCursor` preserve partial inventory, rather than silently truncating it. Errors are categorical; raw provider response bodies and transport exception messages are withheld. [Session list reference](https://developers.openai.com/api/reference/typescript/resources/beta/subresources/agents/subresources/sessions/methods/list), [session retrieval](https://developers.openai.com/api/reference/typescript/resources/beta/subresources/agents/subresources/sessions/methods/retrieve), [turn list reference](https://developers.openai.com/api/reference/typescript/resources/beta/subresources/agents/subresources/sessions/subresources/turns/methods/list).

Output projects only session ID, creation timestamp, status, agent ID/model and required-action count; turns project IDs, timestamps, status and root/subagent attribution. Instructions, inputs, outputs, tool arguments, environment configuration, files and error messages are excluded. JSON results explicitly contain `readOnly:true` and `executionQualified:false`. Session `idle` does not prove environment readiness; turn `completed` does not prove every tool succeeded or a change was accepted. Usage is not reported by this slice, rather than inventing zero token use. [Session contract](https://developers.openai.com/api/docs/guides/agents-api/sessions), [error and completion semantics](https://developers.openai.com/api/docs/guides/agents-api/errors).

This is not a connected fleet seat, autonomous dispatch, event stream, conversation import or personal Dot controller. It has no create/input/steer/cancel/approve/download operation. Successful inventory access does not qualify a model, environment, account or standing grant for execution.

## Provider contract and access boundaries

The official Python/TypeScript clients expose `beta.agents.sessions`; OpenAI manages orchestration, context compaction and recovery. API inference/tools/container charges are separate from ChatGPT or Codex subscription access. Ashlr's existing `codex exec` lane remains distinct. Existing signed metered-spend limits must not be enlarged to accommodate this integration. [Overview](https://developers.openai.com/api/docs/guides/agents-api/overview), [architecture](https://developers.openai.com/api/docs/guides/agents-api/architecture), [quickstart](https://developers.openai.com/api/docs/guides/agents-api/quickstart).

`gpt-6.1-sol` is an official API model identifier. Its appearance in native account catalogs or these session metadata does not establish permission to create managed sessions with it. Managed-session/model qualification still requires the intended project, API access and an explicitly authorized live test. Supported reasoning efforts must follow the selected model's contract. [GPT-6.1 Sol](https://developers.openai.com/api/docs/models/gpt-6.1-sol), [agent configuration](https://developers.openai.com/api/docs/guides/agents-api/configuration).

Managed sessions currently use US data residency and are not eligible for Zero Data Retention, including sessions with self-hosted execution. A model's broader residency availability does not expand this service contract. [Environment security](https://developers.openai.com/api/docs/guides/agents-api/environments/security).

Personal Dots and workspace-agent controls have separate documented surfaces and qualification requirements. The read-only managed API command does not inherit their identities, subscriptions, conversations or permissions. See [Dots companion integration](DOTS-COMPANION.md) for those contracts and remaining gates.

## Concrete next adapter slice

Ashlr's [src/core/verse/adapters/codex.ts](https://github.com/ashlrai/ashlr-hub/blob/master/src/core/verse/adapters/codex.ts) parses CLI JSONL; [src/core/verse/session-store.ts](https://github.com/ashlrai/ashlr-hub/blob/master/src/core/verse/session-store.ts) stores local chat events; [src/core/run/engine-registry.ts](https://github.com/ashlrai/ashlr-hub/blob/master/src/core/run/engine-registry.ts) registers CLI agents and OpenAI-compatible model endpoints. A managed-session harness cannot be treated as a Chat Completions model endpoint. The new [contracts](https://github.com/ashlrai/ashlr-hub/blob/master/src/core/openai-agents/contracts.ts) and [client](https://github.com/ashlrai/ashlr-hub/blob/master/src/core/openai-agents/client.ts) boundary can support a later explicit managed adapter, but currently exposes metadata reads only.

The next implementation should preserve provider session/turn/item/event identity and root/subagent attribution. Open a stream before sending input. Active-session input can steer a turn; idle input starts a turn. Text deltas append, whereas final text events replace accumulated text. Reconnect by buffering a new stream, reading current state/saved items and restoring pending actions from current `required_actions`; do not replay input or approval merely because transport was lost. Stream closure or idle state is not success. [Session events and reconnect](https://developers.openai.com/api/docs/guides/agents-api/sessions/events).

Before any mutation, add an explicit API account/profile identity, signed repo/model/spend/environment scope, revocation and kill checks, pending-action approval custody, durable outcome reconciliation and deployment gates. The provider error guide does not establish an idempotency contract for ambiguous creates or inputs: do not blindly retry them. Test disconnect-after-acceptance and external-effect reconciliation before fleet admission. [Errors and recovery](https://developers.openai.com/api/docs/guides/agents-api/errors).

Self-hosted execution uses OpenAI's harness with `codex exec-server` in an isolated executor. Keep the application key outside that environment. The documented executor key has restricted environment connection permissions and must share the application's organization/project/principal; this is not a reason to copy personal OAuth credentials or the application key into a sandbox. Egress includes the official API and executor WebSocket control host. A separate host-held broker remains necessary for third-party credentials. [Self-hosted environment contract](https://developers.openai.com/api/docs/guides/agents-api/environments/self-hosted).

Hosted artifacts are immutable published copies associated with completed turns; metadata and downloads are separate. Self-hosted files remain in the selected executor/provider filesystem rather than automatically becoming hosted artifacts. Later downloads require enrolled-repo/path confinement, byte budgets and explicit custody. [Files and artifacts](https://developers.openai.com/api/docs/guides/agents-api/environments/files).

Managed subagents share their session's execution environment/filesystem; enabling them does not provide independent isolation. Keep coordinator/subagent IDs and observed tool outcomes separate. Usage is best-effort, may arrive later and is not an invoice; report nullable coverage and measured matched-task comparisons rather than assumed token savings from persistent sessions. [Multi-agent contract](https://developers.openai.com/api/docs/guides/agents-api/multi-agent), [observability](https://developers.openai.com/api/docs/guides/agents-api/observability).

## Current capabilities to consider for later adapters

Verified against official documentation on 2026-10-02. These are research directions; Ashlr's implemented managed integration remains the read-only inventory above.

Responses native multi-agent is a separate beta surface: the application executes function calls, while OpenAI executes hosted delegation actions. Preserve actual child attribution, item/call IDs and encrypted coordination items for replay; do not execute hosted `multi_agent_call` items as functions. Managed Agents API subagents instead share their environment and inherit MCP tools, but do not support function tools. The Agents SDK runs inside the application rather than providing a managed execution seat. [Responses multi-agent](https://developers.openai.com/api/docs/guides/responses-multi-agent), [managed subagents](https://developers.openai.com/api/docs/guides/agents-api/multi-agent), [SDK](https://developers.openai.com/api/docs/guides/agents/sdk).

Responses WebSocket steering can accept updated requirements, but does not undo effects or cancel tools already started. Outcome generation, Stop and exact provider-contact checks remain necessary. Deferred tool discovery and programmatic tool calling could reduce unnecessary context and combine evidence reads; neither grants authority to write or dispatch. These require explicit transport/tool integration, not just changing a model name. [Steering](https://developers.openai.com/api/docs/guides/steering), [tool search](https://developers.openai.com/api/docs/guides/tools-tool-search), [programmatic calling](https://developers.openai.com/api/docs/guides/tools-programmatic-tool-calling).

Published Workspace Agents have a separate authenticated trigger API: `202` means durably queued, beta polling reports run status, and agent responses cannot currently be retrieved through the API. This does not establish a personal-Dot dispatch API or connected Ashlr seat. Dots' documented task delegation and plugins remain separate product capabilities. [Workspace triggers](https://developers.openai.com/workspace-agents/trigger-runs), [Dots](https://learn.chatgpt.com/docs/dots).

## Acceptance

[Read-only contract tests](https://github.com/ashlrai/ashlr-hub/blob/master/test/openai-agents-read.test.ts) uses injected transports and fake provider contracts. It verifies fixed GET/header/redirect behavior, credential laziness, strict identity/pagination/status/timestamp validation, partial/empty distinction, response and deadline bounds, cancellation, safe errors/key-echo rejection, CLI discovery and refusal of unsupported actions. It makes no provider calls and establishes source behavior only. Real API access, live managed-model qualification, dispatch, recovery, artifacts and resident activation remain separate acceptance steps.

# Operator glance

One typed reading of the fleet serves the phone, Telegram, email, and any
agent that imports it.

- Shape and short text: `src/core/fleet/operator-glance.ts` (`OperatorGlance`, `formatOperatorGlance`)
- Files: `src/core/fleet/operator-glance-read.ts`
- HTTP: `GET /api/verse/fleet/runs/glance`
- Orders: `POST /api/verse/fleet/runs/inbox` with `{ "text": "..." }`, which appends `~/.ashlr-runs/leader/MASON-INBOX.md`

The phone opens on that glance. Telegram and email use the same sentences.
Ask "how's the fleet?" and the reply is a few lines. Any other sentence is an
order. Inbound text is logged. It is never run as a shell command.

Outbound messages are only "Release shipped.", "Needs you.", or "Claude lane
is down. It needs you." Ordinary merges and lane holds stay quiet.

## What Mason supplies

Existing paired devices keep working. Unpaired senders get no data or reply.

| Channel | Where the secret lives | What to do once |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Telegram | `TELEGRAM_BOT_TOKEN` in the environment, or `comms.telegram.botToken` in `~/.ashlr/config.json`. Chat id: `comms.telegram.chatId`. | Run `phm comms pair-telegram` locally to enroll the configured private owner. It exclusively initializes a private random operator secret only when absent, never prints/rotates credentials, and uses the same existing pairing proof. Alternatively, from the configured private user id, send `/pair <code>` using the private `PHANTOM_OPERATOR_SECRET` or operator-secret file below. This pairs the user id in `~/.ashlr-runs/queue/telegram-pair.json`. An existing different-owner record is refused and never replaced by setup. The token is never committed or logged. |
| Email | `PHANTOM_OPERATOR_SECRET` in the environment, or mode `0600` file `~/.ashlr/comms/operator-secret`. 16–128 characters, no spaces. | Keep the existing drop folder and `--from` allowlist. The saved `.eml` must include `Authentication-Results` with `dkim=pass` and `header.d=` for the sender's domain. Put the secret on its own line in the first mail. Later mail from that address can be plain language. The secret is removed before the order is logged. |
| Phone | Existing `~/.ashlr/verse-remote.json` (Cloudflare Access) and the Mac pairing code. | Open `/verse/m`. No new step. |

Without an email secret, only an already paired address with a matching DKIM pass is accepted.
The drop folder must be populated by a trusted mail receiver that strips incoming
Authentication-Results headers and writes its own verification result.
A missing or failed DKIM result is refused either way. An invalid secret refuses mail
rather than weakening the check.

Rate limit: 500 messages per 10 minutes per sender. The reply is "Slow down."
and nothing is written.
