# Peer agent products: real programmatic interfaces

Verified against official provider documentation on **2026-10-26**. This is a
research inventory for the Phase 3 proactive-agent adapters sketched in
[Teams](architecture/teams.md#7-roadmap): what interfaces actually exist for
Grok Bot, OpenAI dots and Meta Muse, what each one authenticates and limits,
and whether Phantom should build an adapter. Only surfaces documented by the
provider count as real; a UI feature, a community report or a plausible
endpoint does not. Where a product has no sanctioned programmatic interface
for the job Phantom would ask of it, this document says so plainly instead of
recommending one.

Companion guides cover the operator workflows: [Grok Bot companion](GROK-BOT-COMPANION.md),
[Dots companion](DOTS-COMPANION.md) and [OpenAI Agents integration](OPENAI-AGENTS-INTEGRATION.md).

## Grok Bot (xAI, distributed with Cursor)

Grok Bot gives each account named Bots that work on one shared persistent
cloud computer. It is distinct from the Grok Build CLI seat and from the
metered xAI API. Access comes with paid Cursor plans, linked SuperGrok or
X Premium+, or a Grok Business seat. Sources:
[overview](https://docs.x.ai/grok-bot/overview) and
[plans and billing](https://cursor.com/help/grok-bot/plans), both checked
2026-10-26.

### Interface: routine webhook trigger (dispatch)

- **Type:** inbound HTTPS POST that starts one named routine run on an existing
  Bot. The routine and its instruction are created by asking the Bot in chat;
  the webhook cannot address an arbitrary Bot or inject a free-standing task.
- **Auth model:** a per-routine secret key shown only in the desktop app's
  routine details. Senders use `Authorization: Bearer <key>` and may attach a
  JSON body, which the Bot receives together with the routine instruction.
- **Limits:** HTTP 200 means Grok Bot accepted the call and started a run; it
  is not completion or a result, and no Bot result-polling API is documented.
  Routines run up to 300 times per hour in total and each routine up to 200
  times per hour; a shared provider-side limit can also fail runs and failures
  are not retried automatically. Each run spends the account's weekly usage
  pool or metered top-up credit.
  [Routines](https://cursor.com/help/grok-bot/routines), checked 2026-10-26.
- **Adapter recommendation: Yes.** A one-way dispatch adapter is sanctioned:
  store the key in Phantom Secrets, POST a bounded JSON body (repo, PR, head
  SHA, scope), record acceptance, and read outcomes in the Bot's chat or run
  history. Do not report a 200 as finished work.

### Interface: routine event triggers (provider-mediated)

- **Type:** schedules plus Slack, GitHub, Linear, Sentry and PagerDuty event
  triggers, and inbound email to the Bot's own `@mail.grokbot.com` address,
  all configured through the Bot conversation rather than a public API.
- **Auth model:** connected-app authorizations on the owning Cursor account;
  email routines default to senders that pass standard email authentication.
- **Limits:** same per-routine and hourly run limits as webhooks; one email
  address per account; routine-sent mail waits as a draft for approval.
  [Agent email](https://cursor.com/help/grok-bot/agent-email), checked
  2026-10-26.
- **Adapter recommendation:** none. These are sanctioned surfaces but they are
  configured inside the product, not callable by Phantom.

### Interface: plugins and MCP (incoming tool surface)

- **Type:** connected apps, Marketplace plugins and account MCP policy admit
  tools the Bot can call during its runs. This is a surface Phantom could
  serve (a scoped evidence MCP server), not a surface Phantom can call to
  drive a Bot.
- **Auth model:** per-app OAuth or plugin credentials held by the Bot's
  account; team MCP policy governs custom servers.
  [Settings and notifications](https://docs.x.ai/grok-bot/settings-and-notifications),
  checked 2026-10-26.
- **Adapter recommendation: Yes**, scoped to the read-only evidence server
  already specified in the [Grok Bot companion](GROK-BOT-COMPANION.md#a-possible-future-phantom-connector).

### Interface: inference hooks (Enterprise governance)

- **Type:** outbound inspection webhook, in beta for Enterprise teams. Cursor
  POSTs each governed model request to the team's HTTPS endpoint and waits
  for an `allow` or `deny` verdict before the model sees it.
- **Auth model:** Standard Webhooks signing (`whsec_` secret;
  `webhook-id`, `webhook-timestamp`, `webhook-signature` HMAC-SHA256 headers),
  plus up to 16 custom headers the endpoint requires. The endpoint must be a
  public `https://` URL on port 443 that never redirects.
- **Limits:** Enterprise teams only and Grok Bot coverage only; verdict bodies
  up to 64 KiB, frames up to 64 MiB, verdict timeout 1 to 10,000 ms (default
  5,000), rollout percentage, shadow mode and a circuit breaker.
  [Inference hooks](https://docs.x.ai/grok-bot/inference-hooks), checked
  2026-10-26.
- **Adapter recommendation: No.** It is a governance inspection feed, not a
  way to assign or collect work, and it requires an Enterprise team Phantom
  does not operate.

### Not found

No official documentation describes an API to create Bots, send them
arbitrary messages, poll run results, or read a personal Bot's remaining
allowance. The Cursor Admin API covers team administration, not per-Bot
dispatch. Tagging `@bot` on X is a sanctioned trigger but regional and not
programmatic. Any two-way Bot integration remains unqualified; see
[Sources and limits](GROK-BOT-COMPANION.md#sources-and-limits).

## OpenAI dots

**What "Dot" actually is.** Official OpenAI sources identify the product
Mason calls a Dot: **your dot** is a personal always-on agent inside ChatGPT,
powered by GPT-6 Astra, with its own cloud computer and browser. It is not a
per-Codex-account product: one dot belongs to the ChatGPT account (Pro,
Business Premium or Enterprise workspace) and can delegate to ChatGPT Work or
Codex, including creating or continuing Codex tasks on one connected personal
computer and running tasks in Codex cloud environments. At launch each
eligible account gets one dot; OpenAI says more dots and per-dot scaling are
planned. Conversations with a dot do not count toward ChatGPT usage limits,
but the Work and Codex tasks it starts count against those products.
Sources: [Meet dots](https://learn.chatgpt.com/docs/dots) and
[Getting started with your dot](https://help.openai.com/en/articles/20001530-getting-started-with-your-dot),
both checked 2026-10-26.

### Personal dot dispatch: no sanctioned interface

No official documentation describes an API to create a dot, send it a
message, subscribe to its events, poll its tasks, or retrieve its output.
The documented surfaces are conversational: ChatGPT apps on mobile, desktop
and web, voice calls, connected Slack and Teams channels, and texting as a
limited US Pro beta. Local task delegation flows through the dot's single
connected computer inside the ChatGPT desktop app, not through a network
API. **No adapter recommendation applies** because no real programmatic
interface for the personal dot exists as of 2026-10-26. The supported
companion workflow stays manual; see [Dots companion](DOTS-COMPANION.md).

### Interface: Workspace Agents trigger API (adjacent, real)

- **Type:** authenticated REST trigger for *published workspace agents*, a
  separate surface from personal dots.
  `POST https://api.chatgpt.com/v1/workspace_agents/{id}/trigger` queues a run
  and returns `202 Accepted` with a `conversation_url`. A beta header
  (`OpenAI-Beta: workspace_agent_runs=v1`) adds an `agent_trigger_run_id`
  (`apirun_…`) that `GET …/runs/{run_id}` polls for status.
- **Auth model:** `Authorization: Bearer <workspace agent access token>`
  provisioned per API channel; an `Idempotency-Key` header makes retries of
  the same trigger event safe.
- **Limits:** agent responses cannot currently be retrieved through the API;
  run status polling is beta; statuses are `queued`, `in_progress`,
  `suspended`, `completed`, `failed`, with `dispatch_failed` or `run_failed`
  error codes; scoped failures return 401, 403, 404 or 409.
  [Trigger workspace agent runs](https://developers.openai.com/workspace-agents/trigger-runs),
  checked 2026-10-26.
- **Adapter recommendation: Yes** for workspace agents that a workspace has
  deliberately published with an API channel. Do not represent it as a
  personal-dot dispatch path or treat `completed` as reviewed evidence; the
  response body still requires reading the linked conversation.

### Interface: ChatGPT plugins and MCP events (incoming tool surface)

- **Type:** the dot and ChatGPT can call connected plugins; an authenticated
  MCP plugin can also expose `events/list`, `events/subscribe` and
  `events/unsubscribe` so ChatGPT receives signed event deliveries on a
  verified HTTPS callback.
- **Auth model:** user OAuth 2.1 authorization code with S256 PKCE for the
  plugin connection; per-delivery signatures on event callbacks. A customer
  API key cannot substitute for the user flow.
- **Limits:** delivery acknowledges receipt, not completed work; a public
  HTTPS endpoint is required for publication, with a Secure MCP Tunnel for
  development. [MCP events](https://developers.openai.com/plugins/build/mcp-events)
  and [plugin authentication](https://developers.openai.com/plugins/build/auth),
  checked 2026-10-26.
- **Adapter recommendation: Yes**, as the inbound evidence and
  `fleet.review_ready` event surface specified in
  [Dots companion](DOTS-COMPANION.md#next-implementation-slice).

## Meta Muse

"Meta Muse" names three different products, and adapters differ per product:
the **Meta Model API** (metered inference), **Muse Code** (terminal and CI
agent) and the **personal Muse agent** (consumer app). Source:
[Meta Model API and Muse Code overview](https://dev.meta.ai/docs/overview),
checked 2026-10-26.

### Interface: Meta Model API (metered inference)

- **Type:** OpenAI- and Anthropic-compatible REST at
  `https://api.meta.ai/v1` with three request formats: Responses
  (`POST /v1/responses`), Chat Completions (`POST /v1/chat/completions`) and
  Messages (`POST /v1/messages`), plus Files, Models and an unauthenticated
  Status endpoint. Models include `muse-wonder-1.0` and
  `muse-spark-1.3`/`1.2`/`1.1` with discounted `-contributor` variants.
  [API reference](https://dev.meta.ai/docs/api-reference), checked 2026-10-26.
- **Auth model:** `Authorization: Bearer` with a `MODEL_API_KEY` created in
  the Model API dashboard; the OpenAI SDK works by changing base URL and key.
- **Limits:** per team, not per key. `muse-spark-1.3`: 3,000 requests/min and
  4M tokens/min; contributor variants: 150 requests/min and 3M tokens/min;
  background response submissions capped at 600/min; 429 responses carry
  `Retry-After`. Pricing is per token ($1.25 input / $4.25 output per 1M for
  Spark Standard, $0.15 cached input), plus per-image, per-hour and per-frame
  pricing for Muse Image, Voice Transcribe and SAM. Contributor mode trades a
  steep discount for permission to train on your content, which is a data
  governance decision, not just a price.
  [Pricing and rate limits](https://dev.meta.ai/docs/pricing-rate-limits),
  checked 2026-10-26.
- **Adapter recommendation: Yes**, and it already exists as the opt-in
  `meta-muse` api-model engine (`muse-spark-1.3`, `MODEL_API_KEY`, off by
  default until added to `foundry.allowedBackends`). It is a model engine,
  not a peer-agent dispatch.

### Interface: Muse Code (agent CLI)

- **Type:** several documented programmatic surfaces:
  - `muse exec` headless runs: one prompt or `--prompt-file`, `--json` for
    JSONL events on stdout, `--session-id` to resume an interrupted run
    non-interactively, `--max-model-steps` to cap work, and `muse export`
    for an auditable run document. Exit codes: 0 turn completed (not proof
    the work is correct), 1 failure or cancellation, 2 usage error, 130/143
    on signals. `--disable-approval` keeps the OS sandbox while skipping
    prompts; `--yolo` removes both and trusts the workspace, so it belongs
    only in disposable containers.
  - Session messaging: named local sessions exchange plain-text messages up
    to 8,192 bytes with steer, queue or notify delivery and per-peer
    approval. Same user account and same macOS or Linux machine only; no
    cross-user or cross-machine transport; headless and `--no-session-log`
    sessions cannot participate.
  - Lifecycle hooks: project, user or managed `hooks.json` binds shell
    commands to events (`PreToolUse`, `PostToolBatch`, `SubagentStop`,
    `SessionEnd` and others). Hook commands run outside the sandbox.
  - MCP servers: stdio or streamable HTTP declared in `mcp_servers`, with
    OAuth 2.1 `muse mcp login` for remote servers; MCP tools are approved
    but not sandboxed.
  - Workflows and subagents: parallel children with optional worktree
    isolation; default execution capacity of 8 agents per tree, configurable
    from 1 through 64.
  Sources: [extending and automating](https://dev.meta.ai/docs/muse-code/extending),
  [session messaging](https://dev.meta.ai/docs/muse-code/session-messaging),
  checked 2026-10-26.
- **Auth model:** `META_API_KEY` (environment or `muse auth set`) for
  non-interactive runs, or browser sign-in for interactive use; Meta Managed
  Accounts must use an API key. Billing is pay-as-you-go per token or a flat
  monthly subscription whose key works only inside the Muse Code CLI.
  [Authentication and billing](https://dev.meta.ai/docs/muse-code/auth),
  checked 2026-10-26.
- **Limits:** subscription plans meter in prompt windows (Everyday Usage:
  10-50 prompts per 5 hours; High 5x, Power 20x with Muse Wonder Full,
  Maximum 80x that base) and default to Contributor mode, which must be
  switched off per machine or per run (`--contributor-mode off`) when sent
  content may not train Meta models. Pay-as-you-go runs follow the Model API
  rate limits above. [Subscriptions](https://dev.meta.ai/docs/muse-code/subscriptions),
  checked 2026-10-26.
- **Adapter recommendation: Yes** for a CLI-seat engine adapter in the style
  of the existing Codex or Claude Code seats: dispatch through `muse exec
  --json`, gate on the task's own checks rather than the exit code, keep
  `--disable-approval` (sandbox on) as the automation posture, and resolve
  `META_API_KEY` through Phantom Secrets rather than config. Session
  messaging is a real interface but local-machine coordination only; treat
  it as an optional peer channel, not remote dispatch.

### Personal Muse agent: no sanctioned interface

Muse (the consumer app and web product at `ai.meta.com/muse`) is a personal
agent with its own Connectors to Meta and third-party apps, reminders,
scheduled tasks, approvals, skills, side chats and file access on a
connected Mac. The Meta Help Center documents connection and approval flows
but no API to dispatch work to a personal Muse, poll its activity or read
its results, and no self-serve Connector SDK: Connectors are provided by
Meta or third parties and authorized in the app's settings, so they are an
incoming tool surface, not a dispatch API. Sources:
[How to get started with Muse](https://www.meta.com/help/artificial-intelligence/1331373868832401/)
and [How Muse works with Connectors](https://www.meta.com/help/artificial-intelligence/1687253048996149/),
checked 2026-10-26. **No adapter recommendation**; a saved proactive-agent
profile records identity only and establishes no transport.

## Summary

| Product | Surface | Type | Auth | Limits | Adapter? |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Grok Bot | Routine webhook | HTTPS POST trigger | Per-routine Bearer key | 200 = started; 300 runs/hr total, 200/hr per routine; no result API | **Yes**, one-way dispatch |
| Grok Bot | Schedule/event/email triggers | Provider-configured | Connected-app grants | Same run limits; drafts wait for approval | No Phantom surface |
| Grok Bot | Plugins and MCP | Incoming tools for the Bot | App OAuth + MCP policy | Team policy scoped | **Yes**, read-only evidence server |
| Grok Bot | Inference hooks (beta) | Outbound verdict webhook | Standard Webhooks HMAC + headers | Enterprise only; 64 KiB verdict; 10 s max timeout | **No** |
| OpenAI | Personal dot | None documented | n/a | ChatGPT surfaces only | None to recommend |
| OpenAI | Workspace Agents trigger | REST trigger + beta status polling | Bearer agent access token + Idempotency-Key | 202 accepted; response retrieval unavailable | **Yes**, published workspace agents only |
| OpenAI | Plugins + MCP events | Incoming tools; signed event delivery | OAuth 2.1 auth code + S256 PKCE | Callback receipt, not completion | **Yes**, scoped evidence plugin |
| Meta | Model API | REST inference (3 protocols) | Bearer `MODEL_API_KEY` | 3,000 RPM / 4M TPM per team; 150 RPM contributor | **Yes**, shipped as `meta-muse` engine |
| Meta | Muse Code | `muse exec` headless, JSONL, sessions, hooks, MCP | `META_API_KEY` or browser sign-in | Subscription prompt windows; contributor training default | **Yes**, CLI-seat adapter |
| Meta | Personal Muse agent | None documented | n/a | Connectors curated by Meta | None to recommend |

## Reading notes and caveats

- Acceptance versus completion matters on every dispatch surface: a 200 or
  202 acknowledges a run started or queued, never that work finished or was
  reviewed. Result evidence still lives in each product's own conversation,
  run history or linked conversation URL.
- Every "Yes" above assumes keys and webhook secrets resolve through Phantom
  Secrets at call time, are never stored in profiles or prompts, and that
  dispatch stays behind Phantom's existing spend and signed-authority gates.
- The three consumer agents (personal dot, personal Muse, individual Grok
  Bots) share the same gap as of 2026-10-26: rich in-product automation,
  thin or absent external control planes. Recheck provider documentation
  before commissioning any adapter beyond the webhook and trigger surfaces
  listed here; this inventory reflects one check date, not a standing claim.

# Personal meter provenance

For an installed Phantom, inspect the personal Codex reading directly:

```sh
phm resources personal
phm resources personal --json
phm resources ledger --json
```

`personal` reads local Codex session evidence from `~/.codex-2` by default,
labels it `codex-personal`, and does not write usage history or contact a
provider. Use `--home <absolute-path>` only when the personal session home is
elsewhere. The path must be a non-root absolute path without `..` or a `.codex`
component; inherited `CODEX_HOME` and `CODEX_HOME_ALT` do not select the home
for this command. `personal` supports `--json`, `--home`, and `--help`/`-h`;
it has no watch option. Its exit code is 0 for a current reading, 1 for stale
or unavailable evidence, and 2 for invalid arguments.

Read **Session** and **Weekly** as separate windows, each with its own used
percentage and reset. For example, a weekly 46% can remain 46% after a small
amount of coding even as the session figure changes; the figures are not
interchangeable. In JSON, compare `resources[].session` with
`resources[].weekly`, including `usedPct` and `resetsAt`. An unavailable window
or unknown reset is unknown, not zero. The personal command has no stored
history for computing burn, so an unknown burn or projection is expected.

Check `resources[].observedAt` and `state` before relying on a reading; a
future timestamp is not trustworthy. The
observation is taken from the rate-limit event timestamp; if no usable event
timestamp is available, the collector falls back to the session file's
modification time. The latter is a weaker time indication. `generatedAt` is
when Phantom constructed the report, not when the provider supplied the
reading. A reading over 24 hours old is `stale`; a missing usable window is
`unavailable`. Even `current` is local evidence, not a guarantee of a newly
refreshed provider sample. A busy lane or recent code activity alone does not
prove that a new quota sample arrived. If the timestamp has not advanced, treat
the displayed percentage as the last observation, not proof of current usage.

The ledger supplies lane and status context. Its `generatedAt` is report time;
its top-level `asOf` is the status tick, and `sources.status` describes source
health, not the age of a provider reading. For `codex-personal`, compare the
ledger's **weekly** value with the personal command's weekly value only. In
JSON, when `source` is `codex-personal-sessions`, the lane's
`observation.asOf` identifies the personal observation; top-level `asOf` still
identifies the status tick. The text ledger shows the source but not this
per-lane observation time, so use JSON for provenance.

The ledger replaces an existing personal lane's status value with a valid
personal weekly sample only when its observation is not in the future and is
strictly newer than the status tick. If the tick is unknown, it uses the sample
only when the status weekly value is also unknown. Equal, older, missing, or
incomparable evidence leaves the status value in place. A missing lane is not
created from session evidence. This ordering does not impose a 24-hour age
limit on the replacement: check the observation time independently, including
when the source says `codex-personal-sessions`. A status value without a usable
tick cannot be ranked by freshness. Missing or degraded sources, unknown values,
and stale observations should remain unknown or historical in an agent's
assessment; do not infer a fresh percentage from lane activity.

`phm resources ledger` also supports `--watch`, optionally with
`--interval-ms <1000..60000>` (default 5000 ms); watch with `--json` emits one
JSON object per line. Watch rereads local evidence; it does not itself ensure a
new provider sample. The ledger CLI reads its default `~/.ashlr-runs` data and
the default personal home. It has no CLI home or runs-directory option and
its reader does not consult `ASHLR_RUNS_DIR`; other commands may implement their
own overrides. A custom `personal --home` reading therefore need not match the
ledger's default personal home.

The ledger's Claude lane is weekly; Claude has no five-hour quota represented
by this ledger. Do not substitute a Codex session window for Claude usage or
infer access to an unreported provider meter. Availability and command options
depend on the installed version; use each command's `--help` if needed.

# Phantom by AshlrAI

Phantom is the engineering agent workbench, formerly Ashlr Verse. AshlrAI, Inc. is the company; [ashlr.ai](https://ashlr.ai) remains the company site.

<a id="formerly-verse"></a>
**Formerly Verse.** The desktop app and web console once called Verse (or Ashlr
Verse) are now Phantom: the Phantom app and the Phantom console. `phm verse` (or
the compatible `ashlr verse`) is the command that opens the Phantom console. The
`/verse/` and `/api/verse/` URLs, `verse_*` MCP tool names and other `verse`
identifiers keep their names for compatibility.

The canonical repository is `ashlrai/phantom`, package `@ashlr/phantom` and
project homepage [phm.dev](https://phm.dev). For the published release,
source-candidate status and installation steps, use the
[first-run guide](QUICKSTART.md#open-verse) and
[desktop installation guide](https://github.com/ashlrai/phantom/blob/master/desktop/README.md#install).
Compatibility releases
through 3.25.3 retain their original `@ashlr/hub` package and release evidence.
Both package profiles expose the same five SDK surfaces in their own namespace;
existing imports are not rewritten. `phm` and compatible `ashlr` share one
workbench launcher. The separate `phantom` command belongs to Phantom Secrets.

The bridge accepts only the original legacy and canonical signed identity
profiles. A repository redirect or new download URL is not evidence of a new
package, signing key or grant. Historical manifests and archives retain their
original bytes. Existing `/verse/` and `/verse/m/` routes, `~/.ashlr` data,
credential services, bundle and launch-agent identifiers remain compatible.
Saved grant scopes are not renamed; new repository authority requires the
normal enrollment and approval flow.

The live website separates [Phantom](https://phm.dev) at the root and
[Phantom Secrets](https://phm.dev/secrets) at `/secrets`. On 2026-10-09,
production deployment `dpl_8TZJwqsgHmvxTd5ckob9y1bywHoZ` was READY, the
`phm.dev` alias resolved to that deployment, and both public routes returned
200 with their distinct product identities. Website source revision
`5c2b3992f94495c150b3a18400f8e553abb8dfec` advertised verified workbench 3.29.5
and Secrets 0.7.9. This operator deployment does not commission Phantom's
automatic website publisher or hosted Secrets services. Use the versioned
workbench release and [first-run guide](QUICKSTART.md#open-verse) for installation.

The native window, menus and About identify Phantom. Published 3.25.1 uses `Phantom.app` and `Phantom_3.25.1_aarch64.dmg`; the historical 3.25.0 release retains `Ashlr.app`. The guarded installer requires prior Stop/drain and a closed, identity-verified app, then coordinates the app/current CLI links with a full rollback archive. It refuses conflicting names or uncertain work. The bundle identifier, signing identity, custody keys, grants, data and launch-agent names are retained. This does not activate automatic updates. Published 3.25.2 supplies the verified signed app/CLI feed. The 3.25.2 updater client later reproduced a startup abort. Published 3.25.3 corrects that constructor and supplies the compatibility bridge; existing 3.25.1 installs need a qualified manual update. Feed publication does not establish installed startup or activate automatic updates or resident authority. No notarization is claimed.

## Mark provenance

The blue ghost mark is reused from the first-party `ashlrai/phantom-secrets` repository, clean source commit `bf4b06edd12bbac772d8b56b6001778bb0f910a6`, file `apps/web/public/favicon.svg`, SHA-256 `8cfd1f86237a521ee43e74394712b489ff0cc2adfe70dcf8ac500056314c4269`. Its MIT license copyright notice is preserved next to the SVG copies. It does not replace provider marks or imply provider endorsement.

The current README and landing-page screenshots come from a compiled Phantom build using explicitly labeled sample accounts. They demonstrate the interface and do not establish provider execution or resident autonomy. Existing screenshot filenames and historical package/URL identities are retained.

## Provider and tool identity marks

The landing illustration identifies resources, not endorsements or active accounts. Claude, OpenAI, Grok and Ollama geometry is reused from the existing `ProviderLogo.tsx` Lobe Icons paths with the MIT notice alongside the new SVG assets. Devin retains the exact first-party vendor favicon already stored in `site/assets/devin-mark.svg`.

Vercel's triangle comes from its official [brand assets](https://vercel.com/geist/brands); Supabase's unchanged green icon comes from its official [brand kit](https://supabase.com/brand-assets.zip). These marks preserve vendor geometry and colors. Colored ghosts, routes and islands are Phantom's presentation, separate from the provider artwork. Vercel and Supabase appear as examples of configured tool connections; this scene does not provision either service.

The landing scene uses local SVGs, CSS and one small script, with no visualization framework or provider calls. Playback is optional, pauses offscreen or in the background, and motion is disabled when the viewer prefers reduced motion. Its resource selector describes connection types and cannot sign in, dispatch work or spend credits.

## Display precision

Usage, credit balances, cost estimates, token counts and performance metrics use two significant figures. Exact readings remain in source data and deliberate inspection metadata. Dates, versions, model names and binary capacity names, input limits, navigation positions, exact chart axes and incomplete-history lower bounds retain their meaning; rounding must not change a quota decision or suggest that a resource has reached an endpoint.

# ashlr-plugin Leverage Maximization Plan

**Date:** 2026-06-29  
**Status:** Research complete, implementation ready  
**Scope:** How to extend ashlr-plugin's token savings from interactive-only to the full autonomous fleet + workbench

---

## Part A: How the Plugin Saves Tokens

### Core compression strategies

**1. snipCompact — head+tail truncation (ashlr__read)**

Returns head (80 lines) + tail (40 lines); replaces middle with a single elision marker showing estimated tokens saved (e.g., `[⋯ 312 lines elided · ~4,820 tokens saved ⋯]`). Token estimate uses `chars/4` heuristic. Threshold: files ≥2 KB.

Savings: 60–90% depending on file size.

**2. AST skeleton (ashlr__read, code files ≥6 KB)**

Extracts function/class signatures, type declarations, docstrings — never the bodies. Returns signatures-only "skeleton" of the file. Falls back to snipCompact on parse failure. Confidence badge attached: `high` (snipCompact), `medium` (AST), `low` (LLM summary).

Savings: 75–95%.

**3. LLM summarization (ashlr__read, files ≥16 KB)**

Calls Haiku as summarizer; attaches summary + confidence badge. Most aggressive compression.

Savings: 85–95%.

**4. Genome-aware grep (ashlr__grep)**

With `.ashlrcode/genome/` present: inverted-index lookup over pre-summarized knowledge sections + embedding similarity (cosine threshold 0.68). Returns best-K matches, not raw ripgrep output. Without genome: falls back to ripgrep + result truncation. Genome index cached at `~/.ashlr/genome-index-<repoSha>.cache`.

Savings: ~80%.

**5. Diff-format edits (ashlr__edit, ashlr__multi_edit)**

Returns only a summary + diff after edit, not the full file. Threshold: files ≥2 KB, combined edit ≥80 chars. AST-structural operations (rename, extract-function) available for TypeScript/JavaScript.

Savings: 80–95%.

**6. Hook intercept (PreToolUse/PostToolUse)**

Hooks intercept native Read/Grep/Edit/Write calls. In `redirect` mode (default v1.18+): blocks native call, returns explanation + ashlr equivalent. In `nudge` mode: soft suggestion via `additionalContext`. Throttled ≤1 nudge/60 sec. Guards: in-cwd files only, not plugin tree.

**7. Savings tracking**

`recordSaving(rawBytes, outputBytes, toolName)` in `servers/_stats.ts:L44–90`. Atomic JSON write (tempfile → fsync → rename) with lockfile + mutex. Keyed by `CLAUDE_SESSION_ID`. `ashlr__savings` renders session + lifetime totals with per-tool breakdown, 7-day sparkline, dollar estimate.

**Headline cross-repo average: −57% tokens on instrumented calls.**

---

## Part B: Where It's Leveraged vs. NOT (The Gaps)

### Where it WORKS today

| Context | Status | How |
|---------|--------|-----|
| Mason's interactive Claude Code sessions | ✅ Full | MCP registered in `~/.claude/settings.json`, hooks active |
| Orchestrator (ashlr-hub CLI, the hub process itself) | ✅ Partial | Hub process inherits Mason's MCP env; `mcp-native-engineer.ts` sees ashlr__ tools |
| ashlr__savings display | ✅ Working | `servers/savings-server.ts` reads `~/.ashlr/stats.json` |

### WHERE IT'S NOT — The Critical Gaps

**Gap 1 (biggest): Fleet sandboxed engine invocations — NO MCP**

Every autonomous fleet run spawns `claude -p "<goal>" --model <M> --output-format json --dangerously-skip-permissions --add-dir <cwd>`. No `--mcp-config` flag, no `MCP_CONFIG` env var, no `.mcp.json` written to the engine's working directory.

The engines discover MCP servers from the real `~/.claude/settings.json` (preserved HOME is passed via `buildContainedEnv()`), so IF ashlr-plugin is registered there at the user level it IS inherited. But there is no explicit wiring — it's purely accidental, not guaranteed, and not measured.

Key files:
- `src/core/run/engine-registry.ts:63–66` — claude argv spec (no `--mcp-config`)
- `src/core/run/sandboxed-engine.ts:259–298` — `buildContainedEnv()` + `withToolEnv()`
- `src/core/env-bridge.ts` — `buildToolEnv()` (no MCP vars)

**Gap 2: Fleet token compression is unmeasured**

Even when a fleet engine does use ashlr__ tools (via inherited `~/.claude/settings.json`), `recordSaving()` writes to `~/.ashlr/stats.json` under the session key `CLAUDE_SESSION_ID`. The fleet spawned process has a different session ID than Mason's interactive session. The savings are counted but siloed — they don't roll up to the lifetime counter Mason sees.

**Gap 3: Fleet's own tool usage is uncompressed**

The fleet orchestrator makes its own file reads to build engine prompts (inject context, read worktree state, build M154 context). These happen in the hub process, not via the MCP layer. They use native TS `fs.readFileSync` / direct reads — no snipCompact, no compression.

**Gap 4: Workbench engines (OpenHands/Goose/Aider) — NO MCP**

Workbench adapter invocations don't pass MCP config. These agents have their own tool ecosystems; ashlr__ compression is entirely absent.

**Gap 5: Fleet cost tracking is inference-only, not compression-aware**

`src/core/observability/forecast.ts:L60–90` computes `localSavingsUsd` = "what local tokens would cost if cloud-priced." This measures routing savings (local vs cloud), not compression savings (raw vs compact). The two are tracked in completely separate systems with no cross-link.

**Gap 6: M246 cache metrics are typed but not instrumented**

`GenAiSpan` has `cacheReadTokens`, `cacheWriteTokens`, `cacheHitRate` fields. They exist in `src/core/types.ts:2177–2193` but are not populated in any span emission path (`src/core/swarm/runner.ts:811`, `src/core/run/orchestrator.ts:726`).

---

## Part C: Wiring Plan — Prioritized, Concrete, Non-Destabilizing

### P0 — Guarantee fleet engines inherit ashlr-plugin (1–2 hours)

**What:** Explicitly write a minimal `.mcp.json` into the engine's ephemeral workspace before spawning, so the fleet's claude instances always have ashlr__ tools regardless of the user's global settings.

**Where:** `src/core/run/sandboxed-engine.ts` — in the setup block before `spawnEngine()` is called.

**How:** Before calling `spawnEngine()`, write `<worktree>/.mcp.json`:

```json
{
  "mcpServers": {
    "ashlr": {
      "command": "ashlr-mcp",
      "env": {
        "ASHLR_MCP_HOST": "ashlr-fleet-engine",
        "ASHLR_HOOK_MODE": "redirect",
        "ASHLR_SESSION_LOG": "0"
      }
    }
  }
}
```

Then pass `--mcp-config <worktree>/.mcp.json` in the claude argv (add to `autonomousArgv` in `engine-registry.ts:66`).

**Risk:** LOW. The `.mcp.json` is written to the ephemeral worktree, not the user's real home. The `--mcp-config` flag is standard claude CLI. Clean up the file after engine exit (already handled by worktree teardown).

**Guard:** Check `which ashlr-mcp` exists before writing; skip silently if not installed. This prevents breaking fleet runs in CI/CD where ashlr-plugin is not installed.

**Files to change:**
- `src/core/run/sandboxed-engine.ts` — add `writeMcpConfigIfAvailable(worktreePath)` call
- `src/core/run/engine-registry.ts:66` — add `--mcp-config` to claude's `autonomousArgv`
- `src/core/run/engines.ts` — ensure `--mcp-config` path interpolation is supported

---

### P1 — Fleet savings rollup into ashlr-plugin lifetime counter (2–4 hours)

**What:** Fleet engine runs record savings under their own session IDs. Aggregate those into a `fleet` bucket in `~/.ashlr/stats.json` so `ashlr__savings` shows Mason the full picture: interactive + fleet.

**Approach A (simpler):** Set `CLAUDE_SESSION_ID=ashlr-fleet-<runId>` in the engine's environment so savings land in the plugin's stats file under nameable keys. Then modify `_savings-render.ts` to display a `fleet` aggregate bucket separate from the interactive session bucket.

**Approach B (more accurate):** After each fleet run completes, have the hub process call `ashlr__savings --annotate-fleet --run-id <runId> --tokens-in <n> --tokens-out <n>` to write a fleet annotation directly. This avoids cross-session session-ID collisions.

Recommend Approach A first (minimal change, reversible).

**Files to change:**
- `src/core/run/sandboxed-engine.ts:259–298` — add `CLAUDE_SESSION_ID: 'ashlr-fleet-' + runId` to env
- `ashlr-plugin/servers/_savings-render.ts:74–100` — detect `ashlr-fleet-*` session keys, aggregate into fleet bucket

**Risk:** LOW for Approach A. Session IDs are only used as keys in the JSON file; adding fleet-prefixed keys doesn't break existing interactive session display.

---

### P2 — Compress fleet-internal context building (3–5 hours)

**What:** The orchestrator and swarm runner read worktree files to build engine prompts (M154 context injection). These reads use raw `fs` calls. Replace with snipCompact-equivalent logic so prompt-building doesn't balloon token counts before the engine even runs.

**Where:** 
- `src/core/run/orchestrator.ts` — context-building block (search for `readFileSync` or file-read utilities)
- `src/core/fleet/supervisor.ts` — wherever worktree state is read to build task context

**How:** Import and use the same `snipCompact(content, { head: 80, tail: 40 })` utility that ashlr-plugin uses. This utility should be extractable from `ashlr-plugin/servers/_snip.ts` into a shared package or inlined.

**Alternative:** Add an `ashlr__read` MCP call from the hub process itself during context-building. The hub already has MCP access (it runs in Mason's interactive session context).

**Risk:** MEDIUM. Context truncation could cause engines to miss relevant code sections. Mitigate by: (a) only applying to files ≥4 KB, (b) preserving a larger head (160 lines) for context injection vs the standard 80, (c) A/B testing on a subset of fleet runs first.

**Files to change:**
- `src/core/run/orchestrator.ts` — wrap file reads with snipCompact
- `src/core/fleet/supervisor.ts` — same
- Optionally: extract `snipCompact` into `src/core/utils/snip-compact.ts` (copy from plugin, keep in sync)

---

### P3 — Wire M246 cache metrics in span emission (1–2 hours)

**What:** Populate `cacheReadTokens`, `cacheWriteTokens`, `cacheHitRate` in GenAiSpan emission. These fields exist but are never set.

**Where:**
- `src/core/swarm/runner.ts:811–847` — span emit
- `src/core/run/orchestrator.ts:726–763` — span emit

**How:** The claude CLI's `--output-format json` response includes `usage` with `cache_read_input_tokens` and `cache_creation_input_tokens`. Parse these from the engine's JSON output and populate the span before emitting.

**Files to change:**
- `src/core/run/engines.ts` — parse `usage.cache_*` from claude JSON output
- `src/core/swarm/runner.ts:811` — set `span.cacheReadTokens`, `span.cacheWriteTokens`
- `src/core/run/orchestrator.ts:726` — same

**Risk:** LOW. Additive only — fields go from undefined to populated. No behavioral change.

---

### P4 — Unified savings dashboard in Pulse (4–8 hours)

**What:** Surface both compression savings (ashlr-plugin) and routing savings (fleet local-tier) in a single "Savings" tab in the Pulse dashboard.

**Data sources:**
- Compression: `~/.ashlr/stats.json` (ashlr-plugin, `lifetime.tokensSaved`)
- Routing: `src/core/observability/forecast.ts` `buildForecast()` → `localSavingsUsd`
- Cache: GenAiSpan `cacheReadTokens` after P3 above

**How:**
1. Add a `getSavingsSummary()` function in `src/core/observability/savings-summary.ts` that reads both sources and returns a unified `SavingsSummary` type.
2. Add a `/map` tab sub-panel or a `/savings` route to the Pulse dashboard (`src/cli/dashboard.ts:225`).
3. Display: interactive compression savings + fleet routing savings + cache hit savings as three separate bars with a combined total.

**Files to change:**
- New: `src/core/observability/savings-summary.ts`
- `src/cli/dashboard.ts` — add savings panel
- `docs/PULSE-BRIDGE.md` — document the new data source

**Risk:** LOW. Read-only data aggregation. No changes to save paths.

---

### P5 — Per-run token budget enforcement (future, 1–2 days)

**What:** Give each fleet run an explicit token budget. Abort or downgrade engine if budget exceeded.

**Where:**
- `src/core/fleet/quota.ts` currently tracks dispatch counts. Extend to track `tokensUsed` per repo per day.
- `src/core/governance/trust.ts` — tier-based budget: local tier gets higher budget, cloud tier lower.

**How:**
1. After each run, write `tokensIn + tokensOut` to quota ledger keyed by `(repoId, day)`.
2. Before dispatching, check `quotaLedger.tokensBudgetRemaining(repoId)`.
3. If over budget: skip or downgrade to haiku.

**Risk:** MEDIUM. Changes dispatch behavior. Requires careful calibration to avoid starving legitimate work. Gate behind `cfg.governance.tokenBudgetEnabled: false` default.

---

## Part D: Making Savings Measurable + Meaningful

### What to instrument now (cheap, high signal)

1. **Fleet session ID prefix** (P1 above): Lets you immediately see "fleet contributed X tokens saved this month" in `ashlr__savings`.

2. **Cache hit rate in spans** (P3 above): Reveals how much Anthropic prompt caching is helping fleet runs. This is free money — cache hits cost 10% of normal input tokens.

3. **Per-run token log**: After each fleet engine exits, log `{ runId, goal_hash, tokensIn, tokensOut, cacheHits, model, durationMs }` to `~/.ashlr/fleet-runs.jsonl`. This is ~200 bytes per run, negligible storage. Enables retroactive analysis.

### What the "187M lifetime" number means + how to grow it

The 187M figure is `lifetime.tokensSaved` in `~/.ashlr/stats.json` — the accumulated delta between raw file sizes and snipCompact output sizes across all interactive sessions. It's a compression-layer metric, not an inference-layer metric.

To grow it:
- P0 (fleet MCP wiring) directly adds fleet engine reads to this counter
- P1 (fleet session rollup) makes fleet contributions visible in the display
- P2 (context compression) adds pre-prompt compression to the counter

Expected impact of P0+P1+P2: If the fleet runs 50+ engine calls/day and each reads 5–10 files, fleet compression could add 2–5M tokens/day to the counter, potentially 10× the current interactive session rate.

### Dashboard metric targets (after all phases)

| Metric | Source | Target |
|--------|--------|--------|
| Interactive compression savings | `~/.ashlr/stats.json` session bucket | Existing display, unchanged |
| Fleet compression savings | `~/.ashlr/stats.json` fleet-* buckets | P1: add to `ashlr__savings` display |
| Fleet routing savings (local vs cloud) | `forecast.ts localSavingsUsd` | P4: Pulse dashboard panel |
| Cache hit savings | GenAiSpan `cacheReadTokens` | P3+P4: Pulse dashboard panel |
| Per-run token log | `~/.ashlr/fleet-runs.jsonl` | P1 side effect: retroactive analysis |
| Fleet token budget remaining | `quota.ts` extension | P5: dispatch governance |

---

## Risk Summary

| Change | Risk Level | Why Safe |
|--------|------------|----------|
| P0: Write `.mcp.json` to worktree | LOW | Ephemeral path, guarded by `which ashlr-mcp` |
| P0: Add `--mcp-config` to claude argv | LOW | Standard flag, no behavioral change if file missing |
| P1: Fleet session ID prefix | LOW | Additive key in JSON stats file |
| P1: Render fleet bucket in savings display | LOW | Read-only aggregation, existing display unchanged |
| P2: snipCompact in context building | MEDIUM | Gate behind file-size threshold; test on subset first |
| P3: Populate cache span fields | LOW | Additive only |
| P4: Savings dashboard panel | LOW | Read-only data aggregation |
| P5: Token budget enforcement | MEDIUM | Default-off; requires calibration |

**DO NOT touch:**
- `ashlr-plugin/servers/_stats.ts` — session-critical, atomic writes, any race condition breaks the counter
- `ashlr-plugin/hooks/pretooluse-edit.ts` — live MCP hook, changes affect every interactive session immediately
- `ashlr-plugin/servers/_router.ts` — MCP server entry point; restart required for any change

---

## Implementation Sequence

```
Week 1 (fast wins, zero risk):
  P0 → P3 → P1  (fleet MCP wiring, cache metrics, session rollup)

Week 2 (medium effort, measurable impact):
  P2 (context compression, gated)
  P4 (unified savings dashboard)

Week 3+ (governance layer):
  P5 (token budgets, default-off)
```

P0+P1 alone transforms the fleet from "MCP-invisible" to "MCP-measured" — that's the highest leverage change in this plan.

# Phantom plugins — authoring guide + trust model

Phantom can be extended with plugins that contribute **backlog scanners**,
**project templates**, **model providers**, and **CLI commands** — without
forking Phantom. Commands are shown as `ashlr …`; `phm` runs the same CLI.

## The trust model (read this first)

**Honesty over theater:** an enabled plugin is in-process Node ESM. Once
loaded it runs with the same OS privileges as ashlr itself. ashlr does **not**
claim an OS-level sandbox. The safety posture is *gating + least-privilege
API + tamper evidence + auditability*, not containment:

1. **Default-deny.** `plugins.enabled` defaults to `[]`. Discovery
   (`ashlr plugins list`, `ashlr plugins info <name>`) reads `manifest.json` files only — **no plugin code
   executes** until you have explicitly enabled the name.
2. **Explicit, informed enablement.** `ashlr plugins enable <name>` shows the
   declared capabilities and a trust warning, requires confirmation, and pins
   the entry file's sha256 into your config.
3. **Tamper evidence.** Any later change to the entry file refuses to load
   (integrity mismatch, audited) until you re-run `enable`.
4. **Capability declarations enforced.** A plugin contributing something it
   did not declare in `manifest.capabilities` has that contribution dropped
   and audited — a "scanner" plugin cannot smuggle in a CLI command.
5. **No secrets in the host API.** Plugins receive a frozen, allowlisted
   config *projection* and their own `plugins.settings.<name>` block — never
   the raw `AshlrConfig`, never environment secrets, never Phantom values.
6. **Safety invariants preserved.** No plugin API path reaches inbox
   approval, `applyProposal`, enrollment writes, or config writes. The
   proposal-only mutation flow is unreachable from plugin code via the host.
7. **Kill switch + escape hatch.** The global kill switch (`~/.ashlr/KILL`)
   zeroes plugin loading; `ASHLR_NO_PLUGINS=1` recovers a session when a
   plugin breaks startup.
8. **Everything audited.** Load, refusal, activation, capability violations,
   and command runs all append to `~/.ashlr/audit/` (see `ashlr audit`).
9. **Failure isolation.** Every plugin interaction is try/caught and
   time-bounded (5s activate, 15s per scanner sweep). A broken plugin
   degrades to "skipped + warned" — builtin behavior never breaks.

**Only enable plugins whose source you have read or whose author you trust.**

## Quick start

```bash
ashlr plugins init my-scanner --capability scanner   # working skeleton, ready to edit
```

`--capability` accepts `scanner` (the default), `template`, `provider` or `command`.

This scaffolds a proven-loadable plugin under `~/.ashlr/plugins/my-scanner/`
(every skeleton is integration-tested in test/m33.plugin-init.test.ts). Or by
hand:

```
~/.ashlr/plugins/my-scanner/
├── manifest.json
└── index.js
```

`manifest.json`:

```json
{
  "name": "my-scanner",
  "version": "0.1.0",
  "apiVersion": "^1.0.0",
  "description": "Finds FIXME(security) markers",
  "entry": "./index.js",
  "capabilities": ["scanner"]
}
```

`index.js` (plain ESM; for typed authoring `npm i -D @ashlr/phantom` and import
from `@ashlr/phantom/plugin`):

```js
export default {
  activate(host) {
    host.log('activated');
    return {
      scanners: [{
        id: 'fixme-security',
        async scan(repo) {
          // read files under `repo`, return WorkItem-shaped objects:
          return [{
            id: 'demo', repo, source: 'plugin',
            title: 'FIXME(security) found', detail: 'src/auth.ts:42',
            value: 4, effort: 2, score: 0, tags: [], ts: new Date().toISOString(),
          }];
        },
      }],
    };
  },
};
```

Then:

```bash
ashlr plugins list             # discovery — reads manifests only
ashlr plugins info my-scanner  # manifest detail for one plugin
ashlr plugins enable my-scanner   # confirm + integrity pin
ashlr backlog refresh          # plugin items appear tagged [plugin]
ashlr plugins disable my-scanner
```

## Host API surface

`activate(host)` receives:

| Field | What it is |
|---|---|
| `host.apiVersion` | Phantom's `PLUGIN_API_VERSION` (currently `1.0.0`) (`manifest.apiVersion` is matched against it) |
| `host.pluginName` | Your manifest name |
| `host.log(msg)` | stderr line prefixed `[plugin:<name>]` |
| `host.audit(action, summary)` | Append to the ashlr audit trail (secret-scrubbed) |
| `host.settings` | Frozen copy of `plugins.settings.<name>` from the user's config |
| `host.view` | Frozen allowlisted config projection (`editor`, `staleDays`) |
| `host.dataDir` | `~/.ashlr/plugin-data/<name>/` — the only sanctioned write location |

## Contribution kinds

- **scanner** — `{ id, scan(repo, { signal }) }` → `WorkItem[]`. Wrapped by
  Phantom: 15s timeout, 100-item cap, value/effort clamped, score recomputed,
  titles/details secret-scrubbed, ids namespaced, `source: 'plugin'` forced.
- **template** — a `ProjectTemplate` for `ashlr new`. Id is prefixed
  `<plugin>:`; file paths must be relative, no `..`, never under `.git/`.
- **provider** — `{ id, tier, envKeys?, probe(), createClient() }`. A
  `tier: 'cloud'` provider sits behind the SAME local-first gates as builtin
  cloud providers (`--allow-cloud` + key present); env values are never read
  by the host — only key *presence* is checked.
- **command** — `{ name, description, run(args, host) }`, invoked as
  `ashlr x <name> [...]`. Cannot shadow builtin commands.

## Versioning

The plugin API is semver'd (`PLUGIN_API_VERSION`). Declare a range in
`manifest.apiVersion` (e.g. `"^1.0.0"`); incompatible plugins are skipped with
a clear reason in `ashlr plugins list`.

## Non-goals (deliberate)

- No OS-level sandboxing of plugin code.
- No plugin marketplace, remote fetch, or auto-update of plugins — you place
  the files under `~/.ashlr/plugins/` yourself.

# Provider-neutral coordination backlog

Phantom should own durable assignments, routing evidence, verification and the
operator notification feed. Users declare accounts, agents, capabilities,
preferences and goals; provider adapters establish what can actually run.
Personal assistant names and observed strengths are configuration, not fixed
product roles or authority. Multiple agents may share a provider or account.

## Product acceptance direction

The north star is a unified self-improving engineering workspace and service,
with Ashlr dogfooding its service delivery toward SaaS and autonomous operations.
**Work with me** and **Work for me** must share task identity, context, resources
and evidence. Users can inspect, interject, approve, take over and return work to
agents. This direction is an aspiration, not evidence of a completed product or
measured autonomous performance.

Acceptance for subsequent milestones:

- Ownership changes preserve criteria, context/artifact revisions, budget,
  attempt history and unresolved effects. Human takeover does not silently
  redispatch potentially active work or reset a deadline.
- Priorities and outcome criteria remain inspectable. Allocation across
  subscriptions, CLI/API/cloud/local resources targets verified value, quality,
  time and cost, with exclusion reasons; tokens and activity are diagnostics.
- Independent evaluations pin inputs, evaluator and policy versions. Learned
  routing changes are explainable and reversible; self-reports and synthetic
  routing tests cannot establish production quality or expand authority.
- Operating windows, spending and escalation stay bounded. Agreement across
  task and resource views includes source, identity, observation time, coverage
  and unknown/stale/conflicting values, rather than replacing unknowns with zero.
- Release autonomy retains exact target/artifact evidence, current authority,
  post-release checks and channel-specific recovery. The
  [release evaluator](../src/core/proactive/release-readiness.ts) is a local
  readiness mechanism, not a publisher or proof of successful rollback.
- Team contributions require membership, resource control and explicit
  project/task/source/destination consent. Matching providers or accounts never
  grants sharing rights.

Current [coordination](../src/core/proactive/coordination.ts),
[packets](../src/core/proactive/packets.ts),
[resource projections](../src/core/proactive/resource-evidence.ts) and
[routing lab](../src/core/proactive/routing-lab.ts) implement local evidence and
manual/offline workflows. They do not establish deployed personal-agent
transport, distributed human membership, credit-funded dispatch, provider API
availability, zero-cash execution qualification or measured live improvement.

## Review basis and milestone boundary

This engineering backlog was reviewed on 2026-10-12 in
`/Users/masonwyatt/Documents/Codex/2026-10-12/task/phantom-coordination`, branch
`codex/provider-neutral-companions-20261012`, based on
`ea5f9ac2e6f66b8cece71b91fd9f663c513599f7` (`@ashlr/phantom` source candidate
3.29.13). The first local coordination slice is preserved in commit `18ed964d9`.
Resource projections, offline routing receipts and release readiness extend that
slice. This document records source findings and implementation requirements;
local verification does not claim publication, installation, commissioning or
acceptance with a real provider. Use the milestone verification reports for
their exact source hashes, checked revisions and results.

The local milestone covers extensible profiles, scoped packets, a durable
companion task ledger, manual reports and independent review, observable holds,
one local notification state, pure resource projections, offline routing
evaluations and a read-only release evaluator. It provides evidence without
provider contact. Funding references, declared capabilities and an enabled
profile do not establish entitlements, a connection, transport qualification or
spending permission. A fixture must be labeled simulated; a manual report must
retain its unverified origin even after an operator accepts its result.

No account credentials, private runtime records or session archives were read
for this backlog. No external agent or provider was contacted, and no service,
release target, installed app or account setting was changed.

## Next implementation sequence

The local planning follow-on adds public-snapshot resource DTOs with separate
usage, native funding units/expiry, entitlement and actual/estimated/unknown
costs. The default API reads saved declarations only; host cached-snapshot
integration remains a separate seam because existing collectors can touch
account configuration or assistant sessions. Credit pools use a neutral funding
category and do not imply API access.

The offline routing lab records deterministic shadow previews and a synthetic
closed-choice benchmark with pinned request/input/snapshot/policy evidence,
fallback reasons and local duration. It has no TypeSafe client, model calls,
production preference writes or dispatch consumer. Preference proposals can be
withdrawn as local records. Simulated results stay outside production priors;
verified live outcomes and account/model cohorts remain future work.

### Local resource-display follow-up

This source candidate includes the bounded resource-display slice for 3.29.15.
A source version is not evidence of publication, installation or live
acceptance. Team collaboration, external transports and funding retain
separate operational acceptance gates.

Operator/source acceptance:

- Keep resource count, current-reading count and configured-reference count
  separate. Connections and declared Bot references do not establish distinct
  provider/human identities or control. The qualified independent-account count
  and complete account denominator remain unknown without genuine source-owned
  identity/equivalence evidence; aliases cannot manufacture independent capacity.
- Native quota retains its original `observedAt` and `quotaExpiresAt`; credits
  retain their own observation and original `creditsExpiresAt`. Connection and
  admission stamps are independent. A failed check, health reply, policy change
  or reread cannot restamp a retained observation.
- Recheck at the exact original expiry/reset boundary and when focus returns.
  Display policy may impose a stricter age limit, never extend source TTL.
  Expiry/focus callbacks reevaluate cached evidence without fetching, admitting
  work or spending. Test delayed timers, focus return and quota/credit expiry
  independently, preserving source timestamps and bytes.
- The resource bar, cards, provider groups and usage view must agree on current
  versus retained evidence. Current credit does not refresh expired quota;
  source-qualified pool grouping does not prove account identity or entitlement.
  Missing or conflicting identity evidence stays unknown and effect flags stay
  false. Synthetic acceptance does not qualify a provider or autonomous dispatch.

### 1. Finish local coordination and an honest operator preview

Keep stable identity `(provider, accountId, agentId)` and immutable identity on
profile updates. Capability IDs describe work the user wants assigned, with
source and qualification represented separately. Show configured, connected,
executable, simulated and blocked states distinctly. Unsupported dispatch,
result, status or cancel must remain visible; a generic provider label cannot
enable a hidden transport.

Assignments bind task identity, tenant/project binding, input packet digest,
assignee, attempt, owner and ownership epoch. Record intent before any future
contact. Expected-revision CAS and command-ID/request-digest replay checks
prevent cooperative duplicate dispatch. A timeout after possible contact stays
unknown and held for reconciliation; an expired local lease does not prove a
remote agent stopped. Late reports remain historical and cannot advance a newer
owner. Result review checks exact report/result digests and acceptance criteria;
requesting cancel and confirming cancel are separate facts.

Build a pure capability-routing preview over these records before adding live
dispatch. It should report which candidates match declared requirements and why
execution is blocked. Feed native pools only through their existing admission
and reservation paths. Scoped shared tools must bind account, task and approved
destination. Recheck authorization at actual contact and publication, not only
when preparing a packet.

Minimum acceptance: two generic profiles on one provider, a second account on
that provider, arbitrary configurable assignments, blocked transport, concurrent
claim winner, exact replay, conflicting replay, restart after intent, ambiguous
timeout, stale-owner report, cancellation request/confirmation, failed review,
cross-tenant denial and one deduplicated local notification. Fixtures prove
these local contracts only. No live adapter acceptance follows from them.

### 2. Qualify one read-only companion integration

Use the [Dots evidence slice](DOTS-COMPANION.md) as the first compatibility
target, but implement an adapter contract independent of any assistant's name.
Commission one exact account/agent, one approved project and read-only evidence
operations first. Store operation-specific qualification references, exact
identity, allowed scopes, timestamps, expiry and revocation. A connection test
does not qualify dispatch, result or cancellation. Each additional account is
commissioned independently.

Proactive intake should append source-owned evidence and propose bounded work.
It cannot expand scope, approve spending or treat inbound text as an operator
instruction. Use source event IDs and revisions to deduplicate and handle
out-of-order updates. Phantom owns the durable notification outbox; selected
delivery adapters do not independently notify the user. Record delivery intent
and uncertain delivery before retrying. Local acknowledgement is not proof of
external delivery.

Acceptance: permission revocation between packet build and contact blocks the
operation; identity or scope drift fails; partial source coverage stays visible;
duplicate events/restarts do not create repeated work or notices. This stage
requires account-owner authentication and scoped sharing approval. Two Dots,
GrokBot and Meta Muse/Ash are compatibility targets, not mandatory lanes or
authorization to contact them. The separate Meta API engine does not connect a
personal Muse agent.

### 3. Join planning to resources, accounting and bounded iteration

Add one outcome-level operating contract containing success criteria and a
pinned evaluator/acceptance version, deadline, attempt/concurrency caps, monetary
ceiling, allowed resources, notification/escalation owner and stop conditions.
Null cost means unknown; zero is an explicit zero-dollar ceiling. Exceeding a
deadline, exhausting attempts, missing required evidence or unresolved remote
contact creates a visible hold. Preserve the original deadline and consumed
budget across restart and successor creation. Escalation proposes a change to
the owner; it never silently increases limits.

Reuse [scheduling metadata](../src/core/routing/scheduling-types.ts) and
[reset-aware admission](RESET-AWARE-SCHEDULING.md). Distinguish provider-reported
usage, tariff-based estimates and unknown cost, with model/rate/source/as-of and
coverage. Subscription percentage is not tokens or dollars. Promotional,
purchased and subscription funding are different pools; cloud credit is not an
API grant. Credit expiry and admission cutoff need provider-owned precision and
identity evidence; unknown balance/expiry cannot authorize promo-only spending.
Connection readiness and a display override cannot establish quota or entitlement.

Jev may choose only from the already eligible closed set using approved
metadata, and the caller rechecks current policy, identity, Stop and reservations
after the asynchronous answer. Missing/slow/low-confidence answers use the
deterministic path. Measure real decision latency, tokens, compatible quality and
end-to-end time to verified outcome separately before claiming savings.

The existing REST transport is
[typesafe-client.ts](../src/core/classify/typesafe-client.ts), wrapped by
[decide.ts](../src/core/decide/decide.ts); adding a second client or SDK is not
needed for coordination. Current request types/defaults allow moving aliases
`jev-latest` and `jev-preview`; a reproducible evaluation needs additive concrete
model configuration, response-model checks and cache identity. Compare the
current Score min/max shape to the official rubric contract before using it for
new evaluations. Choice confidence expresses distribution sharpness, not proof
of correctness; this milestone corrects that documentation and comment wording.
Select thresholds
using task-specific held-out evidence. Keep capacity arithmetic, authorization,
budgets and other closed rules deterministic before asking the model.

Before expanding context formats, provide an explicitly typed representation for
SHA-256 artifact heads: the current generic secret detector refuses bare 64-hex
artifact values. Ordinary SHA-1 Git heads and revision-bound local briefs work.
Before large-scale coordination, add worker isolation and measured read budgets
for snapshot-ledger projection, plus safe archival/retention rather than silently
discarding duplicate/recovery evidence when bounded local storage fills.

Run an offline shadow corpus with pinned questions/model expectations,
option-order permutation, misleading/injected state, low-confidence answers,
out-of-vocabulary responses, maximum-choice overflow, timeout, 429 and 529.
The adapter currently falls back without retries, classifies 429 and 503 with
Retry-After as rate limits, and other failed HTTP responses as errors. Retain
those bounded behavior guarantees. After account authorization, separately
measure live classification errors and latency; provider marketing timings are
not an SLA. Source tariff estimates are date/model-specific, not invoice totals.
Learning from provider outputs must respect the provider's current terms; do
not build competing-model distillation into the self-improvement loop.

Acceptance: unknown readings stay unknown, expired credits block, changed
eligibility defeats cached advice, resumed loops preserve caps, and every
dispatch joins its recorded choice to actual/estimated/unknown accounting.
Qualified usage readers, paid API configuration or new funding access need
separate authorization; pure previews and synthetic accounting tests do not.

### 4. Make self-improvement inspectable and reversible

Record policy version, eligible candidate population, chosen action, task/model/
account cohort, input provenance and verified outcome. Quarantine stale,
simulated, self-reported, cross-tenant or incompatible evidence from production
priors. Explain recommendation changes and retain the prior policy version.
Enable shadow comparison and explicit rollback of routing preferences without
rewriting historical receipts. A measured regression triggers a hold or restores
the approved prior policy; it cannot enlarge allowed backends, tools, scopes,
credentials or release authority. Preserve deterministic safety gates.

Acceptance: a routing experiment is reproducible from pinned inputs, its impact
and exclusions can be inspected, rollback restores the prior approved behavior,
and malformed/missing learning receipts leave ordinary routing available.
Reuse verified outcome/production labels rather than counting task volume as
success. The [efficiency roadmap](EFFICIENCY-ROADMAP.md) separates measured local
changes from hosted and installed performance; use that same evidence standard.
