Source: https://verse.ashlr.ai/docs/grokbot-lane.md

# Grok Bot resource lane

Phantom owns task selection. Grok Bot is reserved for `connector`, `browser`,
`desktop`, `message-mason`, and `approval` tasks. Coding, research, shell execution,
and inference are refused. A kind labels capability, not authority: existing
approval and sandbox rules still govern every action. In particular, an approval
result is an observation for Phantom's existing approval flow, never a grant.

The opt-in adapter is `src/core/resources/grokbot/lane.ts`. It exposes
`GrokbotLane.submit(task)` and `GrokbotLane.readResult(task)` for a future daemon
caller. No daemon hooks or dispatchd files change. Dispatchd stays the fallback
until an independently authorized cutover. No provider call or live routine was
enabled by this change.

## Exact request contract

```json
{
  "schema": "grokbot-task.v1",
  "id": "RQ-CONNECTOR-42",
  "kind": "connector",
  "goal": "Find the requested Gmail thread",
  "inputs": { "connector": "gmail", "thread_id": "thread-42" },
  "budget_cap": 1,
  "reply_to": "/absolute/private/grokbot/replies/RQ-CONNECTOR-42.json",
  "deadline": "2026-10-26T19:00:00.000Z"
}
```

All fields are mandatory and extra fields are refused. `id` is 1 to 96 ASCII
letters, digits, underscores or hyphens, starting with a letter or digit.
`goal` is nonempty and at most 4096 characters. `inputs` is a string map with
lowercase identifier keys and values up to 1024 characters. The full request is
limited to 16 KiB. Use public descriptions and opaque connector object IDs;
connector sessions stay inside Grok Bot. Never include mail contents, credential
files, environment dumps, secrets, tokens, or even `phm_` placeholders. The
validator rejects credential-shaped fields and common token formats, but pattern
matching cannot prove arbitrary prose is secret-free. Callers remain responsible
for supplying only public task metadata.

`budget_cap` is exactly **one routine task**, not dollars or model tokens. It
does not authorize paid connector actions or recursive routine spawning.
`deadline` is canonical UTC ISO time, in the future and no more than 24 hours
away. `reply_to` must equal `<stateRoot>/replies/<id>.json` exactly.

Requests use `POST`, `Content-Type: application/json`, and `Idempotency-Key: <id>`.
Only HTTP **202** means accepted, and acceptance is not task completion. No
redirects or automatic retries are allowed. Request timeout is the lesser of
15 seconds and time remaining to the deadline. HTTP errors, timeouts, process
failures, and uncertain delivery retain their task reservation.

## Secrets transport contract and activation dependency

The adapter always launches:

```text
phantom exec -- <node executable> <installed dist/core/resources/grokbot/worker.js>
```

It supplies the validated task on stdin, never a shell command. Child stdout and
stderr are discarded, and errors contain only fixed reason codes. The child
expects a Secrets-owned `GROKBOT_BASE_URL` of the form
`http://127.0.0.1:<port>/grokbot/_phantom/<session-capability>/`. That URL is used
only for transport and never inserted into the task. No plaintext endpoint or
credential environment fallback exists. Local inference configuration is untouched.

**Required upstream auth header: `Authorization: Bearer <existing routine credential>`.**
Phantom Secrets must own the upstream webhook URL in `GROKBOT_WEBHOOK_URL` and
the existing credential in `GROKBOT_WEBHOOK_AUTH`. Secrets must resolve the URL
and inject this header within its proxy; neither value may enter the child,
payload, logs, argv, or agent context. No new credential is created here.

**Current limitation:** the companion source inspected for this change supports
only exact built-in routes under `phantom exec`, refuses custom routes, and has
no built-in `grokbot` route or vault-backed webhook URL routing. Consequently this
transport contract is a dependency seam, not a claim of live support. The worker
fails closed when the route is unavailable. Do not configure a custom route,
extract the vault value, use `phantom start` as a bypass, or loosen a sandbox to
activate it. Secrets needs a reviewed implementation of this exact route and URL
custody contract before live commissioning. The stub tests qualify the HTTP
contract; they do not qualify the Secrets proxy or a real Masbot routine.

## Grok Ultra ledger seam

Construct `GrokbotLane` with an absolute, owned mode-0700 `stateRoot`, a
`secretsProject` working directory, explicit nonnegative integer `caps.day` and
`caps.week`, and `readBudget(): Promise<unknown>`. The latter is the clean
RQ-BUDGET-LEDGER integration point. The current repository has no named budget
ledger interface; the local dispatchd README was unreadable under macOS access
controls. No compatibility with an uninspected private schema is assumed.

`readBudget` must return this projection of the authoritative `grok-ultra` ledger:

```json
{
  "schema": "grok-ultra-budget.v1",
  "pool": "grok-ultra",
  "observed_at": "2026-10-26T18:00:00.000Z",
  "expires_at": "2026-10-26T18:05:00.000Z",
  "not_before": "2026-10-26T18:00:00.000Z",
  "day": {
    "start": "2026-10-26T00:00:00.000Z",
    "end": "2026-10-27T00:00:00.000Z",
    "cap": 5,
    "used": 1
  },
  "week": {
    "start": "2026-10-26T00:00:00.000Z",
    "end": "2026-11-02T00:00:00.000Z",
    "cap": 20,
    "used": 3
  }
}
```

These numbers are examples, not defaults or spend permission. Windows must
contain the current time and last exactly 24 hours and 7 days. The ledger owns
their stable boundaries. Observation freshness and expiry are capped at five
minutes; future observations, invalid data, missing data, and `not_before` in
the future refuse dispatch. Zero cap disables the lane. For each window,
admission requires ledger `used` plus all local reservations in that window to
be below the smaller of the configured and ledger cap. If the shared ledger
already counts local reservations, this deliberately double-counts them until
the window ends. It cannot increase allowance because of reconciliation lag.
The ledger must coordinate other consumers of the same shared allowance.

All adapter instances on a host must share one state root and cap policy.
Reservations are protected by an exclusive directory lock, written and synced
before transport, then atomically renamed and the directory synced. IDs are
retained to prevent replay, including failed sends. The store refuses admission
at 4096 entries rather than forgetting IDs. Missing initial state starts empty;
do not delete or replace initialized state to reset caps. Corrupt state, symlinks,
future reservation times, and a busy lock fail closed. After a crash, an operator
must establish no writer is alive and reconcile delivery before repairing a
leftover lock or `.next` file. No automatic lock stealing or refunds occur.

## Masbot webhook-triggered routine

1. Authenticate the request using the existing credential in the exact auth
   header above. Reject invalid schemas, kinds, credentials and expired tasks
   before starting any work. Persist the idempotency key before acknowledging
   with 202; repeat IDs must not launch a second run.
2. Run only the requested allowlisted capability with existing connector
   sessions and approval controls. `message-mason` targets Mason only. `approval`
   requests Mason's decision; it cannot grant approval to itself. Stop at the
   deadline and never exceed one routine invocation or fan out into child tasks.
3. Produce a bounded, secret-free result with exactly these fields:

   ```json
   {
     "schema": "grokbot-result.v1",
     "id": "RQ-CONNECTOR-42",
     "status": "succeeded",
     "summary": "Requested thread located"
   }
   ```

   `status` is `succeeded`, `failed`, or `needs-approval`; `summary` is at most
   4096 characters. No credential or private connector content belongs here.
4. On the same machine, write a mode-0600 temporary file in the private replies
   directory and atomically rename it to the exact prevalidated `reply_to` path.
   A remote routine requires an independently authenticated file-delivery bridge
   to that directory. This version exposes no callback listener. Do not interpret
   an arbitrary remote `reply_to` as permission to write any filesystem path.
5. The daemon polls `readResult(task)` on its existing tick. Missing files return
   null; malformed, oversized, mismatched-ID, linked or symlinked files refuse.
   Results remain advisory and are never executed. Callers handle deadline
   expiry as timed out, preserve the reservation, and keep dispatchd available.

## Verification and handoff

Run `HOME=$(mktemp -d) npx vitest run test/grokbot-lane.test.ts`, then
`npm run typecheck`, `npm run lint`, and `npm run check:docs`. The test webhook
binds exclusively to `127.0.0.1`; no real webhook, account, or credential is used.
The production child launcher is mocked to verify its fixed `phantom exec`
invocation and failed-delivery accounting.

Live activation requires Secrets route support, a fresh shared ledger projection,
the Masbot routine and an authorized daemon caller. None is silently enabled by
this adapter. Publication remains an operator handoff through `publish.sh` only;
this worktree contains uncommitted changes and creates no PR itself.


<!-- page: lanes/zai -->
Source: https://verse.ashlr.ai/docs/lanes/zai.md

# Z.ai GLM Coding Lite lane

Phantom runs coding tasks on Z.ai models through the GLM Coding Lite lane.
The lane exposes two models, each mapped to a queue tier: **glm-5.3**
(`work`) and **glm-5.3-flash** (`fast`). The lane is part of the published
Phantom package. Tests use loopback fixtures, not live API credits.

## Models and tiers

| Model          | Tier   |
| -------------- | ------ |
| glm-5.3        | work   |
| glm-5.3-flash  | fast   |

A queue router maps `tier=work` to glm-5.3 and `tier=fast` to glm-5.3-flash.
Unknown tier values are rejected; `standard` is normalised to `work`.

## Credit formula

Credit consumption is calculated per request as:

- **glm-5.3:** `(inputTokens*6.9 + cacheReadTokens*1.7 + outputTokens*24) / 10000`
- **glm-5.3-flash:** input credits `2.3`, cache credits `0.56`, output credits `8` (all per 1 000 tokens, no divisor).

The lane reports the dollar-equivalent in usage records. No real spending
information is read, logged, or printed by Phantom. The formula is a
calculation only; it does not prove the account holds sufficient funds.

## Included allowance

Each authenticated Z.ai account receives:

- **2 000 credits** every 5 hours (rolling window).
- **10 000 credits** per week (calendar week).

Credits are consumed in order, starting with the weekly bucket then the
rolling 5-hour bucket. Running out of credits stops new task admission; it
does not cancel an in-flight request. Credits never reset early: a window
expires only when its 5 hours or week elapses.

## Rolling-window pacing

The 5-hour bucket uses a rolling window, not a fixed period. Each task start
advances the window start by five hours. Tasks submitted before the window
expires draw from it; otherwise they wait or fail with `quota_exhausted`.
The weekly bucket is a calendar-week counter that resets on Monday 00:00 UTC.
Phantom does not reorder or prioritise tasks across buckets; it only checks
whether each bucket has remaining credits.

## Error classes

The lane emits three error classes:

| Code               | Meaning                                          | Recovery action                     |
| ------------------ | ------------------------------------------------- | ----------------------------------- |
| `quota_exhausted`  | Both the rolling 5-hour bucket and weekly bucket are at zero. | Wait for a window to replenish.     |
| `auth_failed`      | The authenticated session is missing, expired, or revoked. | Refresh auth through Phantom Secrets. |
| `rate_limited`     | Z.ai returned an HTTP 429 with a retry-after header. | Honour the retry-after window and retry once. |

No retry is attempted on `quota_exhausted`. The lane never exposes a raw
response body, status code, or credential in logs. Only the error code is
recorded.

## Secrets transport

The lane uses a Phantom Secrets-owned endpoint for token injection. The
endpoint URL and bearer token are stored in Phantom Secrets and never appear
in logs, environment variables, or CLI output. Phantom calls the endpoint on
behalf of the lane and injects the token into the request header. No new
secrets are created or printed.

## Test fixtures

Fixture-based tests use a loopback server that returns a fixed credit balance,
a mocked Z.ai response, and each error class. No live API calls, credentials,
or token values are used.


<!-- page: main-guardian -->
Source: https://verse.ashlr.ai/docs/main-guardian.md

# Main Guardian

The main guardian keeps every repo's default branch green after merge.

## How it works

When a PR lands on main, the guardian enqueues a `FIXUP-MAIN` job. A loop
runs detached post-merge verification (CI checks) against that merge commit
and writes pass / fail / unknown results to a state file. Each state entry
is keyed so the next loop iteration skips already-verified work.

## CLI commands

| Command | Role |
|---------|------|
| `ashlr fleet guardian-verify` | Runs verification passes until all manifest entries are pass or fail |
| `ashlr fleet guardian-compact` | Prunes stale entries so the state file reflects only active manifests |
| `ashlr fleet guardian-retry` | Removes a failed entry so it can be re-verified |
| `ashlr fleet main-repair-time` | Measures how long each `FIXUP-MAIN` repair takes |
| `ashlr fleet stuck-fixes` | Lists `FIXUP-MAIN` jobs whose PR is still open past 20 minutes |
| `ashlr fleet guardian-stuck` | Reports repos red for over 60 minutes with no current job; use `--json` for the typed report |
| `ashlr fleet main-red-age` | Reports each repo's guardian state and minutes red from `~/.ashlr-runs/guardian/state.json` (read-only; `--state <file>` overrides) |

Exit codes: `0` pass, `1` fail, `2` invalid args, `3` unknown/cancelled,
`4` timeout, `5` another guardian already holds the state file (retry later).

## Repair escalation

1. **Compact** prunes old entries. Stale state (entries no longer in the
   manifest) is removed so the state file stays under 1 000 entries.
2. **Retry** drops a specific failed entry. The output state is then fed
   back into `guardian-verify`, which re-runs verification for that repo.
3. **Repair time** is tracked via `~/.ashlr/guardian.jsonl` and
   `~/.ashlr/jobs-finished.jsonl` so slow repairs surface in `main-health`.

## Revert behavior

Guardian failures do not auto-revert. A `fail` result records the reason
(`code-failure`, `verification-infrastructure`, `invalid-input`, etc.) and
the failure category (`code`, `infra`, `timeout`). An agent watches the
fleet lanes; red repos with no fix jobs surface through `main-health-needs-you`
as urgent items so a human or agent can act (manual revert, infra fix, or
retry).

## ashlr fleet main-health

`ashlr` exposes a `/api/verse/runs-history/main-health` endpoint that reports:

- Per-repo state: green, red, or unknown (with failing check and SHA).
- `stale` flag: the guardian has not written status recently.
- `guardianOff` flag: the kill-switch (`~/.ashlr-runs/queue/MAIN_GUARDIAN_OFF`)
  is active, pausing all guardian work.

Run the typed CLI to inspect:

```
ashlr fleet main-repair-time --json
```

Agents read this data to decide whether to enqueue a retry, investigate a
code failure, or flag infrastructure for a fleet member.

`guardian-stuck` reads `guardian/state.json` under `ASHLR_RUNS_DIR` (or
`~/.ashlr-runs` by default). It exits 1 for stuck entries or unread/invalid
state, 0 when none are found, and 2 for invalid arguments. Revert status is
unknown unless the state records `revert_status` or a boolean `reverted`.


<!-- page: observability/README -->
Source: https://verse.ashlr.ai/docs/observability/README.md

# Engineering cycle dashboard

Import [cycle-dashboard.json](cycle-dashboard.json) through Grafana's dashboard
import screen and select a Prometheus datasource. The dashboard shows stage
p50/p90, queue wait p50/p90 and CI execution p50/p90 over seven days by default.
Repository and pool filters apply to every panel. It requires classic Prometheus
histograms from an external exporter; Phantom does not currently emit these
metrics. Importing this file does not install an exporter or enable collection.

The router task references a separate spec that is absent from this checkout.
The following is the explicit integration contract used by this dashboard;
confirm metric names with that spec before connecting a production exporter.

| Histogram (seconds) | Observation boundaries |
| --- | --- |
| `phantom_cycle_stage_duration_seconds` | Stage start to stage completion, with a `stage` label naming the stage |
| `phantom_cycle_queue_wait_seconds` | Queue admission to worker start, excluding worker execution |
| `phantom_cycle_ci_duration_seconds` | CI run start to terminal completion, excluding CI queue wait |

All three histograms must carry `repo` and `pool` labels with consistent values;
the stage histogram supplies the filter choices. Attribute CI observations to
the originating work item's pool. Emit standard `_bucket`, `_sum` and `_count`
series, including a `+Inf` bucket. Use identical bucket boundaries across
exporters, chosen to resolve durations from seconds through hours. Labels must
be bounded categories, never task IDs, PR IDs, prompts or credentials.

Observe each completed stage attempt, queue admission and CI run exactly once.
Retries are separate attempts. Include terminal failures and cancellations when
both boundary timestamps exist; omit incomplete or invalid intervals, including
negative durations. Never synthesize zero for missing timestamps. These panels
measure completed observations, so ongoing waits and running stages are absent.
They do not measure proposal-to-merge time or establish release readiness.

Queries apply `rate` before summing histogram buckets, preserving counter reset
handling, and retain `le` for percentile estimation. Stage panels also retain
`stage`; queue and CI panels aggregate across selected repositories and pools.
Percentiles describe the combined observation population, not averages of
per-worker percentiles. Grafana's `$__rate_interval` adapts the rolling sample
window to the datasource scrape interval and zoom level. A point is a rolling
window estimate, not the percentile of the entire selected seven days.

Missing series, empty populations and insufficient samples display as gaps or
“No observations”; gaps are never connected or filled with zero. Inspect the
corresponding `_count` rates in Prometheus before interpreting sparse tails.
The dashboard contains no alert rules or external links.

Validate the dashboard contract locally with an isolated home:

```sh
HOME=$(mktemp -d) npx vitest run test/cycle-dashboard.test.ts
```

# Hop efficiency insights

Read tokens per merged PR and merged PRs per dollar from a local hop-event
journal. From a source checkout:

```sh
npm run dev -- pulse --window 7d --json
```

The additive `hopEfficiency` object appears in `pulse --json`, `GET /api/pulse`
and the activity rollup. `buildSnapshot()` exposes the same object at
`activity.hopEfficiency` in dashboard snapshot JSON. Existing transcript usage
and budget totals remain independent of this ledger, preventing double counting.
The request cache can serve the previous rollup while refreshing it.

## Input contract

The read-only collector reads `~/.ashlr/observability/hops.jsonl`, resolving the
current user's home on each call. This change defines the version 1 interchange
contract; existing run/transcript and fleet-bus producers do **not** automatically
populate this journal. An upstream adapter must supply metadata-only JSONL rows.
Missing input is reported as `missing`, with unknown ratios, rather than a
claim of zero cost or zero engineering output. No credentials or providers are
needed to read a journal.

Each row contains `schemaVersion: 1`, a nonblank stable `id` (up to 256
characters), a canonical UTC timestamp (`YYYY-MM-DDTHH:mm:ss.sssZ`), a repository
slug (`owner/name`, case insensitive, up to 256 characters), and one kind:

```jsonl
{"schemaVersion":1,"id":"hop-1","kind":"hop.completed","ts":"2026-10-25T10:00:00.000Z","repo":"example/phantom","tokensIn":100,"tokensOut":50,"costUsd":2}
{"schemaVersion":1,"id":"merge-7","kind":"pr.merged","ts":"2026-10-25T14:00:00.000Z","repo":"example/phantom","prNumber":7}
```

- `hop.completed` records incremental usage for one completed attempt, including
  failed, cancelled and unmerged work. It must not contain cumulative session
  totals already recorded by another hop. Input and output tokens are
  nonnegative safe integers. `costUsd` is a nonnegative finite recorded dollar
  amount. Missing or `null` accounting values mean unknown; explicit `0` means
  measured zero. Adapters own pricing, including any cache costs; the collector
  does not invent prices or subscription allocations.
- `pr.merged` records a positive integer `prNumber`. Its timestamp must be the
  actual merge time, not the delivery time of a notification. Emit this only
  from confirmed merge evidence. A commit, task completion or generic fleet
  notification does not establish a merge.

Adapters must keep prompts, responses, tool arguments, credentials and file
contents out of the journal. The parser allowlists accounting fields; output
contains aggregate metrics and repository slugs, never raw events or event ids.

## Metric definitions and evidence

Metrics describe the inclusive interval `[since, until]`. They measure interval
productivity, **not** lifetime usage attributed to the cohort of PRs merged in
that interval. Work on an unfinished PR counts in usage; a PR whose work occurred
before the interval counts only as a merge in the interval.

| Field | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| `totals.hops` | Unique hop attempts inside the interval and project scope |
| `totals.mergedPrs` | Unique repository/PR-number pairs merged in the interval |
| `totals.tokens` | Sum of input + output for hops where both are known |
| `totals.costUsd` | Sum of known recorded hop costs |
| `totals.hopsWithTokens`, `totals.hopsWithCost` | Accounting coverage for the two subtotals |
| `totals.tokensPerMergedPr` | Tokens / merged PRs, when token coverage is complete and merges > 0 |
| `totals.mergedPrsPerDollar` | Merged PRs / dollars, when cost coverage is complete and dollars > 0 |
| `byRepo` | Same fields per repository, sorted by canonical slug |

Check `sourceState`, `status`, coverage and `diagnostics` alongside the ratios.
Subtotals with incomplete coverage are not total usage. An overflowed subtotal
is `null`. Ratios are `null` for unknown coverage, no hops, or a zero denominator;
they never emit NaN or Infinity. With known positive cost and zero merges, PRs
per dollar is `0`. With known zero tokens and a merge, tokens per merged PR is `0`.
Token and dollar coverage are independent: one ratio can be known while the other
is unknown.

`status` is `complete`, `partial`, `empty`, `missing` or `unavailable`. Empty
means readable input with no matching events. Partial means missing accounting,
numeric overflow, merge-only input, or invalid/conflicting evidence. A malformed
row or conflicting id conservatively suppresses all ratios, including per-repo
ratios, since its attribution cannot be trusted. Diagnostics include invalid,
duplicate, conflicting and excluded event counts.

Repeated ids are deduplicated within each repository; reuse the original id on
delivery retries. Conflicting payloads for the same id are excluded. Merge rows
with different ids still count once per repository/PR-number pair, using the
earliest timestamp **before** interval filtering. Retain that original merge
evidence when rotating journals so later notifications cannot earn fresh credit.
Future and old events are excluded. No merge is inferred from usage.

`--project owner/name` and `--project name` filter hops exactly, ignoring case.
For indexed checkout paths or other matching index filters, the rollup reuses
indexed GitHub origins to select canonical repository slugs. An unindexed path
or an indexed repo without a recognized GitHub origin has no matching hops;
the collector never guesses from a worktree directory name or probes a remote.

The collector reads at most 8 MiB from a regular file. Missing input is distinct
from unreadable, oversized or concurrently resized input (`unavailable`); it
never silently summarizes a tail. Keep the journal bounded while retaining the
selected interval's full usage and original merge evidence. No automatic
rotation, backfill, remote fetch or accounting completeness attestation occurs.

## Verification

The fixture in `test/fixtures/hop-events.jsonl` covers multiple repositories,
failed work, retries and interval exclusions. Run from the repository root:

```sh
HOME="$(mktemp -d)" npx vitest run test/hop-rollup.test.ts
```

Tests also exercise malformed and missing data, numeric limits, the file reader,
project-path mapping and real `pulse --json` serialization. Dashboard projection
coverage lives in `test/m13.dashboard.test.ts`.

# Inner loop research

This note records how long the edit-to-verified-result loop takes today in seven public Ashlr repos, and ranks the changes most likely to bring a typical edit under 5 seconds. Every timing below was measured on this VM on 2026-10-26, or it is quoted from a linked source and marked as such. This pull request adds this note only. It does not change code, CI, workflows, or package files.

A loop under 5 seconds is local feedback. The merge gate stays the existing CI for each repo. No test set is dropped on the way to a green merge. Tier-1 and security tests still run before merge. Where a repo already has a local gate that keeps those tests, the plan keeps that gate.

## How the numbers were taken

hyperfine 1.19.0, `--warmup 1 --runs 5`, with `CI=1` and `NO_COLOR=1`. One heavy command at a time. Tables list the hyperfine mean, standard deviation, min, and max in seconds. Those rows are 5-run means.

Rows marked **one run** are a single observation: a cargo `Finished` line, a tool's own duration line, or a wall-clock bracket. They are not means.

The one-line edit stripped any previous `INNER_LOOP_PROBE` line and appended `// INNER_LOOP_PROBE <timestamp>`. Each timed run therefore changed file content. `git checkout` restored the file afterward.

"Added means" means the commands were timed separately and the means were added on paper. That sum was not timed as one pipeline.

The serial sum of the two phantom TypeScript 7 means is 6.766 s. `57.204 / 6.766 = 8.45`. That compares a serial pair of native `tsc` runs with `npm run typecheck`, which runs both projects. A parallel wall time was not measured. Default TypeScript 7 checkers is 4, which matches this VM, so the two projects would contend for the same cores if launched together. Both native runs exited 0. Diagnostics were not diffed against tsc 5.9.3.

The incremental tsc 5.9 mean of all five runs is 7.374 s and is pulled by the 20.971 s first run. The mean of the last four times is 3.975 s. That is backend only. `npm run gate` already uses incremental `tsc` for the backend (`--tsBuildInfoFile .ashlr-gate/tsc.tsbuildinfo`). In the one gate run, that incremental `tsc` completed (the gate build log shows `tsc` then asset copy).

The rule sets differ (oxlint reported unicorn rules, among others). `57.577 / 0.358 = 161`, and that ratio is a stopwatch ratio of two different checks. It is not a measured replacement of ESLint.

Biome on phantom is slower than oxlint and far noisier than ESLint. It is not a drop-in.

ashlr-md TypeScript 7.0.2 failed with TS2322 at `src/lib/export.ts:936` and `src/lib/pasteImage.test.ts:84` (`Uint8Array<ArrayBufferLike>` not assignable to `BlobPart`). ashlr-stack failed with TS5102 (`baseUrl` removed) at `tsconfig.json:16` and TS5090 (non-relative paths) at lines 18 and 19. Neither was timed.

The lexicon esbuild and Rolldown rows bundle one entry. `npm run build` is a `tsc` emit of the project and took 0.686 s. The SWC row transforms one file. It is not a project build. The plugin `bun build` row emits one file. The project has no compile step for a server change. bun runs TypeScript directly.

`5.155 / 0.680 = 7.58` for the plugin typecheck, both exit 0 on this tree. Diagnostics were not diffed.

### Rust

| Candidate | Where | Result | Kind |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| mold 2.30.0, `RUSTFLAGS='-C link-arg=-fuse-ld=mold' cargo build --workspace` | locus, after a one-line edit | 9.458 s (sd 0.162) | 5-run |
| default linker (rust-lld), same workspace build | locus | 9.539 s (sd 0.155) | 5-run |
| mold warmup | same flag change, full rebuild | cargo `Finished` in 27.23 s | one run |
| Cranelift nightly, `-p locus-core`, fresh target dir | `CARGO_PROFILE_DEV_CODEGEN_BACKEND=cranelift` | 5.671 s (sd 0.148) | 5-run |
| nightly LLVM, `-p locus-core`, a different fresh target dir | control for the row above | 7.407 s (sd 0.259) | 5-run |
| long-lived `target/` package build | `cargo build -p locus-core`, directory was 5.5 G after the workspace and mold runs | 6.564 s (sd 0.110) | 5-run |
| fresh ext4 target, `-p locus-core` | warmup then the edit | warmup cargo `Finished` in 18.99 s, then 1.457 s (sd 0.016) | warmup one run, then 5-run |
| fresh tmpfs target, `-p locus-core` | same shape | warmup cargo `Finished` in 18.87 s, then 1.361 s (sd 0.015) | warmup one run, then 5-run |

mold minus the default linker is 0.081 s, smaller than either standard deviation. No measured win. The mold flag change forced a full rebuild first (27.23 s). Only the runs after that warmup are the incremental comparison.

`7.407 / 5.671 = 1.31` for Cranelift against nightly LLVM, package `locus-core` only, separate target directories. This is not a comparison with the stable workspace build of 9.539 s. Tests were not run on Cranelift output.

The 6.564 s package build and the 1.457 s fresh-directory build both printed only `Compiling locus-core`. A later single rebuild on the long-lived directory took 7.78 s and also compiled only that crate. The fresh directory is faster. The cause was not isolated past "the long-lived directory had been through workspace builds and a mold relink, and it was 5.5 G". tmpfs versus a fresh directory on ext4 is 1.457 s versus 1.361 s (0.096 s). That is a real small gap on this VM. It is not the gap between 6.564 s and 1.361 s.

`/dev/shm` is mounted `noexec`. A cargo build there failed with `Permission denied` executing build scripts. A tmpfs mounted as root, without a uid, failed with `Permission denied` creating the target path. The successful tmpfs row used a tmpfs mounted with the user's uid and gid.

### Cache hit

A Python sha256 compare of `pending-authority.ts` against a stamp file took 0.019 s (sd 0.001). That is the cost of noticing an unchanged file. It is not a verifier. A miss still pays the full command being skipped.

## Published numbers (other machines, other repos)

These are not measurements of Ashlr repos.

TypeScript 7 announcement, [Announcing TypeScript 7.0](https://devblogs.microsoft.com/typescript/announcing-typescript-7-0/), says full builds typically land between 8x and 12x. Their table, TypeScript 6 versus TypeScript 7 with the default of 4 checkers:

| Codebase | TypeScript 6 | TypeScript 7 | Their speedup |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| vscode | 125.7 s | 10.6 s | 11.9x |
| sentry | 139.8 s | 15.7 s | 8.9x |
| bluesky | 24.3 s | 2.8 s | 8.7x |
| playwright | 12.8 s | 1.47 s | 8.7x |
| tldraw | 11.2 s | 1.46 s | 7.7x |

The same post says TypeScript 7.0 ships no programmatic API. The API is expected in 7.1. typescript-eslint still needs the TypeScript 6 API, via the `@typescript/typescript6` package, installed side by side. Source: [microsoft/typescript-go](https://github.com/microsoft/typescript-go).

Oxlint's benchmark page says Oxlint is 50x to 100x faster than ESLint depending on core count, and points at [oxc-project/bench-javascript-linter](https://github.com/oxc-project/bench-javascript-linter). Source: [oxc.rs benchmarks](https://oxc.rs/docs/guide/benchmarks) and [oxc-project/oxc](https://github.com/oxc-project/oxc). Our phantom run was a different rule set, so their multiplier is not applied here.

cargo-nextest's [benchmarks](https://nexte.st/docs/benchmarks/) report 1.37x (penumbra) to 3.38x (crucible) against `cargo test`, excluding build time and doctests, on a Ryzen 9 7950X (16 cores / 32 threads), 64 GB RAM, Rust 1.66. The recorded value is the minimum of runs 3, 4, and 5. Source: [nextest-rs/nextest](https://github.com/nextest-rs/nextest). On this VM, warm locus-core tests were 22.720 / 17.975 = 1.26x for nextest. Warm broker tests were faster under `cargo test` (6.239 s versus 6.498 s).

The Cargo book, [Optimizing Build Performance](https://doc.rust-lang.org/cargo/guide/build-performance.html), says Cranelift should generate code faster than LLVM, needs nightly and `-Z codegen-backend`, produces slower code at runtime, and may not support unwinding. It also says an alternative linker such as mold or wild can help, and that on `x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu` the linker Rust already uses is often fast enough that switching is not worth it. Our mold result matches that second sentence. Cranelift source: [rust-lang/rustc_codegen_cranelift](https://github.com/rust-lang/rustc_codegen_cranelift). mold source: [rui314/mold](https://github.com/rui314/mold). wild source: [davidlattimore/wild](https://github.com/davidlattimore/wild). wild was not installed.

## Ranked wins

Ranking is measured seconds saved against the size of the follow-up pull request. Hour counts were not estimated. "Small" means one pull request with a narrow diff. "Medium" means a command plus tests and a cache. A win that drops tests is not ranked, whatever its stopwatch says.

The merge rule for every repo: the existing CI stays the bar. A local shortcut that skips tests is feedback only.

### phantom

Today's verified loop for the median core file is `npm run gate`. One run took 690 s of wall time and 572.97 s inside backend vitest, because the import graph selected 1036 files. `src/core/` is on the full-qualification list in `.github/scripts/ci-impact-policy.mjs` (`fullChangeReason` returns `backend-or-authority-change`). That policy is advisory (`activationEnabled: false`). GitHub CI still runs `npm run test:ci`, lint, and build. A 5 second loop for this file can be feedback. It cannot replace that gate.

1. **Side-by-side TypeScript 7.0.2 for typecheck.** Measured: backend 3.289 s and web 3.477 s, both exit 0, serial sum 6.766 s, against `npm run typecheck` at 57.204 s (8.45x on that comparison). Effort: small. Risk: no programmatic API until 7.1, so ESLint and anything that imports `typescript` stay on 5.9 or on `@typescript/typescript6`. Both native runs exited 0 here, which is not a diagnostic diff. `--checkers` defaults to 4 and the announcement says more checkers use more memory. The serial sum is still over 5 s before lint and tests.
   Plan: one pull request adds a script that runs the native `tsc` on `tsconfig.json` and `src/web-ui/tsconfig.json`, leaves the `typescript` dependency on 5.9, and fails CI only when the native compiler and tsc 5.9 disagree. A later pull request can make the native binary the default typecheck once a diff on `master` is empty.

2. **Point `npm run typecheck` at the incremental tsc the gate already uses.** Measured: warm backend incremental runs at 3.940 s to 3.996 s (mean of those four, 3.975 s) against a cold incremental run of 20.971 s. Effort: small. Risk: a stale `.tsbuildinfo` after a config change. The gate path already exists.
   Plan: one pull request changes the backend half of `npm run typecheck` to the same `--incremental --tsBuildInfoFile` invocation `scripts/gate.mjs` uses, and runs the web project at the same time. Keep `npm run gate` as the test selector.

3. **Oxlint as a prefilter in front of ESLint.** Measured time: 0.358 s versus `npm run lint` at 57.577 s. The checks differ (oxlint 1 error and 384 warnings, ESLint 0 errors and 206 warnings). Effort: small. Risk: a green oxlint gets treated as a green lint. Biome at 8.753 s, with tens of thousands of findings and a diagnostic cap, is a worse fit.
   Plan: one pull request adds `lint:fast` that runs oxlint on `src` and `test` and prints that ESLint is still `npm run lint`. CI keeps `npm run lint`.

4. **A content-hash stamp around `npm run gate`.** Measured: the hash compare itself was 0.019 s. The thing it can skip is the gate, which was 690 s of wall time in one failing run and is the right local verifier. Effort: medium. Risk: a stamp that forgets an input (lockfile, vitest config, toolchain, `CI`) will skip a run that should have happened. A hit is allowed only for a previous green run of the same command.
   Plan: described in the agent section below. The smoke set, including the tier-1 closure test, stays inside the command that gets stamped. CI does not read the stamp. `src/core` changes still take the full `test:ci` lane before merge.

5. **Keep the direct vitest file as a scratch check, and keep the related set for anything that will merge.** The direct file was 1.318 s. The related set was 1036 files and 572.97 s in one run. Effort: none for the measurement, and a pull request would be wrong if it made the direct file the gate. Risk of switching: almost all coverage for a `src/core` edit disappears. `pending-authority.ts` is also imported by tests other than `m504`.

`npm run build` did not finish on this VM, so a bundler swap is not ranked. Vite's own "built in 2.17 s" line is one observation inside a failing `npm run build`, after `tsc` had already run.

### lexicon

Lexicon is already on TypeScript 7.0.2. A second install of the same compiler, pointed at the root tsconfig, took 1.318 s against `npm run lint` at 1.365 s. There is no compiler upgrade left to rank.

1. **Stop paying for lint as a second root `tsc`.** Typecheck is 1.681 s and already runs the root project plus the extension. Lint is 1.365 s and runs the root project again. Effort: small, in the lexicon repo. Risk: low while `npm run typecheck` remains in CI. The two scripts are not identical, because typecheck also builds the extension project.
   Plan: one pull request makes `lint` a real linter, or makes it call the typecheck the CI job already runs, so a local loop does not typecheck the root twice. Add oxlint or ESLint only if the project wants lint findings. The 0.063 s oxlint timing is a different check and was not compared finding-for-finding.

2. **Keep `vitest related` as the verify step, and cut its fixed cost.** Related tests were 25.408 s. The one file that imports `prompt.ts` was 1.153 s. Typecheck plus that one file is under 5 s (added means 2.834 s) and is the right scratch loop. Effort: medium. Risk: running only `tests/review.test.ts` misses other importers.
   Plan: one pull request in lexicon adds a warm path that caches the related file list for a content hash of the import graph, then runs that same list. The list is recomputed when the graph changes. CI keeps `vitest run` of the whole suite.

3. **Leave the build alone.** `npm run build` is 0.686 s. esbuild bundled one entry in 0.083 s and Rolldown in 0.273 s. Those are not the project emit. A bundler pull request saves less than a second on a loop that is already under 5 s for the direct path.

### phantom-secrets

1. **`cargo check` is the edit feedback.** Measured 1.746 s after the edit, against a cold check of 50.60 s. Effort: small (document it, or have the agent tool run it first). Risk: check is not tests.
   Plan: one pull request in phantom-secrets adds a `just` or npm script named for the local loop that runs `cargo check --workspace --locked` and prints the next command (`cargo nextest` with the affected filterset) rather than replacing it. CI is unchanged.

2. **Package tests for local feedback, reverse-deps before merge.** Package nextest after the edit was 6.901 s. The no-edit run was 6.498 s, so the tests themselves are most of that time. Reverse-deps nextest was 90.493 s. The broker crate has dependents (the workspace filter pulls them in). Effort: small to script the split, zero to adopt nextest (CI already uses it). Risk: shipping on the package run alone misses breakages in dependents.
   Plan: local default is check, then `-p phantom-secrets-broker` when the agent wants tests. The pre-merge command stays the existing affected filterset, which expands to reverse deps. Do not switch the runner to `cargo test` for the 0.259 s noop gap.

3. **Clippy stays off the keystroke path.** Measured 5.080 s, which is the whole 5 second budget by itself. CI already runs it with `-D warnings`.

4. **Do not spend a pull request on the linker.** Workspace build was 3.821 s. The 90 s test run is the wall. mold did not beat rust-lld on locus (see above), and this crate's check is already 1.746 s.

The npm wrappers are already under 2 seconds (`0.520 s` and `1.122 s`).

### locus

1. **`cargo check` for feedback, nextest for verify.** Check was 4.695 s (cold check 15.09 s). Package nextest after the edit was 28.462 s, and with no edit 17.975 s, so a warm test run with nothing to compile is still 18 s. Reverse-deps was 44.354 s. Nextest versus `cargo test` on the warm package was 1.26x (22.720 / 17.975), in the same direction as the upstream benchmarks and smaller than their 1.37x to 3.38x range. CI already uses nextest. Effort: small. Risk: treating check as the merge gate.
   Plan: same shape as secrets. Local first command is `cargo check --workspace --locked`. Pre-merge stays `scripts/ci/affected-filterset.sh` plus nextest, which CI already runs.

2. **A fresh target directory, not a linker swap.** On the long-lived 5.5 G `target/`, `cargo build -p locus-core` was 6.564 s. On a fresh ext4 directory the warmup was 18.99 s and the incremental build was 1.457 s. tmpfs incremental was 1.361 s after an 18.87 s warmup. mold versus rust-lld on the workspace build was a tie (9.458 s versus 9.539 s). Effort: small. Risk: a fresh directory costs the warmup, and a second `CARGO_TARGET_DIR` uses disk.
   Plan: one pull request documents that a mold or rustflags experiment should use a separate target dir, and adds a script that builds `-p <crate>` into a scratch dir when the developer asks for a fast package rebuild. It does not change the default `target/` CI uses. tmpfs is optional. The measured gain over a fresh ext4 dir was 0.096 s.

3. **Cranelift only if package builds dominate and nightly is acceptable.** Measured 5.671 s versus 7.407 s nightly LLVM, a 1.31x on `locus-core` alone. The Cargo book flags slower runtime and missing unwinding. Tests were not timed. This does not bring the 18 s warm test run under 5 s. Effort: medium, because it is nightly and unstable. Ranked under check-first and under a clean target dir.

4. **Fix the npm test invocation.** `node --test npm/test` failed on Node 22.23.4. The two files passed in 0.142 s (14 tests). Effort: small. Risk: low if the file list matches what CI intended.
   Plan: one pull request in locus changes the CI and package script to pass the test files (or a glob Node 22 accepts) and keeps `node --test scripts/check-crypto.test.mjs`.

### ashlr-md

The web loop and the Rust loop are different edits.

1. **Rust: `cargo check` is already the 5 second loop.** Warm check was 1.806 s. Clippy was 2.702 s. Cold check was 48.23 s. Package nextest with no edit was 1.836 s, and `cargo test` was 1.872 s. After the one-line edit, package nextest was 11.989 s and the workspace build was 9.239 s, so the extra time is the test-profile rebuild. Effort: small. Risk: none for using check as feedback. CI already runs check and clippy.
   Plan: one pull request in ashlr-md adds a local script that runs `cargo check --workspace --manifest-path src-tauri/Cargo.toml` and leaves clippy and the web jobs on the CI path. Adopting nextest is not ranked. The noop gap was 0.036 s, and CI does not use nextest today.

2. **Web: separate typecheck from the vite bundle.** Typecheck was 5.304 s, Biome 0.440 s, one vitest file 0.607 s. Added means of those three: 6.351 s. `bun run build` was 21.462 s, of which vite alone was 16.364 s. Effort: small. Risk: a logic change that only shows up in the bundle waits for CI. That is the right trade for an edit loop, because CI already runs the vite build.
   Plan: one pull request documents the local web command as `bun run typecheck`, `bun run lint`, and `bunx vitest run <file>`, and keeps `bun run build` on CI. Biome is already the linter. Do not replace it.

3. **TypeScript 7 is blocked on two errors.** The native compiler exited 1 and was not timed. The errors are the two TS2322 `BlobPart` assignments named above. Effort: small once those two types are fixed, then a remeasure. Risk: the speedup is unknown until it is timed. Plugin's similar-sized typecheck went from 5.155 s to 0.680 s, which is a different repo. Do not copy that ratio onto ashlr-md.
   Plan: one pull request fixes the two assignments (or adjusts the lib types if the project agrees), then runs the same hyperfine. Switch `bun run typecheck` only after the native compiler exits 0 and a diagnostic diff against tsc 5.8.3 is empty.

### ashlr-stack

The measured cli edit is already under 5 seconds. Added means: typecheck 2.313 + lint 0.224 + one test 0.138 + cli build 0.044 = 2.719 s. These were separate commands.

1. **Keep the full `bun test` on CI, and use the one file locally.** Full suite was 31.685 s. The one file was 0.138 s. Effort: small. Risk: the one file misses packages that import `agent-preflight.ts`.
   Plan: one pull request in ashlr-stack adds a local script that maps a changed file to the test file that imports it and runs `bun test` on that set. CI stays `bun test` with no filter. The root build, including the site, was not timed, so this plan does not claim the site rebuild is under 5 s.

2. **Leave the compiler alone.** TypeScript 7.0.2 failed on `baseUrl` and `paths` and was not timed. Typecheck is already 2.313 s. A paths migration is a larger pull request than the time it could save. Revisit only if the site build, once measured, is dominated by `tsc`.

### ashlr-plugin

1. **TypeScript 7.0.2 for `bun run typecheck`.** Measured 0.680 s versus 5.155 s, both exit 0, 7.58x on this tree. That is the step over 5 seconds. One file of tests was 0.081 s. `mdx-lint` was 0.018 s. Added means of native typecheck plus the one file: 0.761 s, timed separately. Effort: small. Risk: exit 0 is not a diagnostic diff against tsc 5.9.3.
   Plan: one pull request adds the native `tsc` beside the current one, fails if they disagree, and switches the script after a clean diff. `bun run check` (smoke, typecheck, mdx lint, root tests, and the server, site, and vscode checks) stays the pre-merge command.

2. **Keep the full suite before merge.** One `bun run test` on this VM exited 1 in 33.53 s with the two environmental failures above. Effort: a follow-up to make those two tests hermetic, separate from the speed work. Risk of skipping the suite: the 0.081 s file does not cover the other 245 files.

3. **Do not add a bundler to the edit loop.** `bun build` of the one server file was 0.004 s and is not a project rebuild. bun already runs the TypeScript. Oxlint at 0.063 s with 311 warnings is a different check from `mdx-lint`. It is not ranked as a replacement.

## Agent loop: `ci-local` and a verified-result cache

Phantom agents already have `npm run gate`, which plans vitest related tests plus the smoke set. The smoke set always includes the tier-1 authority closure test. A core edit still cannot shrink the merge suite: `fullChangeReason` treats `src/core/` as a full qualification, and `activationEnabled` is false, so CI does not inherit a reduced set.

Proposed follow-up, one medium pull request in phantom, after this note:

- A thin CLI handler and the logic in `src/core/`, named `ci-local`. The local mode runs the same planner as `scripts/gate.mjs`.
- An `--impacted` mode is that local planner. It is feedback. It is not the merge command.
- A stamp directory keyed by a hash of every gate input: the sorted canonical changed-file paths and their bytes, the selected base ref and merge-base SHA, `scripts/gate.mjs`, `scripts/gate-smoke.json`, the lockfile, the tsconfig and vitest config, and the toolchain version. A change to any of these inputs produces a new key, so it invalidates the stamp. The hash compare measured here was 0.019 s for one file. A hit prints the previous green result and exits 0. A miss runs the real gate and writes the stamp only when that run exits 0. A red run is recorded as red so the next call does not report green.
- CI jobs keep calling `npm run test:ci`, `npm run lint`, and `npm run build`. They do not read the stamp.
- A second, smaller pull request can expose the same command as an MCP tool next to `ashlr_impact` in `src/core/mcp-native.ts`. Until that exists, an agent can run the CLI.

The same stamp shape fits the Rust repos, with the cargo fingerprint and the affected filterset as the command being cached. phantom-secrets and locus already compute that filterset in CI. The local win is running `cargo check` immediately and caching a green nextest only when the fingerprint matches. A leaf crate still runs reverse-deps before merge, because a package-only green run missed dependents in the measurements above (secrets reverse-deps 90.493 s versus package 6.901 s).

## Surveyed and not timed

| Idea | Why it was not timed | What the sources say |
| --- | --- | --- |
| wild linker | not installed | Cargo book lists it with mold. mold tied rust-lld on the locus workspace build, so a second linker is unlikely to move these crates. [wild](https://github.com/davidlattimore/wild) |
| sccache | not installed | Caches artifacts for crates that did not change. The crate you just edited still compiles. The nextest benchmark page mentions build caches so that test time becomes a larger share of the total. [mozilla/sccache](https://github.com/mozilla/sccache) |
| `split-debuginfo` and `debug = "line-tables-only"` | not changed | Cargo book recommends less debug info for faster codegen and linking. Worth a later measurement on the locus long-lived target, where one crate took 6.564 s. No speedup is claimed here. |
| bacon, cargo-watch | not installed | They rerun a command when files change. They do not shorten that command. [bacon](https://github.com/Canop/bacon), [cargo-watch](https://github.com/watchexec/cargo-watch) |
| turborepo, nx | not installed | Phantom is one package. ashlr-stack already uses bun workspaces. A task graph helps when outputs are cached. The only cache timed here is the 0.019 s hash compare. [turborepo](https://github.com/vercel/turborepo), [nx](https://github.com/nrwl/nx) |
| tsserver, vitest watch, a pre-forked test runner | not left running as a daemon | The warm incremental tsc result is the closest measurement. Lexicon's related run (25.408 s) versus one file (1.153 s) is mostly extra tests and the graph walk, which a warm process can avoid recomputing only if it runs the same tests. |
| coverage-based test impact | not built | Phantom already selects tests by import graph. On the median core file that selected 1036 backend files. A coverage map can be tighter and can miss a test that never imports the file. The gate smoke set exists for that reason. Building one is a later experiment, and it does not replace CI. |

# Personal usage proof — diagnostic recipe

How an agent collects evidence that the **personal** Codex weekly meter is
actually moving, without confusing it with the CMP seat or with a Claude
quota. This serves the Oct 30 23:45 order (prove personal usage is moving)
and the Claude five-hour-removal order (no Claude session cap exists to
rediscover).

All commands are read-only and local. Use `--json` output for provenance.

## Boundaries

- The personal home is `~/.codex-2`. `~/.codex` is the CMP seat
  (`codex-cmp`): never read, list, or merge it into personal evidence. Both
  commands below scope themselves to `~/.codex-2`; `personal --home` rejects
  any path containing a `.codex` component.
- The `claude` lane is weekly-only. Claude has no five-hour session cap;
  values in historical rows, screenshots, or notes from before the removal
  are history, not a contract. Do not infer a new Claude session cap from
  them, and do not substitute a Codex session window for a Claude one.
- No command here performs an authenticated provider call, and none exists
  for that purpose. `auth.json` is never opened; the only provider evidence
  is the rate-limit snapshot the codex CLI already writes into its own
  session logs. Do not invent a direct-provider auth call — no credential
  reads, no usage API requests.

## What each command reads

| Command | Evidence kind | Source read |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `phm resources personal [--json] [--home <absolute-path>]` | Samples **local provider evidence** | Newest `rollout-*.jsonl` under `~/.codex-2/sessions/` (allowlisted rate-limit fields only; nothing else in the home is opened). No history written, no provider contacted. |
| `phm resources ledger [--json]` | Reads **dispatch status** plus the same local sample | `~/.ashlr-runs/queue/status.json` lanes and budget, `metrics/api-spend.jsonl`, `metrics/jobs.jsonl`; then merges a `~/.codex-2` session sample into the `codex-personal` lane when strictly newer than the status tick. |
| `examples/agents/personal-usage-follow.ts` | Bounded **repeat observation** of the local sample | Same `~/.codex-2` collector; emits JSONL `sample` records and a `summary` with `weeklyUsedPctDelta`. |

## Recipe

1. **Baseline.** `phm resources personal --json`. Record
   `resources[0].observedAt` (the provider snapshot timestamp),
   `resources[0].weekly.usedPct`, `resources[0].weekly.resetsAt`, and
   `resources[0].state`. Exit 0 means `state: "current"`; exit 1 means stale
   or unavailable evidence — an unknown, not a reading, and never a success.
2. **Dispatch context.** `phm resources ledger --json`. For
   `lanes[]` where `lane === "codex-personal"`, record `running`, `target`,
   `usedPct`, `source`, and `observation.asOf`. Lane `running`/`target` show
   what dispatch is doing, not what the meter did. `source:
   "codex-personal-sessions"` means the lane carries a local session sample
   stamped `observation.asOf`; `source: "status"` means it carries the
   dispatcher's own figure. Top-level `asOf` is the status tick;
   `generatedAt` on either command is report construction time — neither is
   a provider observation.
3. **Repeat observation.** After the agent does work, take a second
   `personal` reading (or run
   `npx tsx examples/agents/personal-usage-follow.ts --samples 2
   --interval-ms 60000`, which prints `weeklyUsedPctDelta`, `null` when the
   samples are not comparable).
4. **Judge.**
   - *Measured change:* the second reading is `current`, its `observedAt`
     is strictly later, `weekly.resetsAt` is unchanged (same window), and
     `weekly.usedPct` differs. Report it as "weekly moved A% → B% between
     observations T1 → T2".
   - *Same snapshot re-read:* equal `observedAt` means the provider has not
     written a new sample; a changed `generatedAt` alone is nothing.
   - *Unknown:* `state` is `stale` or `unavailable`, `observedAt` is missing
     or in the future, `usedPct` is `null`, or the window reset between
     samples. Report unknown — never 0%, never "unchanged", never success.
5. **Freshness gate (optional).** `phm resources ledger --json
   --check-fresh-seconds N` adds `freshnessCheck` (`pass`/`stale`/`unknown`,
   exit 1 unless `pass`) on the status tick. A stale tick means the lane
   rows are historical even when they print numbers.

## Measured change versus a projection

`burnPctPerHour`, `runwayHours`, and `projectedExhaustionAt` are computed
from stored samples and are **projections**. The `personal` command keeps no
history, so they are `null` in its output — expected, not an error. In the
ledger they may arrive via the status file's own observation history. A
projection says where usage would land at the measured rate; it is not proof
the meter moved. Only two timestamped `current` readings constitute
measured change.

## Stale and unknown handling

- `state: "current"` — a reading exists and `observedAt` is at most 24 h old.
- `state: "stale"` — a reading exists but is older (or has no timestamp);
  the command exits 1 and the figure is a last-known value, not evidence.
- `state: "unavailable"` — no usable window; exits 1. Unknown is never
  reported as 0%.
- A future `observedAt` is not trustworthy: the ledger refuses to merge it,
  and the follow helper refuses to compare it.
- The ledger merges a personal session sample into the `codex-personal`
  lane — creating the row when the status file reports none — only when the
  sample is not future-dated and is strictly newer than the status tick (or
  the tick is unparseable and the status weekly value is unknown). Older or
  equal evidence leaves the `source: "status"` figure in place.

## What does not count as proof

A busy lane (`running` > 0), recent commits, an advancing `generatedAt`, or
an approaching `projectedExhaustionAt` do not show a fresh provider sample.
CMP (`~/.codex`) values must never appear in a personal proof. A Claude lane
percentage is a weekly figure only — there is no Claude session meter to
cross-check against.

# Chat-first assistant child jobs

This is the planning handoff for **RQ-PLAN-NORTHSTAR**, not a claim that the
features are delivered. The [job manifest](chat-first-north-star.json) is the
canonical list of proposed child jobs: stable IDs, parent, repository, priority,
tier, dependencies, concrete deliverables, acceptance criteria and validation.
It is a planning artifact, not an executable router payload. No jobs have been
enqueued by this change.

## Product outcome and current evidence

One conversation should turn engineering intent into scoped, observable,
interruptible work and a reviewable result. Users can inspect the evidence,
correct context and continue from the result without managing the fleet's
internal machinery. This translates the [north star](../NORTH-STAR.md) into a
chat-first delivery sequence; it does not replace the broader product factory.

The [user guide](../VERSE.md) already describes Work with me, Work for me,
Automatic and Review. [Automatic work](../AUTOMATIC-OUTCOMES.md) describes
Manager delegation, resource selection and durable outcomes. The source files
listed on each job are inspection entrypoints, not assertions of missing
implementations or permission to modify protected code. Start each child by
checking its acceptance scenarios against the current source. If already met,
retain the regression evidence and close the gap without building a duplicate
system. Source presence alone is not installed or live-provider proof.

## Delivery order

| Child | Mergeable slice | Depends on |
| --- | --- | --- |
| RQ-NS-CONTRACT | Journey identities, state ownership and baseline fixtures | None |
| RQ-NS-FIRST-TURN | First useful turn and readiness recovery | CONTRACT |
| RQ-NS-CONTINUITY | Reconnect, interruption and replay | CONTRACT |
| RQ-NS-CONTEXT | Inspectable and correctable project evidence | CONTRACT |
| RQ-NS-DELEGATE | Durable scoped Manager handoff receipt | CONTRACT, CONTINUITY |
| RQ-NS-PROGRESS | Task state and acknowledged controls in chat | DELEGATE |
| RQ-NS-REVIEW | Exact artifact, checks and follow-up | CONTEXT, PROGRESS |
| RQ-NS-RESOURCES | Account-specific Automatic explanation | FIRST-TURN |
| RQ-NS-COMPANIONS | Seat-specific companion capability recovery | CONTEXT, RESOURCES |
| RQ-NS-MEASURE | Fixed-corpus comparison and coverage report | REVIEW, RESOURCES |
| RQ-NS-ACCEPT | Combined journey and failure-path acceptance | All implementation children |

Dependency labels abbreviate the RQ-NS- prefix. Land CONTRACT first. After it,
FIRST-TURN, CONTINUITY and CONTEXT are independently ready. Dependencies express
required accepted interfaces and evidence, not authority to dispatch or a reason
to override declared priority. P2 work can follow the P1 core loop, but the full
north-star acceptance still requires it. Reserve integration and review capacity
before launching more work. Use one writer per task and serialize overlapping
file edits, particularly SourceList, chat startup and shared fixtures.

## Handoff and boundaries

A router operator can translate each manifest entry into its native queue schema,
using the stable ID to reconcile existing work before creating anything. Copy
its problem, deliverable, acceptance, validation and non-goals together. Do not
infer a pool or account from the parent's execution pool: use current eligible
capacity and the child's frontier tier. Every child begins planned; dependency
completion must come from accepted evidence, not from this document's ordering.

RQ-NS-DELEGATE touches protected Manager surfaces and requires the owner lane.
A worker under a no-Tier-1 instruction must leave those files untouched and hand
off that slice; it must not bypass the boundary via a new alternate dispatcher.
Any other child discovering a protected change must likewise split and route it
for owner review. No child may enable dormant execution, widen grants, weaken
checks, change CI, provision paid resources, or publish a release as a shortcut.
Phantom Secrets supplies opaque secret references; Locus handles access needs.
Companion evidence must reflect actual per-seat availability.

Each child should fit one concern and one reviewable PR. If discovery expands a
slice, split it with new stable IDs and explicit dependencies before execution.
Attach the base/candidate revisions, changed paths, exact validation commands,
pass/fail counts, limitations and result artifacts to its handoff. Run typecheck,
lint and affected tests with an isolated HOME; run web tests for UI changes and
documentation checks for changed guides. Preserve existing regressions. New
behavior needs positive, refusal and recovery coverage, not text-only assertions.

## Completion and measurement

The parent planning task is complete when the manifest covers the journey,
forms an acyclic graph with resolvable references, and gives every child a
bounded deliverable and testable acceptance. The accompanying manifest tests
check these structural contracts and source references. They do not prove any
planned product behavior.

Product delivery is complete only after RQ-NS-ACCEPT runs the whole journey on
one combined candidate, including unavailable resources, local-only scope,
stale context, interruption, duplicate events, failed checks and Stop. Compare
baseline and candidate with fixed acceptance fixtures. Report scenario success
with denominators, time, rework and token coverage separately. Unknown usage
remains unknown; message count and inferred hours saved are not accepted value.
Live-provider, installed-app and user acceptance remain distinct evidence gates.
The measurement child connects this work to recursive improvement, the completed
journey serves the product-factory pillar, and the companions child covers
composition without requiring every companion to be available.

# Remote agent transport: watching and steering the fleet

How an integrator's agent — a mobile remote or an agent-native client — uses
the existing authenticated remote transport to read fleet state and issue
pause/resume/Stop. Everything below already exists on `master`:
`createRemoteFleetFeed` and `RemoteFleetTransport`
([source](../src/core/web/remote-fleet-feed.ts)) against the opt-in phone
gateway ([source](../src/core/web/remote-gateway.ts)) and its route policy
([source](../src/core/web/remote-gateway-policy.ts)). No new endpoints.
Executable proof: [test/phx-remote-agent-recipe-31ac0.test.ts](../test/phx-remote-agent-recipe-31ac0.test.ts).

## Gateway URL vs loopback endpoints — never interchangeable

There are two HTTP servers on the Mac, and a remote client may speak to only one:

- **Hub (loopback only)** — `http://127.0.0.1:7777`, the desktop's local
  server. Its GETs take the local read token, its mutations the separate local
  mutation token, both in `X-Ashlr-Token`. Those credentials are server-side
  secrets: they exist to carry the gateway's own loopback hop to Hub, and a
  remote client must never possess, send, or log them. The gateway's envelope
  check rejects any remote request that bears `x-ashlr-token` or
  `x-ashlr-read-client` before routing.
- **Remote gateway** — the only door for remote clients. It binds loopback
  (`http://127.0.0.1:<gatewayPort>`) and is published exclusively as the
  configured `access.publicOrigin` (for example `https://phone.example.com`)
  through Cloudflare Tunnel fronted by Cloudflare Access. A remote agent calls
  the **public origin**; a same-Mac integration may call the gateway's own
  loopback port. It must never call the Hub port.

`RemoteFleetTransport` is implemented against the gateway only:

```ts
interface RemoteFleetTransport {
  get<T>(path: string): Promise<T>;                      // GET `${gateway}${path}`
  mutate<T>(method: 'POST', path: string, body: unknown): Promise<T>;
}
```

The feed adds nothing of its own: no headers, credentials, retries, fallbacks,
or alternate routes. Every gateway rejection reaches the caller as a rejected
promise; a transport must not swallow or reclassify it.

## What every gateway request must carry

- A Cloudflare Access assertion for an `allowedSubjects` identity (the
  `cf-access-jwt-assertion` header or the Access session cookie).
- A live device session cookie (`__Host-ashlr-remote`) obtained from
  `POST /remote/auth/finish` after a WebAuthn passkey login. Sessions are
  short-lived; `GET /remote/session` reports `authenticated`, `deviceId`,
  `scopes`, `csrfToken`, `expiresAt`, and `capabilities`.
- `host` equal to the `publicOrigin` host and `origin` equal to `publicOrigin`
  (`sec-fetch-site: same-origin` when the client sets it).
- `x-ashlr-remote-csrf: <csrfToken>` on every POST — the token returned by
  `/remote/session` or the auth finish response.

## Reads — reviewed GET routes only

Each feed method issues exactly one GET on a route the gateway policy lists
individually; there is no general `/api/*` proxy. `classifyRemoteRoute` must
return `{ kind: 'read' }` or the request is refused with `ROUTE_DENIED`.

| Feed call | Request | Response type |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `feed.list()` | `GET /api/verse/fleet/live` | `FleetLiveSnapshotV1` |
| `feed.runs()` | `GET /api/verse/fleet/runs` | `FleetRunsV1` |
| `feed.laneTargets()` | `GET /api/verse/fleet/control/lanes` | `LaneTargetsV1` |
| `feed.switches()` | `GET /api/verse/fleet/control/switches` | `RunsSwitchesV1` |
| `feed.inbox({ limit?, source? })` | `GET /api/verse/fleet/runs/inbox?limit=N[&source=S]` | `FleetInboxReadV1 \| null` |
| `feed.queue({ limit? })` | `GET /api/verse/fleet/live/queue[?limit=N]` | `FleetQueueV1` |
| `feed.bus({ limit? })` | `GET /api/verse/fleet/live/bus[?limit=N]` | `FleetBusFeedV1` |

Option contract (validated locally before any request): `limit` is an integer
from 1 to 200 (inbox defaults to 50 and always sends `limit`); `source` matches
`^[A-Za-z0-9 ._-]{1,40}$` and is URL-encoded. Unknown option keys throw.

## Mutations — pause, resume, Stop

| Feed call | Request | Meaning |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `feed.pause()` | `POST /api/verse/daemon` `{ "action": "pause" }` | Set the daemon pause sentinel: running jobs finish, nothing new dispatches. |
| `feed.resume()` | `POST /api/verse/daemon` `{ "action": "resume" }` | Clear only the pause sentinel. **Resume never clears Stop and grants no new authority.** |
| `feed.kill()` | `POST /api/verse/authority` `{ "action": "stop" }` | Engage the global Stop. Clearing Stop is a deliberate owner act, not something `resume()` does for you. |

All three classify as writes requiring **step-up**: a direct POST is answered
`403 STEP_UP_REQUIRED`. A transport completes the mutation through the
existing ceremony, which binds one WebAuthn assertion to the operation's exact
bytes:

1. `POST /remote/step-up/begin` with `{ "method": "POST", "path": path, "body": JSON.stringify(body) }` → `{ challengeId, options }`.
2. The paired device's passkey signs `options` (user verification required).
3. `POST /remote/step-up/finish` with `{ method, path, body, challengeId, response }` → the gateway re-verifies pairing, act scope, and the bound body, forwards the mutation to Hub over loopback, and returns the result (204 or JSON).

One assertion authorizes one operation once — approving `pause` does not cover
`resume`, and a consumed challenge cannot be replayed. Never try to skip
step-up, and never try to "fix" a `STEP_UP_REQUIRED` by switching credentials;
prompt for the passkey instead.

## Pairing ownership — who may do what, and from where

`createRemotePairing` ([source](../src/core/web/remote-pairing.ts)) splits the
ceremony into a **`mac` facade** and a **`phone` facade**:

- **Mac-owned** (`invite`, `pending`, `approve`, `deny`, `revoke`) is reachable
  only through the private Mac-local operator socket — the
  `phm verse remote invite <Access-subject> [read|act]`,
  `pending`, `devices`, `approve <id>`, `deny <id>`, `revoke <id>` commands.
  No remote HTTP route performs approval or revocation.
- **Phone-reachable** — `POST /remote/pair/claim` (one-use code + label),
  `POST /remote/pair/complete` (registration response), and
  `GET /remote/pair/status?pendingId=<id>` are bound to the preauth session
  that claimed the code; another session cannot observe or finish the
  registration. `POST /remote/auth/begin` / `/remote/auth/finish` then logs the
  paired device in and issues the device session.
- **Scopes** — every device has `read: true`; `act` is granted only by an
  `invite ... act`. A read-scoped device gets `403 ACT_DENIED` on any write.

## Device revocation

`phm verse remote revoke <device-id>` marks the device in the durable
registry; the gateway drops its sessions and open streams immediately, and the
device store is re-read per request, so the next read or write fails with
`401 DEVICE_SESSION_REQUIRED` (`GET /remote/session` reports
`DEVICE_REVOKED`). A transport surfaces the 401 and stops — it must not retry,
re-pair, or fall back to another credential on its own.

## Errors the caller can receive

`ACCESS_REQUIRED` (401), `DEVICE_SESSION_REQUIRED` (401), `DEVICE_REVOKED`
(401/403), `ACT_DENIED` (403), `STEP_UP_REQUIRED` (403),
`REMOTE_ENVELOPE_DENIED` (403; host/origin/CSRF mismatch or a local Hub token
on the request), `ROUTE_DENIED` (404; unlisted path or stream route),
`INVALID_MUTATION` (400; body failed the reviewed shape),
`HUB_UNAVAILABLE`/`HUB_BAD_RESPONSE`/`HUB_READ_UNAVAILABLE` (502/503),
`PREAUTH_REQUIRED`/`PAIRING_DENIED`/`PAIRING_NOT_FOUND` (401/403/404).

## Never do

- Never send `X-Ashlr-Token`, `x-ashlr-read-client`, or any loopback Hub
  credential on a remote request — it is refused outright and indicates the
  token has already escaped.
- Never point a remote transport at `http://127.0.0.1:7777` or Tunnel directly
  at the Hub port; Tunnel targets the gateway port only.
- Never bypass or auto-satisfy step-up, cache an assertion for a different
  operation, or treat `resume()` as a Stop-clear.
- Never invent paths or query shapes — the gateway reviews each one
  individually and denies everything else.
